title: Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)
bodyText:
In most New Jersey residential rentals a landlord can remove a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, only for one of the good causes listed in N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1, proven in court. The causes include nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct or rule violations after a written notice to cease, willful damage, habitual late payment, refusal of reasonable lease changes at renewal, certain criminal convictions, and owner occupancy in buildings of three or fewer units.

Most causes need an advance written notice of a set length: three days, one month, two or three months, or longer. The Act does not cover owner-occupied buildings with no more than two rental units or transient and seasonal rentals. A lease term that waives these protections is unenforceable.

Where the Act applies, the end of the lease term does not by itself end the tenant's right to stay; a holdover tenant can be removed only for good cause under the Act. Where the Act does not apply, a holdover tenant can be removed after the tenancy is ended by a notice to quit whose length depends on the tenancy: three months for a tenancy at will or from year to year, one month for a tenancy from month to month, and one full term for any other periodic tenancy, such as week to week (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-56).

title: Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal
bodyText: A New Jersey landlord may not change the locks, remove a tenant's belongings, shut off heat, water or electricity, or otherwise force a residential tenant out without a court judgment executed by a court officer. Doing so is a disorderly persons offense, and a repeat offense within five years is a fourth-degree crime. The tenant may reenter with a police officer present and can sue for possession, damages, costs and attorney's fees, or treble damages where returning is not appropriate. A court officer may execute a warrant for possession only between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., and no earlier than the third business day after it is served.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: Except in owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, a New Jersey landlord may not serve a notice to quit, sue for possession, or substantially change the terms of a tenancy in reprisal for a tenant's efforts to enforce the lease or the law, a good-faith complaint to a government agency (after first telling the landlord and allowing reasonable time to fix the problem), or tenant-organization activity. Taking one of these steps after such activity creates a presumption of retaliation. The presumption does not arise from refusing a renewal requested more than 90 days before the lease ends. The tenant can win the eviction case and sue for damages and other relief.

title: Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early
bodyText:
New Jersey lets a residential tenant end a lease early in several situations. After the tenant's death (or the spouse's), the tenant, the estate, or the surviving spouse where husband and wife signed the lease jointly, can end a lease of one year or more on written notice, effective 40 days after the landlord receives it; this applies unless the lease expressly provides otherwise.

A disabling illness or accident, or acceptance of a tenant or spouse aged 62 or older into assisted living, a nursing home or low- and moderate-income housing, allows the same 40-day termination of a lease of one year or more, with documentation.

So does a unit that isn't accessible for the tenant or a household member with a disabling illness or accident that is likely not temporary, where you were asked to make the unit accessible at your expense and were unable or unwilling to; the notice must include a physician's certification and a statement of that request.

A domestic-violence victim facing an imminent threat can end any residential lease with written notice and documentation, effective 30 days after receipt; this right cannot be waived, and the landlord must keep the documents confidential. A court can also order the landlord to change the locks for a domestic-violence victim within 48 hours.

title: Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs
bodyText: When a New Jersey rental has a lack of heat, water, light, electricity or sewage service, or another serious code or safety violation, the tenant or a municipal officer can ask a court to order rent paid into court and used for repairs. The landlord's defenses are that the condition did not exist or has been fixed, that the tenant caused it, or that the landlord was refused entry to fix it. Separately, a court may appoint a receiver to run a multifamily building with persistent code violations. Lease terms waiving these rights are void.

title: Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)
bodyText:
In a New Jersey building of three or more units, the owner must keep each unit at least 68 degrees from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. and at least 65 degrees overnight, from October 1 to May 15.

In smaller buildings, the State Housing Code (which local officials use to judge fitness for occupancy) sets the same 68/65-degree minimum from October 1 to May 1 for any unit you've agreed to heat, and you must provide heat when you control the heating facilities or two or more units share one, unless an agreement says otherwise.

A local board of health may also set heat rules and, where you fail to restore heat, act as your agent to get the heating equipment repaired. The owner cannot shift the cost of heating fuel to a tenant unless the unit has its own separately billed heating equipment and the tenant agrees in writing.

The owner must get rid of insects and rodents when an infestation is in two or more units or in common areas, and must arrange professional pest-prevention service at least once a year. Tenants are responsible for conditions within their own unit that they cause or control.

Owners must install carbon monoxide alarms near the sleeping area of every unit in buildings with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, and a visual alarm for a deaf or hard-of-hearing tenant on request. A lease cannot relieve the owner of these duties.

title: Tenant Screening Limits
bodyText: New Jersey limits how landlords screen applicants. Landlords covered by the Fair Chance in Housing Act (all rentals except owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units) may not ask about criminal history until after a conditional offer, must disclose in writing before taking an application fee whether they consider criminal history, may consider only certain convictions within set look-back periods, and must follow an individualized-assessment and written-notice process to withdraw an offer. Applicants may not be required to take drug or alcohol tests. Military and veteran housing allowances must be counted as income. You may not refuse to rent because of a record of nonpayment or late payment of rent, or a related court filing, from the COVID-19 covered period, or report that rent to another landlord, a debt collector or a credit bureau. Information from the sex-offender registry may not be used to deny housing except as another law authorizes. Since May 1, 2026, a landlord or its agent may not charge more than $50, adjusted each year for inflation from 2027, as an application or similar fee, except for a unit in a one- or two-family home or a real estate licensee who is not the landlord. Landlords may not refuse Section 8 vouchers or other lawful sources of income, and any minimum-income requirement must be based only on the tenant's share of the rent. Refusing to rent because a household includes children, or leasing terms that end a tenancy on the birth of a child, are unlawful except in qualifying housing for older persons.

title: Tenants in Foreclosed Properties
bodyText: A person who takes title to a New Jersey rental through a sheriff's sale or a deed in lieu of foreclosure must give every tenant a prescribed notice, in English and Spanish, within 10 business days after taking title. The notice must be in at least 14-point bold type on paper at least 8½ by 11 inches. Foreclosure is not a ground to evict a tenant. A foreclosing party or new owner may try to get a tenant to leave only by a bona fide cash offer, which the tenant has five business days to consider, and may not pressure the tenant. Where the foreclosed owner is an individual, a tenant who has secured financing or assets to meet the terms has a right of first refusal to buy the property at the sheriff's sale for the original upset price or the final starting upset price, whichever is less, exercised by paying a 3.5% deposit before bidding opens. Violations expose the owner to treble damages or $2,000 per violation, plus fees.

title: Unlawful Lease Terms Carry Penalties
bodyText: New Jersey prohibits a landlord from offering or signing a lease containing a provision that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities under New Jersey law at the time of signing. A tenant may ask a court to terminate a lease containing such a provision, and the landlord faces a penalty of up to $100 for each offense. A general sentence elsewhere in the lease saying that nothing in it limits the tenant's rights does not make an unlawful term safe. This does not apply if the tenant proposed the provision. Several New Jersey laws also make specific lease waivers void, including waivers of the tenant's implied right to recover attorney fees when the lease gives you one (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.66), waivers of plain-language rights (a lease may not contain one), security deposit rights, landlord registration rights, eviction protections, repair-escrow rights and domestic-violence termination rights.

title: Local Rent Control and Registration
bodyText:
Many New Jersey municipalities have rent control or rent leveling ordinances, and many require rental registration, licensing or inspections. State law does not set a general cap on rent increases, but an increase must comply with any local ordinance and must not be unconscionable, or it cannot support an eviction.

In a building of four or more rental units (not housing built for senior citizens) constructed under a construction permit issued after the 1987 exemption law took effect, local limits on periodic or regular increases in base rent do not apply for 30 years after construction is completed, or until the initial mortgage would be paid off if that is sooner. The exemption does not reach rent controls a municipality imposes on substandard multiple dwellings under the 1966 substandard-housing rent control law.

While the exemption lasts, the lease must say the building is exempt, and the tenant must get a written statement saying so before signing. Check the municipality's ordinances before setting or raising rent.

title: No Radon Rule for Landlords
bodyText: New Jersey statutes do not require a residential landlord to test for radon or to disclose radon information to a tenant. Radon rules in the statutes cover home sales, schools, child care centers, new construction in high-radon areas, and certification of radon testers and mitigators. If you do test a rental you own, you may do it yourself without certification.

title: No Mold Rule for Landlords
bodyText: New Jersey statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose or remediate mold as a separate duty. The only housing-related mold provision concerns real-estate agents in home sales. Mold in a rental is handled under general habitability law and local housing codes.

title: Smoke Alarms
bodyText: New Jersey requires smoke alarms in every rental. In a building with three or more units, the owner must install and maintain smoke detectors or alarms as the Department of Community Affairs requires by rule. A home for no more than two households must have a smoke alarm on each level and outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and, if it has a secondary power source, a warning label within 18 inches of the main electrical panel and meter. Before leasing it or letting a new tenant move in, the owner must get a certificate showing it complies: from the municipal official who issues the certificate of occupancy or inspection where a local ordinance requires one, and otherwise from the local fire safety enforcing agency. The state fire code rules also require working carbon monoxide alarms before the certificate issues. Leasing without compliance can bring a fine of up to $500.

title: No Tenant EV-Charging Right
bodyText: New Jersey statutes do not give a residential tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger, and do not require a landlord to allow one. Separate state law requires certain newly built multifamily projects to provide charger-ready parking spaces as part of site plan approval; that is a construction requirement, not a tenant right.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: New Jersey statutes do not contain a rule specifically addressing whether a landlord may ask about or act on a tenant's immigration status. Discrimination based on national origin, nationality or ancestry is prohibited under the Law Against Discrimination, and threatening someone based on immigration status can be evidence of coercive control in a domestic violence case.

title: Owners Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText: New Jersey requires the owner of a rental unit to carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 for combined property damage and bodily injury, or at least $300,000 for an owner-occupied multifamily home of four or fewer units. Owners must register the certificate of insurance with the municipality each year. A municipality can fine a noncompliant owner $500 to $5,000.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText:
A New Jersey landlord cannot simply have a tenant's or visitor's car towed because the lease allows it. On most rental properties, a tow without the vehicle owner's consent is lawful only if the landlord has a private-property towing contract with the tow company, has authorized removal of that particular vehicle, and has posted a sign at least 36 by 36 inches at every vehicle entrance stating when and for what parking is allowed, that violators will be towed at the owner's expense, and the tow company's name, contact details, charges and storage address; the car must go to secure storage within a reasonable distance.

In a residential community with clearly marked assigned spaces, a simpler entrance sign is allowed, but the landlord must still document approval of each tow. These rules do not apply to a single-family home, an owner-occupied building of six or fewer units, or a car blocking a driveway or garage entrance.

title: Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
New Jersey's Rent Security Deposit Act controls deposits, and a lease term waiving it is void (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19 et seq.). It covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, and even there it applies once the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it.

Amount: no more than one and a half months' rent, and any added security in a year may not exceed 10% of the current deposit.

Holding: keep it in trust (the account and investment requirement doesn't apply to a seasonal rental of not more than 125 consecutive days to someone with a permanent residence elsewhere; you bear the burden of proving the rental is seasonal), unmixed with your own money, in a New Jersey interest-bearing account or fund of the required kind.

Notice: within 30 days of receiving it, tell the tenant in writing the institution's name and address, the type of account, the current rate and the amount; give the same notice within 30 days after moving it (unless the move is within 60 days of the annual interest payment, when the annual notice covers it), after any transfer of ownership or control, and with each annual interest payment.

Interest belongs to the tenant: pay it in cash each year, or credit it toward rent on the renewal or anniversary date, or on January 31 if you've told the tenant in writing.

If you fail to hold it, give a notice or pay interest, the tenant may give written notice to apply the deposit plus 7% interest to rent, after which you can't demand another deposit (for a missed annual payment or notice alone, the tenant must first give notice and allow 30 days).

Use: make no deduction while the tenant is in possession.

Return: within 30 days after the lease ends, return the deposit plus interest, less lawful charges, by personal delivery or registered or certified mail, with an itemized statement of the interest and each deduction; a shorter timetable applies if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation (46:8-21.1) or ends the lease as a domestic violence victim (46:8-9.6).

title: Senior and Benefit-Recipient Grace Period
bodyText: If rent is due on the first of the month and a tenant is a senior citizen receiving Social Security Old Age benefits, Railroad Retirement or another government pension in lieu of Social Security, or receives Social Security Disability, Supplemental Security Income or Work First New Jersey benefits, you may not charge a late fee until after a five-business-day grace period (excluding weekends and state or federal holidays) (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-6.1). Use it as a guardrail when you set the grace period.

title: Rent Payment Rules
bodyText:
If you are a landlord under the Truth-in-Renting Act (it excludes rental premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, and transient or seasonal hotels and guest houses), you may not require a tenant to pay by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers, so accept at least one other method (N.J.S.A. 46:8-49.1 et seq.); accepting a non-electronic method is the safe course for every landlord.

For each cash payment, give a printed or emailed receipt stating the amount, purpose, date received, the printed names of landlord and tenant, and who accepted it. A missing receipt is a defense to a nonpayment eviction for the months it covers, and the penalty rises by $100 for a second violation and $200 for each later one within five years.

If a warrant for removal has been posted or a lockout executed for nonpayment, accept payment of all rent due within the next three business days by cash, certified check or money order, or from a government rental assistance program or bona fide charity, and give a dated receipt (2A:42-10.16a).

title: Property a Tenant Leaves Behind
bodyText:
If a tenant leaves belongings after a warrant for removal is executed, or after giving written notice of voluntarily giving up possession, you may dispose of them only if you reasonably believe the tenant does not intend to claim them, and only as N.J.S.A. 2A:18-72 through 2A:18-84 allow: first send the tenant written notice by certified mail or receipted first-class mail, to the last known address and any other address you know, marked "Please Forward"; store the property with reasonable care; and don't sell or dispose of it until the date in the notice, which must be at least 30 days after the notice is delivered or 33 days after mailing, whichever comes first (75 or 78 days for a manufactured or mobile home).

While you store it you may promptly dispose of perishable food, and you must let an animal control agency or humane society remove any abandoned pets or livestock. The tenant may reclaim it in that time without paying unpaid rent, but must reimburse your reasonable storage and removal costs.

If you sell the property, you may deduct the reasonable costs of notice, storage and sale and any unpaid rent and charges the security deposit doesn't cover; send the tenant the rest with an itemized accounting, or, if the tenant can't be found after due diligence, deposit it with the Superior Court. If you keep a tenant's property without following these steps, you lose those costs and may owe up to twice the tenant's actual damages.

title: Private Well Testing
bodyText: If the property's drinking water comes from a private well that no other State law already requires to be tested, have it tested at least once every five years as the Private Well Testing Act requires, give each rental unit a written copy of the results within 30 days of receiving them, and give each new tenant a written copy of the most recent results. For a seasonal rental, you may instead post the results where they are easy to see inside the unit (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-32).

title: Fire and Other Casualty
bodyText: In New Jersey, if the property is damaged by fire without the tenant's fault, you must repair it as quickly as possible, and if you don't, rent stops until it is completely repaired; if the building is totally destroyed without the tenant's fault, rent is owed only to the date of destruction and the lease ends (N.J.S.A. 46:8-6, 46:8-7). Neither rule applies where the tenant caused the damage, and both give way to a lease that provides otherwise; this library's lease does not vary them, except the optional tenant-caused-damage clause, which addresses only damage the tenant's side caused.

title: Good-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: New Jersey is a good-cause state. In most residential rentals a landlord may remove a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, only for one of the causes the Anti-Eviction Act lists, proven in court; the end of a lease term is not a cause. The Act does not cover owner-occupied buildings with no more than two rental units or transient and seasonal rentals. The full rules are in the Anti-Eviction Act entry.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: New Jersey court rules add duties to an eviction case. A default judgment for possession needs the landlord's affidavit stating the facts that give good cause and that every charge claimed as rent, other than base rent, is allowed to be charged as rent by the lease and by law; a landlord's attorney must certify the same, and any required notice to quit must be attached with a statement that it was served and is true. A business entity other than a sole proprietor, or a partner in a general partnership, must appear through an attorney. A consent judgment for possession against an unrepresented tenant must be reviewed and signed by a judge that day. When the landlord believes service at the rental may fail, the landlord must also ask for service by mail at another address. A warrant of removal cannot issue until three business days after judgment (two days for a seasonal tenancy) and cannot be executed before the third business day after it is served; if the landlord does not apply for it within 30 days of judgment, or it is not executed within 30 days of issuance, the landlord must apply to the court with seven days' written notice to the tenant. A court may stay a warrant for up to seven days for an orderly move. A levy on belongings inside a home may be made only between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.

title: Eviction Records Kept From Public Access
bodyText: New Jersey court records of a landlord-tenant case are not public if the case ended without a judgment for possession, or if the judgment for possession was entered seven or more years ago. Eviction records for nonpayment during the COVID-19 emergency period are also shielded and may not be used in screening. No statute gives a landlord a right to object.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: New Jersey's electronic-transactions law applies only when both sides have agreed to do business electronically, and either side may later refuse further electronic dealings. It does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's home, so those must go by the methods the eviction statutes require (personal delivery, leaving a copy at the home with a family member over 14, or certified mail, with regular mail if certified mail is not claimed). An electronic record the sender stops the tenant from printing or saving cannot be enforced against the tenant.

title: Plain Language Rules for New Jersey Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's plain-language law applies to residential leases: a lease must be written in a simple, clear, understandable and easily readable way, judged as a whole. Courts and the Attorney General look at guidelines such as confusing cross-references, needlessly long sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, and illogical order, and whether sections are logically divided and captioned, a lease over 3,000 words has a table of contents or index, and conditions and exceptions get the same prominence as the main promise in at least 10-point type. Technical terms alone are not a violation, and wording a law or agency requires or approves is protected. A landlord who violates the law owes the tenant actual damages if the tenant was substantially confused, plus up to $50 and attorney's fees up to $2,500, but not if both sides performed, the landlord tried in good faith to comply, the contract follows an Attorney General opinion, or the tenant supplied the wording. A lease may not contain a waiver of these rights, though a violation does not make the lease void or voidable. A court may also reform or limit a provision to avoid an unfair result if it violates the law, substantially confused the tenant about rights or obligations, and caused or is likely to cause the tenant financial harm, so long as the claim is brought before the lease is fully performed; the tenant must keep paying meanwhile. The Attorney General will certify a form on request for a fee of up to $50.

title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's Consumer Fraud Act makes it unlawful to use any unconscionable commercial practice, deception, fraud, misrepresentation, or knowing omission of a material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise or real estate, and the Act defines a sale to include a rental. It is also unlawful to ask a consumer to sign a document evidencing a transaction without giving a full and accurate copy at the same time, so give each tenant a complete copy of the signed lease when they sign. A person who loses money or property because of an unlawful practice recovers three times the damages plus attorney's fees and costs. The Act lists no rule about blank spaces in a lease.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText:
If a New Jersey tenant, occupant or guest causes damage, the statutory protections tied to damage do not help the tenant: rent stops after a fire only if the damage happened without the tenant's fault, the lease ends on total destruction only if it happened without the tenant's fault, and a rent-into-court case fails if the condition was caused maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use by the petitioning tenant or family.

Willful or grossly negligent damage is a cause for removal on three days' notice, with no notice to cease first. You may apply the security deposit to damage after the tenancy ends, never while the tenant stays, and you may sue for the cost of repair. Lost rent after the tenancy ends is recoverable as damages, subject to your duty to try to re-rent.

title: Fees Treated as Rent
bodyText: In New Jersey, late fees, attorney's fees and other charges count as rent in an eviction for nonpayment only if the lease expressly says so, and never for Section 8 or public-housing tenants. This library's lease does not call any fee rent, so an unpaid fee cannot support an eviction for nonpayment; collect it another way. In a default judgment for possession, the landlord must swear, and a landlord's attorney must certify, that every charge claimed as rent other than base rent may be charged as rent under the lease and the law.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting Ban
bodyText: From July 1, 2027, New Jersey's FAIR Act makes it a violation of the state antitrust law for a rental property owner, or its agent, to pay for, subscribe to or contract for the services of a "coordinator", and for anyone, including an owner acting for its own benefit, to perform a "coordinating function". A coordinating function is using an algorithm or other automated process to set or recommend rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels from competitively sensitive, nonpublic information of two or more owners, or from such information of any other owner, or setting or recommending them for two or more owners through the same or a substantially similar algorithm in a way that facilitates parallel pricing. Tacit or express price coordination between owners is also barred. Publicly available free rent estimates, research that is not used to set rents or lease terms, equal-access brokerage listing databases that don't set or recommend rents, and government affordability controls are excluded, as are spreadsheets without artificial intelligence that need human analysis and databases that only query stored data.

title: Forms and Wording New Jersey Supplies
bodyText: New Jersey prescribes the exact wording or form of several lease items: the Department of Community Affairs Flood Risk Notice, the renter's flood-insurance sentence every lease must contain, the window-guard notice for buildings of three or more units, the Truth in Renting statement, the condominium or cooperative conversion statement, the bold tenant attorney-fee sentence, and the foreclosure notice to tenants. The library's entries for each carry the required text. Eviction complaints must use the court's form.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Adult cannabis use is legal in New Jersey, but a landlord may still limit it. The owner of a building with three or more units may prohibit or regulate smoking, vaping or aerosolizing cannabis there; the owner of other property may prohibit or regulate eating or otherwise consuming cannabis on the property, but that power is not given for multi-unit buildings. A landlord may not refuse to rent to someone, or penalize a tenant, because cannabis metabolites are found in the person's body from lawful use, unless that would break a federal contract or cost federal funding. The cannabis law does not change landlord-tenant law otherwise.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets a lease remove a habitability requirement or lets a tenant accept substandard conditions in exchange for lower rent. In a building of three or more units (a multiple dwelling, with some exclusions), the state maintenance rules say no owner, agent or superintendent is relieved of any maintenance duty by the terms of any lease, contract or agreement. For rentals other than owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units (the act's 'housing space' also excludes public housing and hotel, motel or guest-house space), a tenant or a municipal officer can ask a court to have rent paid into court and used for repairs when there is a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, or another substantial code violation or danger to life, health or safety; a lease term waiving that right is void. Offering a lease with a term that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities can cost up to $100 per offense and lets the tenant ask a court to end the lease (this applies to landlords covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act; see "Unlawful Lease Terms Carry Penalties"). The judge-made implied warranty of habitability is not covered here. The cautious course: put no clause in the lease by which the tenant accepts defects, gives up repairs, or waives habitability rights. A lease may give the tenant some upkeep tasks; see "What a Lease Can Shift to the Tenant".

title: Smoking in Common Areas and Smoke Drift
bodyText:
New Jersey's Smoke-Free Air Act bans smoking in indoor public places and workplaces. Its definition of an indoor public place expressly includes an apartment building lobby or other public area in an otherwise private building, and a passenger elevator in any building other than a single-family home. A workplace is any enclosed place where someone performs any service or labor. Smoking includes vaping (electronic smoking devices) and lighted tobacco or anything else that can be smoked.

Private homes and private residences are exempt, so the Act does not reach smoking inside a tenant's own unit.

As the person in control of the building, you must tell anyone smoking in a covered area to stop; a person who keeps smoking after being told faces fines of $250, $500 and then $1,000. Only the health authorities enforce the Act; tenants have no private lawsuit under it.

No New Jersey statute deals with smoke drifting between units or lets a lease make a tenant give up a nuisance or other claim for drifting smoke. Whether such a waiver would hold is case law not covered here, and a court could treat it as a term violating clearly established tenant rights.

The cautious course: do not put a smoke-drift waiver in the lease. Your own smoking rules for units and outdoor areas are a separate choice.

title: Eviction Notices Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, a lease cannot shorten or waive the notice to cease or the notice to quit. The Act lets a court enter judgment for possession only on one of its good-cause grounds and, except for nonpayment of rent (including failure to pay a lawful rent increase after a valid notice to quit and notice of increase), only after the written notice the Act requires, which must state the cause in detail and be served as the Act directs. Any lease provision by which the tenant agrees the tenancy can end for other than good cause, or waives any other right under the Act, is against public policy and unenforceable. The Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, hotels, motels or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal guests, or certain units occupied by an owner's family member with a developmental disability. For those tenancies, when you seek possession because the tenant held over after the tenancy ended, the court needs proof of a notice to quit: one month for month-to-month, three months for year-to-year or at will, and one term for other periods. No statute says whether a lease may waive that notice; that is case law not covered here. The cautious course for every New Jersey lease: do not include a notice-to-quit waiver. If a tenant moves out after a notice that relies on a lease clause contrary to law and misstates that the tenant would be evicted, the owner can owe three times the tenant's damages plus attorney's fees. See "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)".

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Any lease or agreement term by which a tenant gives up any part of New Jersey's security deposit law is absolutely void. That covers the 1.5-month cap and the 10% yearly limit on added security, the holding and interest rules, the ban on deductions while the tenant stays in possession, and the 30-day itemized return with double damages. The law applies to all dwelling rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, unless the tenant of such premises gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it. For the rules themselves, see "Security Deposit Rules" and "Security Deposit: Amount and Use" clause.

title: Tenant Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: New Jersey has no single landlord-tenant code with one anti-waiver rule. Instead, each major law carries its own. A lease term waiving any of these is void or unenforceable: good-cause eviction protections and every other right under the Anti-Eviction Act; security deposit rights; landlord identity and registration rights; the right to have rent paid into court for repairs of serious code violations; the domestic-violence lease-termination rights; the tenant's implied right to recover attorney's fees and expenses when the lease gives the landlord fee rights. Separately, a lease may not contain a waiver of plain-language rights. A tenant's waiver or refusal of the Truth in Renting statement does not change your duties. In buildings of three or more units, no lease relieves the owner of state maintenance duties. On top of these, a landlord covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act may not offer or sign a lease with any term that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities: up to $100 per offense, and the tenant may ask a court to end the lease, unless the tenant proposed the term. Habitability: no statute lets a lease waive or reduce the owner's habitability duties; see "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived" and "What a Lease Can Shift to the Tenant". The judge-made implied warranty of habitability is not covered here. See also "Unlawful Lease Terms Carry Penalties".

title: Jury Waivers in New Jersey Leases
bodyText: The New Jersey Constitution says the right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate. An eviction (summary dispossess) case is heard in the Special Civil Part; if it is transferred to the Law Division, the statute says it shall be tried before a jury unless a jury is waived. No New Jersey statute either allows or bars a jury waiver written into a residential lease, and none requires a separate signed writing for one (the statutes that mention jury waivers deal with criminal cases, arbitration agreements and motor vehicle franchises). Whether a pre-dispute jury waiver in a residential lease is enforceable is case law not covered here, and a court could treat it as a term violating clearly established tenant rights. This library's New Jersey lease does not include a jury waiver.

title: No Confession of Judgment in Leases
bodyText: Do not put a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney in a New Jersey lease. New Jersey law says no judgment by confession shall be entered on a warrant of attorney that is included in the body of a bond, note or any instrument for the payment of money, and that no judgment shall be entered on a warrant of attorney in an action on a bond or other instrument for the payment of money except on motion after notice to the defendant. A lease that obliges the tenant to pay rent is very likely such an instrument; the statute does not say so in words, so that last step is case law not covered here. Many consumer-credit laws also ban confession clauses outright. Eviction must go through the court process in any case. This library's lease has no confession clause.

title: Attorney's Fees Work Both Ways
bodyText: If a New Jersey residential lease lets you recover attorney's fees or expenses when the tenant breaks the lease, including as additional rent, the court reads in a matching promise: you must pay the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees or expenses, to the same extent, when the tenant successfully defends a case you bring over an alleged lease breach, or successfully sues you for failing to keep the lease. The tenant chooses whether to take the award as money or as a credit against future rent. Any waiver of this rule is void. A tenant who simply pays the rent due after you file, and has no other good defense, has not successfully defended a nonpayment case. Expenses means litigation costs such as court costs and witness costs, not travel, missed work or child care. A lease clause giving you fee rights must also contain the statute's reciprocity sentence, in bold type at least one point larger than the rest of the clause or 11 point, whichever is larger. The library's Default by Tenant clause already carries that sentence; do not add a second fee clause. Fees are never labeled rent in this library's lease ("Fees Treated as Rent").

title: No Statute on Collection Fees
bodyText: No New Jersey statute sets or bans a collection fee that a residential landlord may charge on unpaid rent or other amounts. The collection-fee statutes that exist cover consumer loans, retail installment contracts, home repair contracts and similar credit, not residential leases. Limits still apply. If the lease lets you recover attorney's fees or expenses for the tenant's breach, the tenant gets the same right when the tenant wins (see "Attorney's Fees Work Both Ways"). An unpaid fee cannot support an eviction for nonpayment in this library's lease, which labels no fee as rent ("Fees Treated as Rent"). A flat or percentage fee that is not tied to your actual costs could be challenged as a penalty under case law not covered here. The cautious course: recover only reasonable costs you actually incur, as the library's Default by Tenant clause provides.

title: No Statute on Notice or Filing Fees
bodyText: No New Jersey statute authorizes or bans a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice to cease, a notice to quit, or for filing an eviction. If the lease lets you recover expenses of a court case, the tenant gets the same right when the tenant wins, and court costs count as expenses (see "Attorney's Fees Work Both Ways"). Fixed charges set in advance for a breach can be challenged as a penalty under case law not covered here; New Jersey's statutory liquidated-damages rules cover other kinds of contracts, not residential leases. The cautious course: do not charge a flat notice or filing fee; recover only reasonable costs you actually incur, through the court where possible. An unpaid fee cannot support a nonpayment eviction under this library's lease ("Fees Treated as Rent").

title: Charging the Tenant for an Eviction
bodyText: No New Jersey statute expressly bans a lease clause that charges the tenant a penalty or fee because of an eviction notice or case. Several laws limit what you can do. If the lease lets you recover attorney's fees or expenses, the tenant gets the same right when the tenant wins ("Attorney's Fees Work Both Ways"). In a nonpayment case, if the tenant pays all rent due within three business days after the warrant of removal is posted or a lockout, you must accept it, no late fee may exceed the amount stated in the warrant application, and the case is dismissed. If a tenant moves out after an eviction notice relying on a lease clause that is contrary to law and misstating that the tenant would be evicted, you can owe three times the tenant's damages plus fees. A fixed eviction charge could also be challenged as a penalty under case law not covered here. The cautious course: no flat eviction or notice charge in the lease ("No Statute on Notice or Filing Fees").

title: No Statute on Lease Liquidated Damages
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute governs liquidated damages, early-termination fees or other damages fixed in advance in a residential lease. The statutes that mention liquidated damages cover sales of goods, employment, public contracts and similar matters. Whether an agreed amount is a valid estimate or a void penalty, and whether you must try to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, are case-law questions not covered here.

Some rules are fixed by statute. The security deposit belongs to the tenant, is held in trust, and is returned within 30 days less only charges spent under the lease, itemized; it cannot simply be kept as a forfeit. Certain tenants may end a lease early by statute for death, disability or domestic violence.

The cautious course: claim your actual losses rather than a fixed sum.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: No New Jersey statute decides whether accepting rent after a notice to cease or notice to quit, or with knowledge of a breach, waives the notice or the breach. That is case law not covered here. The cautious course: after you serve a notice to quit, do not accept rent for any period after the termination date unless you state in writing, when you accept it, that you accept it as use and occupancy only and do not waive the notice; if in doubt, return it. Statutes do require you to take payment in some cases. A tenant may stop a nonpayment case by paying the rent claimed plus costs to the court clerk on or before final judgment. In a nonpayment eviction, you must accept all rent paid within three business days after a warrant of removal is posted or a lockout, notify the court within two business days, and the court then dismisses the case.

title: Plain Language: No Waiver Statement Required
bodyText: New Jersey's plain-language law applies to residential leases, and its usual $50,000 limit does not apply to real estate, so every lease is covered (see "Plain Language Rules for New Jersey Leases"). It does not require a separate statement listing the tenant's waivers or restrictions, and no New Jersey statute does. Two rules to know: a lease may not contain a waiver of any right under the plain-language law, and a court may reform or limit a material term that substantially confused the tenant and is likely to cost the tenant money. Optional review: the Attorney General can certify a lease form as compliant for a fee of up to $50; a certified form is deemed to comply. The separate Truth-in-Consumer Contract, Warranty and Notice Act, including its rule against saying a term may be void 'in some jurisdictions' without naming New Jersey, does not apply to residential leases.

title: Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms
bodyText: New Jersey penalizes offering or using a lease with an unlawful term, and it does not require proof that you knew the term was unlawful. A landlord covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act may not offer to a tenant or prospective tenant, or sign, a written lease with a provision that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities under New Jersey law at the time of signing. The penalty is up to $100 for each offense, collected in a summary proceeding that the Commissioner of Community Affairs, the Attorney General or any other person may start, and the tenant may ask a court to end the lease. Neither applies if the tenant proposed the term. Covered landlords exclude rental premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, and transient or seasonal hotels, motels and guest houses. Separately, if a tenant moves out after an eviction notice that relies on a lease clause contrary to law and misstates that the tenant would be evicted, you owe three times the tenant's damages plus attorney's fees and costs. See "Unlawful Lease Terms Carry Penalties".

title: Clauses Releasing the Landlord From Liability
bodyText: No New Jersey statute generally addresses a residential lease clause that releases the landlord from liability or makes the tenant hold the landlord harmless. Two rules apply. In a building of three or more units, no owner, agent or superintendent is relieved of any state maintenance duty by the terms of any lease, contract or agreement. And a covered landlord may not offer or sign a lease containing a term that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities (up to $100 per offense; the tenant may ask a court to end the lease). Whether a clause releasing you from your own negligence is enforceable is case law not covered here. The cautious course: do not include a clause releasing you from liability for your own negligence or for failing to maintain the property. A narrow statute does protect a landlord who complies with the senior-citizen pet law from damages for injury caused by a senior tenant's lawful pet, except for willful or wanton acts.

title: Unconscionable Terms and Rent Increases
bodyText: New Jersey has no general statute that voids an unconscionable residential lease term. Three statutes use the idea. The Consumer Fraud Act makes any unconscionable or abusive commercial practice in connection with the sale or advertisement of real estate unlawful, and the Act defines a sale to include a rental (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). Under the Anti-Eviction Act, failure to pay a rent increase is good cause for eviction only after a valid notice to quit and notice of increase, and only if the increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws and local rent ordinances. Changes of substance to the lease that you propose at renewal must be reasonable, and for certain protected tenants you must also prove they do not substantially reduce the tenant's rights. The plain-language law also lets a court reform or limit a confusing material term that is likely to cost the tenant money. The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability sections cover sales and leases of goods, not apartments. How courts judge an unconscionable lease term or rent increase is case law not covered here.

title: What a Lease Can Shift to the Tenant
bodyText: A New Jersey lease can give the tenant some upkeep tasks, but it cannot relieve the owner of habitability duties. In buildings of three or more units, the state maintenance rules make owners and occupants each responsible for their own duties, and no lease relieves either one. An occupant is responsible for violations caused by the occupant's own willful act or gross negligence, neglect or abuse, or that of household members or guests. The State Housing Code, which local officials use to judge whether a dwelling is fit to live in, lets a lease decide a few things: who keeps the premises orderly, who takes garbage out weekly in buildings of three or fewer units, and who provides heat where an agreement says otherwise. Every duty the Housing Code does not assign to occupants stays with the owner. In buildings of three or more units, heating fuel cost can be shifted only where the unit has its own separately billed heating equipment and the tenant agrees in writing ("Tenant-Supplied Heat" clause; "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)"). Topic note: no New Jersey statute lets a lease waive a water or hot-water duty.

title: Lease Completeness
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires that a residential lease have no blank spaces at signing. The statutes that ban blanks cover consumer loans, retail installment and home repair contracts, and rental-purchase agreements for goods.

Fill in every blank before the tenant signs anyway: the plain-language law applies to residential leases, and, as the cautious course, give the tenant a full copy of the signed lease when they sign (the Consumer Fraud Act's copy rule is written for sales of merchandise).

title: What a New Jersey Lease Must Contain
bodyText: New Jersey has no single list of required lease terms, but several statutes put specific content in the lease. Every residential lease of a covered landlord must contain the statutory flood-insurance notice, and the flood-risk notice must be given in writing before signing; if it is in the lease, it must be a separate rider, individually signed or acknowledged, in at least 12-point type (seasonal rentals under 120 days are exempt). If the lease lets you recover attorney's fees or expenses, the fee clause must contain the statutory reciprocity sentence in bold. Rules can support an eviction only if they are reasonable and the tenant accepted them in writing or they were in the lease at the start of the term; a lease covenant can support an eviction only if it is reasonable, was in the lease at the start, and the lease reserves a right of reentry. Other required items have their own rows: Truth in Renting statement, landlord registration statement, window guard and steam radiator cover notices, lead-safe certification, private well results, and condominium conversion and rent-control exemption notices. No New Jersey statute requires the start and end dates on the first page. The whole lease must be in plain language.

title: Where New Jersey Law Depends on Your Lease
bodyText: Some New Jersey rules turn on what the lease says. Rules and lease covenants can support an eviction only if they were in the lease at the start of the term (or, for rules, accepted by the tenant in writing), are reasonable, and, for covenants, the lease reserves a right of reentry. A tenant's refusal of changes of substance is good cause for eviction only if you proposed them at the end of the lease term, by written notice, and they are reasonable. If the lease gives you attorney's fee or expense rights, the tenant gets matching rights and the lease must say so in bold. The security deposit may be up to 1.5 months' rent, with added security each year of no more than 10% of the current deposit. If you are a landlord covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act (not premises of two or fewer units, owner-occupied premises of three or fewer, or transient or seasonal hotels), you may not require payment by electronic funds transfer, even if the lease says so. The flood-risk notice may be placed in the lease only as a separately acknowledged rider. Fees count as rent in a nonpayment eviction only if the lease expressly says so; this library declines that option ("Fees Treated as Rent"). No New Jersey statute specifically governs a residential lease with an option to purchase, apart from laws on buying a homeowner's property in foreclosure.

title: No Homestead Waiver in New Jersey Leases
bodyText: New Jersey has no general homestead exemption; the Legislature has said so in a 2025 law. That law exempts the primary and one secondary residence owned by a veteran, service member or military spouse from creditors, which protects owners, not a tenant's lease. Tenants have the general exemption for personal property up to $1,000 plus all wearing apparel, and household goods and furniture up to $1,000 are exempt from attachment, except for a debt incurred to buy them. No New Jersey statute lets a lease waive these exemptions, and you may not seize a residential tenant's belongings for unpaid rent (distraint is barred for a lease of property used solely as the tenant's residence). Do not put an exemption or homestead waiver in the lease; a court could treat it as a term violating clearly established tenant rights.

title: Keeping Domestic-Violence Documents Confidential
bodyText: If a tenant ends a lease under New Jersey's Safe Housing Act and gives you documents showing domestic violence, you must not disclose that information. Don't enter it into any shared database, and don't give it to any person or entity. You may use it only when it is required as evidence in an eviction case or in a lawsuit for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, with the tenant's consent, or as otherwise required by law. A lease term can't waive this. The statute covers the documents given to you for a Safe Housing Act termination; it says nothing about other abuse information a tenant shares with you, but treating that the same way is the cautious course. If the municipal clerk returns a deposit for you after a domestic-violence termination, the clerk may not knowingly disclose the victim's personal information. The Act doesn't apply to seasonal leases of 125 consecutive days or less to a person with a permanent home elsewhere (housing for seasonal or migrant farm workers is not excluded). Federally assisted housing programs may add their own confidentiality rules.

title: Deposit Return After a Domestic-Violence Termination
bodyText: When a tenant ends a lease under the Safe Housing Act (see "Domestic-Violence Lease Termination"), a faster deposit rule applies. Within 15 business days after the lease terminates, you must have the security deposit, plus the tenant's share of interest or earnings, available and return it to the tenant or the tenant's designated agent on demand. You may subtract only charges the lease allows and rent due and owing at the time the lease terminates. Within three business days after the termination, give the victim written notice, by personal delivery or by mail to the tenant's last known address, stating where, and on which days and hours, the money is available. Keep it available on demand during normal business hours for 30 days at a location in the same municipality as the rental, with an itemized statement of interest or earnings and deductions. You may arrange with the municipal clerk for the clerk to return it. The statute also calls for a duplicate notice to the municipal relocation officer (or the municipal clerk if there is none); it is unclear whether that applies to a domestic-violence notice, and sending it is the cautious course, since the clerk may not disclose the victim's information. Money not claimed within the 30 days must be redeposited in the account it came from. The clock runs from the date the lease terminates (the 30th day after you receive a complete notice, unless you agree on an earlier date), not from the date everyone moves out. The co-tenants' lease ends at the same time. The statute requires return of the deposit 'including the portion' due to the victim but doesn't say how to handle co-tenants you let stay; the cautious course is to return at least the victim's portion on time and settle the rest in writing with the remaining tenants. A court that finds for the tenant in a suit for the money must award double the amount, plus costs, and may award attorney's fees. These rules apply wherever the Rent Security Deposit Act applies (it excludes owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units unless the tenant invokes the Act by 30 days' written notice), and not to seasonal leases the Safe Housing Act excludes. For public housing or a publicly funded housing assistance contract, deposit terms must also follow the program's State or federal rules.

title: No Eviction Protection for Abuse Victims
bodyText: No New Jersey statute bars evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or stops you from relying on abuse-related incidents (such as police calls or damage) against the victim. The Anti-Eviction Act's good causes contain no victim exception, and the Law Against Discrimination doesn't name abuse victims. New Jersey law protects victims in other ways. A victim can end the lease early on 30 days' notice, and that also ends the co-tenants' lease even though the Anti-Eviction Act would otherwise protect them ("Domestic-Violence Lease Termination"). A Family Part restraining order can give the victim exclusive possession of a home the parties lease jointly or that either leases alone, bar the abuser from the residence, require the abuser to keep paying rent, and order you to change the locks ("Lock Changes Under a Restraining Order"). If a tenant shows you such an order, follow it: don't let a restrained person back in or give that person a key. For a unit in a federally assisted housing program, the federal Violence Against Women Act adds protections.

title: Domestic-Violence Lease Termination
bodyText: Under the New Jersey Safe Housing Act, a tenant may end a residential lease early if the tenant or the tenant's child faces an imminent threat of serious physical harm from another named person if the tenant stays. The tenant must give you written notice saying so, together with one of the documents the Act lists (see "Documents a Domestic-Violence Victim May Provide"). The termination takes effect on the 30th day after you receive a notice that complies, unless you and the tenant agree on an earlier date. Rent is owed pro rata up to that day. The lease ends this way only if the tenant acts in good faith and follows the Act's steps. If there are other tenants on the lease, their lease ends too, even though the Anti-Eviction Act would otherwise protect them; you may offer them a new lease for a new term, or let them hold over, at your option. The Act doesn't limit who the threatening person may be: it says only 'another named person', not a household member or partner. It covers any lease of residential property used by the tenant only as a home for the tenant or the tenant's family. It doesn't cover seasonal leases (125 consecutive days or less to a person with a permanent home elsewhere; housing for seasonal or migrant farm workers is not excluded), and you must prove a lease is seasonal. In public housing the tenant gives notice under the public-housing rules, and under a publicly funded housing assistance contract the notice and deposit terms follow that program's State or federal rules. No lease term can waive these rights. Keep the documents confidential ("Keeping Domestic-Violence Documents Confidential") and return the deposit on the special schedule ("Deposit Return After a Domestic-Violence Termination"). The Act has no separate route for a tenant abused by the landlord. New Jersey's other early-termination rights are summarized in "Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early".

title: Lock Changes Under a Restraining Order
bodyText: New Jersey gives an abuse victim a lock change through a court order, not on the tenant's own say-so. When the Family Part issues a temporary or final domestic-violence restraining order, it may order the landlord to change the locks on the unit where the victim lives. The victim must tell you in writing that the order has been granted. If you have not installed new locks within 48 hours after receiving that written request, the victim may change them. A victim who does must notify you and give you a copy of the new keys within 48 hours after the change. The victim pays for a change the victim makes, but can recover the cost from the abuser in the restraining-order case. The law doesn't say who pays when you make the change yourself; don't charge the victim a fee for it, and check the order. If the victim changes the locks, you aren't liable to the victim, another tenant of the unit or a guest for damage to the unit, to personal property in it, or to those persons while there, but only for damage that occurs more than 48 hours after the change, before the victim tells you and gives you new keys, and while the victim still lives there. Don't give a key to a person the order bars from the residence. The Safe Housing Act's ban on waivers doesn't expressly cover this lock-change law, but a lease term can't change what a court orders.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey's landlord-tenant domestic-violence laws point to the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act of 1991 (N.J.S.A. 2C:25-17 and following), and those cross-references are current. The Safe Housing Act's termination documents cite the final restraining-order section, N.J.S.A. 2C:25-29. The 2023 lock-change law cites both the temporary-order section, 2C:25-28, and 2C:25-29, and 2C:25-29 itself was amended in 2023 to list the landlord lock-change order and lock costs. One wording point: the Safe Housing Act asks for a certified copy of a 'permanent' restraining order, while 2C:25-29 calls them 'final' orders. Treat a final restraining order as the permanent order the Act means. A temporary restraining order is not one of the Act's listed court orders, but a tenant with only a temporary order may still qualify with another listed document, such as a police record or a domestic violence specialist's certification. The Safe Housing Act doesn't define 'domestic violence'; the definition in the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act (2C:25-19) is the natural reference. Protective orders under the Victim's Assistance and Survivor Protection Act (2C:14-13 and following) are not among the Act's listed orders, though another listed document may still qualify.

title: Documents a Domestic-Violence Victim May Provide
bodyText: To end a lease under the Safe Housing Act, the tenant must give you a written notice that the tenant or the tenant's child faces an imminent threat of serious physical harm from another named person if the tenant stays, plus any one of these: (1) a certified copy of a permanent (final) restraining order issued by a New Jersey court under N.J.S.A. 2C:25-29 protecting the tenant from the person named in the notice; (2) a certified copy of a permanent restraining order from another jurisdiction, issued under its domestic-violence laws, protecting the tenant from the person named; (3) a law enforcement agency record documenting the domestic violence, or certifying that the tenant or the tenant's child is a victim; (4) medical documentation of the domestic violence from a health care provider; (5) a certification from a certified Domestic Violence Specialist or the director of a designated domestic violence agency that the tenant or the child is a victim; or (6) other documentation or certification from a licensed social worker that the tenant or the child is a victim. One document is enough. The Act sets no time limit on how recent the document must be, and the 30-day termination period runs from when you receive a notice that complies. The lock-change law is different: it works only through a temporary or final restraining order that orders the lock change, and the victim's written notice to you that the order was granted ("Lock Changes Under a Restraining Order"). Keep every document confidential ("Keeping Domestic-Violence Documents Confidential").

title: Lease Breaches: Notice to Cease and Removal Grounds
bodyText:
In rentals the Anti-Eviction Act covers (most New Jersey rentals), a lease breach supports removal only as the Act allows, and several grounds give the tenant a chance to stop first.

For disorderly conduct, breaking your rules and regulations, breaching a lease covenant, or habitually paying rent late, you must first give a written notice to cease. Only if the conduct continues after that notice may you serve a notice to quit and file: three days' notice for disorderly conduct; one month's notice for rule violations, covenant breaches and habitual late payment.

Rules count only if they are reasonable and were accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the start of the term. A covenant breach counts only if the breach is substantial, the covenant is reasonable and was in the lease at the start of the term, and the lease reserves a right of reentry for its breach. The lease can't decide these questions for the court by calling a term 'material', and any lease term waiving the Act's rights is unenforceable.

Some grounds have no notice to cease: willful or grossly negligent damage to the premises, and the drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking grounds, need only three days' notice to quit, and nonpayment of rent needs no notice.

Each notice to quit must state the cause in detail and be served personally, left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail (then regular mail if unclaimed).

For premises the Act doesn't cover (owner-occupied with two or fewer rental units, or rented to transient or seasonal guests), a tenant who is disorderly, willfully damages the premises, constantly breaks rules accepted in writing or made part of the lease, or breaches a covenant for which the lease reserves reentry may be removed after a written notice ending the tenancy and demanding removal within three days; no notice to cease is required. That notice must state the cause and be served personally or left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or posted on the door if neither is possible.

title: Notice Before a Nonpayment Case
bodyText: In rentals the Anti-Eviction Act covers, you don't have to give the tenant any notice before filing an eviction case for nonpayment of rent: the Act requires a written notice to quit for most grounds, but not for nonpayment. Two related grounds do need notices. Nonpayment of a rent increase requires a valid notice to quit and notice of the increase first, and the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any law or rent-control ordinance. Habitual late payment requires a written notice to cease and then one month's notice to quit. For premises the Act doesn't cover (owner-occupied with two or fewer rental units, or rented to transient or seasonal guests), a tenant who holds over after defaulting in rent under the lease may be removed, and the statute sets no notice before filing. New Jersey statutes supply no required wording for a nonpayment notice, and a lease term waiving the Act's protections is unenforceable. A tenant can still stop the case by paying (see "Tenant's Right to Pay and Stay"): for premises outside the Act, by paying the rent claimed and costs to the court clerk on or before judgment; and in every Anti-Eviction Act nonpayment case, by paying all rent due within three business days after the warrant of removal is posted or the lockout is carried out. The complaint may claim only the rent the tenant must pay under the lease and federal, State or local law, and this library doesn't treat fees as rent ("Fees Treated as Rent"). Rent that accrued during the COVID-19 'covered period' can't support eviction of a very low-, low-, moderate- or middle-income household; it may be pursued only as a money claim. A federally backed property may need a 30-day federal notice ("Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). For a senior or benefits recipient whose rent is due on the 1st, no late charge may fall within the five-business-day grace period ("Senior and Benefit-Recipient Grace Period").

title: Ending a Tenancy by Notice
bodyText: How a tenancy ends by notice depends on whether the Anti-Eviction Act covers the rental. Where it applies (most New Jersey rentals), you can't end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, or refuse to renew a lease, just by giving notice: you need one of the Act's good causes, with the notice the Act sets for that cause ("Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)"). A lease term letting you end the tenancy without good cause is unenforceable. Where the Act doesn't apply (owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotels, motels or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal guests; units held in trust for, or occupied by, an owner's immediate family member with a developmental disability), you end the tenancy with a written notice to quit: three months for a tenancy at will or from year to year, one month for a month-to-month tenancy, and one full term for any other periodic tenancy, such as week to week. Serve that notice personally or leave it at the tenant's home with a family member over 14; posting on the door is allowed only if those methods can't be used. New Jersey statutes don't set how much notice a tenant must give to end a periodic tenancy. A tenant who gives notice to leave on a stated date and doesn't leave owes double rent from that date (see "Holdover" clause).

title: Contents and Service of Good-Cause Notices
bodyText: Where the Anti-Eviction Act applies, each notice to quit it requires must be in writing, must specify in detail the cause of the termination, and must be served on the tenant personally, left at the tenant's usual home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail; if the certified letter isn't claimed, send it by regular mail. The notice must give the full period the Act sets for the ground: three days, one month, two or three months, 18 months or three years (see "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)"). Nonpayment of rent and failure to pay a lawful rent increase need no notice to quit, though the increase itself needs a valid notice to quit and notice of increase. Several grounds also need an earlier written notice to cease ("Lease Breaches: Notice to Cease and Removal Grounds"); the Act doesn't say how a notice to cease must be served, so using the same methods is the cautious course. Attach copies of all notices you rely on to the eviction complaint. If you seek a default judgment, your affidavit must attach every required notice and state that the notices were served as required and that their facts are true. If a tenant moves out after a notice that claims a cause the law doesn't provide, or rests on a lease term that is unlawful under the Truth-in-Renting Act, and misrepresents that the tenant would be evicted, you can owe three times the tenant's damages plus attorney's fees and costs. For email or text delivery, see "Electronic Notices".

title: Self-Help Eviction Ban
bodyText: New Jersey bans self-help eviction. You may not enter or retake a property occupied solely as a residence by the person in possession, without that person's consent, except through a court eviction case; doing so is a disorderly persons offense. Padlocking or changing the locks, putting the occupant's belongings outside, shutting off heat, electricity or water to regain possession, or using any means other than a court officer's lawful execution of a warrant for possession is forcible entry and detainer. Doing it, or refusing to let the occupant back in, after a police or other public official warns you it is illegal is a disorderly persons offense, and a second conviction within five years is a fourth-degree crime. A displaced occupant may reenter with a police officer present, and the officer must stop you from blocking it. The occupant can also sue for possession, damages, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or treble damages if returning isn't appropriate. Only a court officer may execute a warrant of removal, between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. unless the court orders otherwise, and no earlier than the third business day after it is served. The full rule is in "Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal"; lockouts for unpaid rent are covered in "No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent".

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: New Jersey doesn't let a landlord lock a residential tenant out for unpaid rent, and a lease clause can't create that right. Entering or retaking a home occupied solely as a residence without the occupant's consent, except through a court eviction case, is a disorderly persons offense. Padlocking or changing the locks, or shutting off utilities to regain possession, is forcible entry and detainer; doing it after a police or other public official warns you is a disorderly persons offense, and a repeat within five years is a fourth-degree crime. The tenant may reenter with a police officer present and can sue for possession, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or treble damages. Where the Anti-Eviction Act applies, a lease term waiving its protections is unenforceable. For unpaid rent, file a nonpayment case ("Notice Before a Nonpayment Case"). After judgment, only a court officer executes the warrant of removal, and the tenant still has three business days after the lockout to pay all rent due and have the case dismissed ("Tenant's Right to Pay and Stay"). The warrant itself warns that padlocking or blocking entry while a tenant is in possession is illegal, except in a distraint involving nonresidential premises.

title: Tenant Property After an Eviction
bodyText: After a court officer executes a warrant of removal and you get possession back, belongings the tenant leaves are handled under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-72 to -84, summarized in "Property a Tenant Leaves Behind" (written notice by certified or receipted first-class mail, safe storage with reasonable care, and at least 30 days after delivery, or 33 days after mailing, before disposal). The same law also says: you may promptly dispose of perishable food, and you must let an animal control agency or humane society remove any abandoned pets or livestock. If the tenant tells you, in writing or orally, by the date in the notice, that he or she will remove the property, the tenant has until that date or 15 days after the response, whichever is later. After the deadline the property is conclusively presumed abandoned; you may sell it at a public or private sale conducted under the Uniform Commercial Code, destroy or dispose of it if you reasonably decide its value is so low that storage and a sale would probably cost more than the sale would bring, or do both. From sale proceeds you may deduct reasonable costs of notice, storage and sale, and unpaid rent and charges the security deposit doesn't cover; send the rest to the tenant with an itemized accounting, or, if the tenant can't be found after due diligence, deposit it with the Superior Court. Storage and removal charges can't exceed local fair market value, and you aren't responsible for loss in storage unless you caused it deliberately or negligently. Good-faith compliance is a complete defense to a tenant's claim for loss of the property; seizing and keeping it without complying costs you your storage and removal charges and up to twice the tenant's actual damages. The law doesn't apply to abandoned motor vehicles or to property that must be handled under the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. For 10 days after the warrant is executed, the court keeps jurisdiction to hear the tenant's applications for relief.

title: Hardship and Other Stays of Eviction
bodyText: After a judgment for possession of a dwelling, the judge may stay the warrant of removal if the tenant would suffer hardship because other housing isn't available, but never for longer than six months after the judgment. No stay can be granted or continued unless the tenant pays you all rent arrears and the amount that would have been due as rent if the tenancy had continued, plus accrued costs; keeps paying rent as it comes due during the stay; and doesn't become so disorderly as to destroy other tenants' peace, or willfully damage the premises, during the stay. (Two nearly identical statutes say this: one for units under State rent control on June 30, 1956, the other for all other dwellings.) The court's hardship-stay order also has the tenant give up further applications for more time and the right to pay within three business days after the lockout. Separately, a court may grant an orderly-removal stay of up to seven days for good reason; you may move to dissolve or change it on two days' notice. Other stays: in a holdover case for premises outside the Anti-Eviction Act, a terminally ill tenant (certified by a physician) who has rented from you for at least two years, fulfills all lease terms, and would likely suffer serious medical harm by moving may get one-year stays, during which the tenant may renew at the end of the term subject to your reasonable written changes; the court must consider undue hardship to you, and this doesn't apply to hotels, motels or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal guests or to residential health care facilities. A tenant removed for a condominium or cooperative conversion gets one-year stays (no more than five) until offered comparable housing. For a furnished seasonal unit in premises of five or fewer units, in a case for disorderly conduct or damage, the warrant issues within two days of judgment and may be stayed only with your consent.

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers
bodyText: New Jersey court rules set how eviction papers are served. In a summary eviction case, the summons and complaint are served by ordinary mail and by personal delivery under R. 4:4-4. If the officer can't deliver them personally, they may be affixed to the door of the tenant's unit or, if that isn't possible, another conspicuous part of the premises. If you have reason to believe service may fail at the rental, you must also ask for service by certified and regular mail at another address where you believe the tenant will be served, and give the clerk two extra copies for each defendant. A statute also allows notices and papers to be served on any person actually occupying the premises, or posted, when the usual methods fail. New Jersey's statutes and Part VI court rules contain nothing that lets a lease name someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant. The personal-service rule, R. 4:4-4(a)(1), allows delivery 'to a person authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process on the individual's behalf', but whether a clause in your own lease is a valid appointment of that kind is a case-law question. Don't rely on one: serve the tenant by the methods above.
