A tenant enrolled in New Jersey's Address Confidentiality Program has designated the program director as agent for receiving process and mail.

title: Criminal-Activity Eviction Grounds
bodyText:
New Jersey has no separate fast-track court for criminal-activity evictions, but the Anti-Eviction Act gives criminal grounds a short notice and no chance to cure. You may file after three days' written notice to quit, with no notice to cease, where the person:
- has been convicted of, pleaded guilty to, or as a juvenile been adjudicated delinquent for, a drug offense under the Comprehensive Drug Reform Act involving use, possession, manufacture, dispensing or distribution of a controlled dangerous substance, analog or drug paraphernalia on the leased premises or the building, complex or grounds, unless he or she has completed, or is on probation while completing, a court drug rehabilitation program
- has been convicted of, pleaded guilty to, or as a juvenile been adjudicated delinquent for, assault or terroristic threats against you, your family or your employee
- has been convicted of, pleaded guilty to, or as a juvenile been adjudicated delinquent for, theft of property from you, the leased premises or other tenants in the building or complex
- is found liable by a preponderance of the evidence, in the eviction case itself, for one of those theft, assault or drug offenses
- is found in a civil action to have committed human trafficking on the premises or in the building, complex or grounds.

Each ground also reaches a tenant who knowingly harbors such a person or lets the person live there (with a limited exception for a juvenile adjudicated only for drug use or possession).

Drug and assault cases based on a conviction must be brought within two years after the conviction or adjudication or the person's release from incarceration, whichever is later; trafficking cases within two years after the violation ended.

A public housing authority also has a ground for a substantial breach of lease terms on illegal drug use or other illegal activity, without a reserved right of reentry.

These grounds apply only where the Act applies. The ordinary summary eviction procedure and warrant rules still apply.

title: Removing an Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: New Jersey has no special squatter-removal procedure outside court. You may not enter or retake a property occupied solely as a residence by the person in possession, without that person's consent, except through court process, and lockouts or utility shut-offs are forcible entry and detainer ("Self-Help Eviction Ban"). Court routes: (1) If the person came in under your tenant (a subtenant, assignee or other occupant), you may name the tenant and the other occupant in one summary eviction complaint for the unit, identifying each and stating each one's interest separately. (2) Against a person who took possession without your consent or any color of title and stays after your written demand and notice to deliver possession, you may bring an unlawful detainer action, heard in a summary manner, and recover possession, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees; title isn't tried, but three years' peaceable possession is a defense. (3) A possession action in the Superior Court is available to anyone claiming a right of possession; the Special Civil Part hears it summarily where the occupant has no colorable claim of title or possession, and damages may include the value of use and occupation for up to six years. Criminal trespass law makes it an offense to enter or secretly remain in a dwelling knowing one isn't licensed or privileged to, or to stay after actual notice against trespass, but it is a defense that the person reasonably believed the owner would have permitted it; whether to charge is for the police and prosecutor. If the person claims to be a tenant or a tenant's guest, use the court routes.

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a New Jersey summary eviction case, the tenant can't file a counterclaim or third-party complaint, no answer is permitted, and the case can't be joined with any other claim. A tenant who has money claims against you brings them separately. New Jersey's statutes and Part VI court rules contain nothing that makes a tenant pay rent into court to raise a defense in an eviction case. Payment into court works mainly to end a case: for premises outside the Anti-Eviction Act, a tenant sued for holding over after a rent default stops the case by paying the rent claimed plus accrued costs to the court clerk on or before final judgment, and the clerk pays it to you (see "Tenant's Right to Pay and Stay"). If either side moves to transfer the case to the Law Division, where it is tried by jury unless waived, the court may require security for rent while the motion is pending. Defenses based on the unit's condition, and any court-ordered deposit of rent that goes with them, come from court decisions. Tenants, or a public officer, can also ask the court to have rents deposited with the court and used for repairs under the tenant rent receivership law ("Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs").

title: Minors as Tenants and Defendants
bodyText: In New Jersey a person 18 or older is an adult for all purposes relevant here, with the same capacity to contract, sue and be sued as anyone older, so an 18-, 19- or 20-year-old can sign a lease and is bound by it; the law abolished the right of 18- to 21-year-olds to disaffirm contracts because of age. New Jersey's statutes contain nothing addressing leases signed by people under 18 (in them, the only rental rule for minors concerns safe-deposit boxes). The general rule that a minor may undo a contract comes from court decisions; if a prospective tenant is under 18, the cautious course is to have a parent or guardian sign as a tenant or guarantor. In an eviction case, the clerk can't enter a default judgment for possession against a minor or mentally incapacitated defendant; you must apply to the court, and the judgment can't be entered without five days' written notice to the minor's guardian or a guardian ad litem appointed for the minor. A minor's own signed acknowledgment of service doesn't count as personal service.

title: Business Landlords Need a Lawyer in Eviction Court
bodyText: In a New Jersey summary eviction case, a corporation, LLC or other business entity landlord can't appear or file papers on its own; it must appear through an attorney. A sole proprietor may represent himself or herself, and a partner in a general partnership may file papers and appear for the partnership. A landlord without a lawyer who asks for a default judgment for possession must state in the affidavit that it isn't a corporation or other business entity barred from appearing without one. Money claims are different: in the Small Claims Section (landlord-tenant claims for rent, a security deposit or damages up to $5,000), an authorized officer or employee of a business entity may bring or defend the entity's own claims (not claims acquired by assignment), as long as that person isn't a suspended or disbarred attorney or one who has resigned. That exception names only the entity's own officers and employees.

title: Tenant's Right to Pay and Stay
bodyText: New Jersey gives a tenant chances to pay and keep the home in a nonpayment case. Before judgment: for premises outside the Anti-Eviction Act, a tenant who pays the court clerk the rent claimed plus accrued costs on or before final judgment stops the case. An older statute for a landlord owed a full year's rent who has a right of reentry also requires dismissal if the tenant pays or tenders all rent arrears and costs before trial. Whether a covered tenant can stop the case by paying before judgment rests on court decisions; accepting full payment of the rent and costs tendered before judgment is the cautious course. After a lockout: in every Anti-Eviction Act nonpayment case, the tenant has three business days after the warrant of removal is posted on the unit or the lockout is executed to pay the rent. You must accept every rent payment made in that period. Within two business days after the rent due is paid, give the court written notice that it was paid, with a copy to the tenant; the court then dismisses the case with prejudice. If you don't send the notice, the tenant may move to dismiss. If all rent due is paid within the three days, you may not charge a late fee above the amount stated in your application for the warrant. These statutes set no limit on how often a tenant may use these rights. A hardship stay requires paying all arrears and costs, and the court's stay order has the tenant give up the three-day payment right ("Hardship and Other Stays of Eviction").

title: Application Fee Cap
bodyText: For applications made on or after May 1, 2026, you or your agent may not require an application fee or other similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a home that is more than $50 (N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). The State adjusts the cap for inflation each January 1, starting in 2027, and the Division of Consumer Affairs posts the current figure on its website; check it before you set your fee. The cap does not apply to a unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling, or to a licensed real estate licensee who is not the landlord. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later one, and the overcharge is paid back to the applicant from the penalty. No New Jersey statute requires you to refund an application fee if you do not rent to the applicant. If the Fair Chance in Housing Act covers you (every rental except owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units), before you accept any application fee you must tell the applicant in writing whether you consider criminal history and that the applicant may give you evidence of errors in the record or of rehabilitation (46:8-55). In a mobile home park, a fee for checking a prospective tenant's credit may not exceed your actual cost (46:8C-2). The screening rules are summarized in the Tenant Screening Limits row.

title: Mobile Home Park Fee Disclosure
bodyText: If you own or operate a mobile home park, you must fully disclose in writing all fees, charges, assessments, rules and regulations before a resident takes occupancy and before any lease is signed (N.J.S.A. 46:8C-2). Every fee, however named, must relate to and be identifiable with your actual costs, and a credit-check fee may not exceed your actual cost. To raise a disclosed fee or change a rule, give all tenants written notice with an implementation date at least 30 days later. You may not collect a fee you did not disclose, and a resident's refusal to pay an undisclosed charge cannot be grounds for eviction. Outside mobile home parks, no New Jersey statute requires a lease to list every fee; the Fees and Charges clause is the library's recommended list.

title: No Fee Transparency Statute
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to advertise or state rent as one all-in figure, put fees on the lease's first page, or itemize mandatory fees in the lease, except in mobile home parks, where every fee must be disclosed in writing before occupancy (N.J.S.A. 46:8C-2).

You still may not offer a lease term that violates clearly established tenant rights (46:8-48), and misleading statements about charges can raise Consumer Fraud Act issues. Listing every fee with its amount in the lease, as the Fees and Charges clause does, is the cautious course.

title: Pet Deposits and Fees
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute names or caps a pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent. A refundable pet deposit is money you hold as security, so treat it as part of the security deposit: hold, notify, pay interest on and return it under the Rent Security Deposit Act, and keep the security deposit and the pet deposit together within the one-and-a-half-months' rent cap (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.2).

New Jersey case law is reported to count pet deposits toward the cap, so follow that cautious course. The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (46:8-26).

You may not charge extra for a service or guide dog, including a retired one kept as a pet, though the tenant is liable for damage it causes (10:5-29.2). In a senior citizen housing project, the pet rules in the Pet Policy clause apply.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute authorizes or regulates a fee, insurance product or bond offered in place of a security deposit. Be cautious: the Rent Security Deposit Act covers money 'or other form of security' given as security for the lease, so a bond or a payment that works as security may be treated as a deposit, with the trust, interest, cap and return rules (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.2), and a lease term waiving the Act is void (46:8-24). If you offer an alternative, make it optional, do not count a nonrefundable fee as replacing the tenant's statutory protections, and get legal advice on the product.

title: No General Late Fee Cap
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute caps the amount of a residential late fee or sets a grace period for all tenants.

Two limits apply. If rent is due on the first of the month and the tenant is a senior citizen receiving Social Security Old Age, Railroad Retirement or another government pension in lieu of Social Security, or receives Social Security Disability, Supplemental Security Income or Work First New Jersey benefits, no late charge may be made before a five-business-day grace period ends (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-6.1, -6.3); a violation is a disorderly persons offense (2A:42-6.2).

After a warrant for removal is posted or a lockout carried out for nonpayment, if the tenant pays all rent due within three business days you may not impose a late fee above the amount in the warrant application (2A:42-10.16a).

No separate late-fee cap applies to mobile home parks. Under this library's lease a late fee is not rent, so an unpaid late fee cannot support an eviction for nonpayment.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: Give the tenant a printed or emailed receipt for every cash payment of any amount due under a residential lease, renewal or extension. The receipt must show the amount, what it was for, when you received it, the printed or typed names of both landlord and tenant, and who accepted it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-49.2). Penalties are up to $100 per offense, $100 more for a second violation within five years and $200 more for each later one, and in an eviction for nonpayment the tenant has a defense for any month in which you failed to give a required receipt. After a warrant for removal is posted or a lockout executed, give a receipt showing the payment date for every rent payment made in the three-business-day window, however paid (46:8-49.3; penalty up to $500 per offense). No statute requires receipts for check or electronic payments outside that window, though keeping a record is wise. The receipt duty sits in the Truth-in-Renting Act, whose definition of landlord excludes buildings of not more than two units and owner-occupied buildings of not more than three; give receipts anyway, because the defense and the penalty cost far more than a receipt. Payment rules are also summarized in "Rent Payment Rules".

title: No Rent-Receipt Anti-Waiver Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute says that whoever receives the rent carries the duty to keep the home habitable, or bars separating the right to collect rent from that duty by lease, assignment, deed or security instrument. That does not let you contract out of your duties: you may not offer a lease term that violates clearly established tenant rights or landlord responsibilities (N.J.S.A. 46:8-48; see "Unlawful Lease Terms Carry Penalties"), and a lease term waiving the Rent Security Deposit Act is void (46:8-24). A buyer or assignee who takes over the property also takes over the security deposits (46:8-20, -21; see "Deposits When the Property Is Sold").

title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText:
You may not require more than one and one-half months' rent as security. If you later collect additional security, the amount added in any year may not exceed 10% of the current deposit (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2).

Count every payment held as security toward the cap, including a refundable pet deposit and rent paid in advance as security; case law is reported to count pet deposits, so take that cautious course.

The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: Holding the Security Deposit
bodyText: A security deposit stays the tenant's property. Hold it in trust and never mix it with your own money (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19). If you receive deposits for 10 or more rental units, invest them in an insured New Jersey-based money market fund of the kind the statute describes, or deposit them in an insured New Jersey bank, savings bank or savings and loan in an account paying a variable rate set at least quarterly. With fewer than 10 units, deposit them in an insured New Jersey bank, savings bank or savings and loan in an account paying the current rate on time or savings deposits, unless the Commissioner of Banking and Insurance requires the stricter method. The investment rule does not apply to a seasonal rental of not more than 125 consecutive days to someone with a permanent home elsewhere (not farm-worker housing); you must prove a rental is seasonal. Written notices to the tenant, interest payments and the tenant's 7% rent-offset remedy are set out in "Security Deposit Rules". Knowingly diverting deposit money is a disorderly persons offense (46:8-25), and if you become insolvent or bankrupt the tenant's claim is a statutory trust (46:8-23). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell the property or assign your lease, or the property is sold at a foreclosure sale, turn the deposits plus the tenants' share of interest over to the buyer, assignee or foreclosure purchaser at delivery of the deed or assignment or within five days after, and notify each tenant by registered or certified mail of the transfer and the new holder's name and address (N.J.S.A. 46:8-20). In an insolvency or bankruptcy, the five days run from the court order discharging the receiver or trustee. Once you turn the deposit over, you are released from liability to the tenant for it (46:8-21). The buyer, assignee or purchaser must get the deposits and interest from the seller, and whether or not they are transferred is responsible for investing them, giving the notices, paying interest and returning them, unless it transfers them again under the same rules before the lease ends (46:8-20, -21). The new holder must give the tenant the written deposit notice within 30 days after the transfer (46:8-19). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: Deposit Violation Consequences
bodyText: If a tenant sues you for deposit money due under N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1 and wins, the court must award double the amount, full costs, and in its discretion reasonable attorney's fees. Deposit cases up to $5,000, including penalties, can go to small claims (46:8-21.4). If you fail to hold the deposit as required, give a required notice or pay interest, the tenant may give written notice to apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest to rent and need never pay you another deposit; for a missed annual interest payment or annual notice alone, the tenant must first give you notice and 30 days to comply (46:8-19). Knowingly diverting deposit money is a disorderly persons offense, with a fine of at least $200, up to 30 days in jail, or both (46:8-25). Willfully withholding a deposit paid for a tenant by a State or federal assistance program can bring a civil penalty of $500 to $2,000 per offense, and such a tenant need not sue to keep program benefits (46:8-21.1, -21.5). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to post or disclose the standards you use to set different security deposit amounts for different tenants. Any amount must stay within the one-and-a-half-months' rent cap (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2), and applying different standards because of a protected characteristic or a lawful source of income is unlawful discrimination (see "Tenant Screening Limits"). Applying one written standard to everyone is the cautious course.

title: Using the Security Deposit
bodyText:
You may deduct from the deposit only charges actually spent in accordance with the lease, and you may not deduct anything while the tenant remains in possession (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). So you cannot apply the deposit to unpaid rent during the tenancy, and a tenant cannot be required to top it up after a deduction mid-tenancy.

After the lease ends, itemize each deduction and the interest and deliver it with the balance within 30 days by personal delivery or registered or certified mail.

The statute does not list permitted uses or define ordinary wear and tear; the State's tenant guidance describes damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and money owed under the lease. The deposit clause in this library states the permitted uses and the in-possession bar.

The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute allows or forbids a lease schedule of pre-set cleaning, carpet or repair charges to be taken from the deposit. The statute lets you deduct only 'charges expended' in accordance with the lease (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1), so the cautious course is to deduct only what you actually spent for a charge the lease allows, itemized, and not a flat amount you did not spend. A tenant who wins a deposit case recovers double the amount due (46:8-21.1).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A security deposit refund you owe but cannot deliver is unclaimed property under New Jersey's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, which lists security deposits (N.J.S.A. 46:30B-6). If it stays unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable, and the tenant has not contacted you about it, it is presumed abandoned (46:30B-7, -7.1), generally when the tenant's last known address is in New Jersey (46:30B-10). You must then report it to the State Treasurer before November 1 each year as of June 30 and pay it over with the report (46:30B-49, -57). Between 60 and 120 days before filing, send the tenant written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, if the amount is $50 or more and you have an address (46:30B-50). You may not deduct dormancy charges unless a written contract allows them and the other conditions are met (46:30B-7.2). Late reporting or payment carries interest and a civil penalty of $200 a day, up to $100,000 (46:30B-104). A lease term letting you keep an unclaimed deposit would conflict with the deposit law, and a term waiving it is void (46:8-24). If a displaced or domestic violence tenant does not collect the deposit within 30 days, redeposit it in the same institution (46:8-21.1).

title: Deposit Installments After Displacement
bodyText: New Jersey gives tenants no general right to pay a security deposit in installments. One statutory schedule applies: if a tenant displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation got the deposit back and then resumes occupancy, the tenant must redeliver one-third of the deposit immediately, one-third in 30 days and one-third 60 days after reoccupying. If the tenant fails to make those payments, you may sue for possession in the same way as for nonpayment of rent (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). You may agree to installments in other cases. Any additional security you collect in a year may not exceed 10% of the current deposit (46:8-21.2). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: New Jersey's deposit law covers money given as security or to be applied to lease payments when due, so last month's rent you collect in advance as security is held, noticed, earns interest and counts toward the one-and-a-half-months' cap like the rest of the deposit (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.2). No statute lets a tenant withhold the last month's rent and tell you to use the deposit, and none penalizes a tenant for doing so. Because you may not deduct from the deposit while the tenant remains in possession (46:8-21.1), unpaid last-month rent is collected the ordinary way, and the deposit is applied only after the lease ends, with the itemized 30-day accounting. The tenant's statutory right to apply the deposit plus 7% interest to rent arises only if you fail to hold it, notify or pay interest as required (46:8-19). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: No Surrender-Notice Condition
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets you condition the deposit's return on the tenant giving notice of surrender or a forwarding address. The 30-day period runs from the end of the lease, and return is by personal delivery or registered or certified mail (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). A lease term making the refund depend on a move-out notice would risk being void as a waiver (46:8-24). You may ask the tenant for a forwarding address so you can send the refund, without making it a condition; if none is given, send it to the last known address. Some towns' ordinances require owners to register tenants' forwarding addresses in certain eviction situations (2A:18-61.1f).

title: Fast Deposit Return Deadlines
bodyText: Two faster deadlines replace the usual 30 days. Displacement: within five business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation and either a public official posts the premises against occupancy or a building inspector certifies within 48 hours that displacement will likely last more than seven days and notifies you in writing, have the deposit plus interest, less lawful lease charges and rent owed at displacement, available and return it on the tenant's or agent's demand. Domestic violence: within 15 business days after a lease ends under the domestic violence termination law (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.6), do the same, less lawful charges and rent owed at termination. In both cases keep the net sum available on demand during business hours for 30 days at a location in the same municipality, with an itemized statement (the municipal clerk may hold it by agreement). Within three business days, give the tenant written notice by personal delivery or mail to the last known address stating where and when the money is available, send a duplicate to the relocation officer or, if none, the municipal clerk, and if the tenant's mailbox at the vacated address is not accessible, also post the notice at each exterior public entrance. Money not collected within 30 days must be redeposited in the same institution. (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1.) The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: No Holding Deposit Statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute addresses a holding deposit, binder or earnest money taken before a residential lease is signed. Be cautious on two points. Money paid on an agreement to lease as security for performance may be a security deposit under the Rent Security Deposit Act, so hold it in trust and, when the lease is signed, credit it to the security deposit within the cap (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.2). And where the application fee cap applies, a nonrefundable charge required to apply for the unit may be an 'other similar fee' limited to $50, adjusted for inflation from 2027 (46:8-18.1). Put any holding agreement in writing, say when it is refunded, and refund it if you do not offer the lease.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: No New Jersey statute allows any part of a security deposit to be nonrefundable or prescribes a notice for one. Money given as security remains the tenant's property held in trust, and you may keep only charges actually spent in accordance with the lease, itemized after the lease ends (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.1); a lease term waiving that is void (46:8-24). Do not label deposit money nonrefundable. Whether a separate nonrefundable fee (for example a pet fee) is really security is not settled by statute; the cautious course is to state any such fee's amount and purpose in the lease and keep it modest, and never to require more than the application fee cap where it applies (46:8-18.1). The Act covers every rental except a unit in an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units, unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26), and a lease term waiving it is void (46:8-24).

title: No Separate Nonrefundable Notice
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a separate written notice for a nonrefundable deposit or fee, because New Jersey law does not provide for nonrefundable deposits at all; see the No Nonrefundable Deposits row. Security money stays the tenant's property and is returned less charges actually spent under the lease (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19, 46:8-21.1).

title: Abandoned Property Procedure
bodyText: New Jersey's procedure for a tenant's abandoned belongings is set out in the row "Property a Tenant Leaves Behind" (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-72 to -84). It applies only after a warrant for removal has been executed and possession restored to you, or after the tenant has given written notice of voluntarily giving up possession, and only if you reasonably believe the tenant does not intend to claim the property. Points to add to that row: after giving notice you must store the property with reasonable care, but you may promptly dispose of perishable food, and you must allow an animal control agency or humane society to remove any abandoned pets or livestock. If you sell the property, the sale must follow the Uniform Commercial Code's sale rules (N.J.S.A. 12A:9-601 et seq.). From the proceeds you may deduct reasonable costs of notice, storage and sale and any unpaid rent and charges not covered by the security deposit; you must send the tenant any remainder with an itemized accounting. If the tenant cannot be found after due diligence, deposit the remainder with the Superior Court. The procedure does not cover abandoned motor vehicles or property that must be handled under the Uniform Unclaimed Property Act. Good-faith compliance is a complete defense to the tenant's claim for the property.

title: Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute sets a landlord's duty to re-rent (mitigate damages) when a residential tenant abandons the property or leaves before the lease ends, or says whether the lease stays enforceable for the rest of the term. The rule comes from court decisions.

The cautious course: if a tenant leaves early, make and document reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit at a fair rent, as you would any other vacant unit; credit rent you receive from a new tenant against what the old tenant owes; and do not put a clause in the lease saying you have no duty to re-rent.

For belongings the tenant leaves behind, follow the row "Abandoned Property Procedure". Do not treat the unit as given up, change locks or remove belongings unless the tenant has given written notice of giving up possession or a warrant for removal has been executed.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires towns to allow accessory dwelling units (in-law or backyard apartments), bars owner-occupancy rules for them, or sets special rental terms for them. State law mentions them only in the affordable housing laws: it defines an accessory dwelling unit, and the State Affordable Housing Trust Fund may fund units occupied by low- and moderate-income households. Whether you may build or rent one is up to your town's zoning and housing rules; check them before you rent. A rented accessory unit is an ordinary residential tenancy, but the unit count matters: if you live in the house and it has no more than two rental units, the Anti-Eviction Act does not apply (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1), and the Rent Security Deposit Act does not apply unless the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26). A unit created with affordable housing funds may carry its own occupancy and rent restrictions.

title: Agreeing on Extra Notice Methods
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute lets a landlord and tenant agree on an extra way (such as a text message) to give a notice the law requires, or says that an agreed method counts as actual notice.

For eviction-related notices to tenants covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (all residential tenancies except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest-house rentals), the notice must be served personally, left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail, with regular mail if the certified letter is not claimed (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2).

A lease may add email or text as a courtesy copy for everyday notices, but do not rely on it in place of the method a statute requires. Electronic delivery is covered in the row "Electronic Notices".

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you, as a residential landlord, to tell your tenants generally about a lawsuit, foreclosure, code-enforcement case or other proceeding that could affect their tenancy. Specific notices are required in some situations:
- (1) after a sheriff's sale or deed in lieu of foreclosure, the new owner must give tenants a prescribed notice within 10 business days (see "Foreclosure and Tenant Rights")
- (2) a foreclosure summons served on a tenant, and a foreclosing creditor's first contact with a tenant, must include the court-rule notice of tenant rights
- (3) before applying to register a condominium or cooperative conversion, you must give the municipal agency a tenant list, stamped envelopes and copies of the notice, and the agency notifies each tenant
- (4) if the State grants a multiple dwelling an exception to a regulation that affects occupant safety, you must give every applicant and occupant a written notice of it, attached to the lease of each affected unit (to all leases for common-area exceptions)
- (5) when you serve an eviction notice because you cannot comply with housing inspectors' citations without removing the tenant, you must at the same time notify the Department of Community Affairs.

Cautious course: tell tenants promptly in writing of any proceeding you know will affect their possession or rent, and whom to pay.

title: Fees for Tampering With Alarms
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute authorizes a set fee or penalty that a landlord may charge a tenant for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke alarm or carbon monoxide alarm. The state's alarm laws put the duty on the owner: a one- or two-household dwelling must have smoke alarms (and a carbon monoxide alarm where required) and a fire-safety certificate before a new occupancy, with a fine of up to $500 for renting without them; every hotel and multiple dwelling (three or more units) must have smoke detectors and carbon monoxide sensors under State rules.

The library does not offer a fixed tampering fee. You may use the optional clause "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors", which has the tenant agree not to disable an alarm and to pay the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing one the tenant or a guest damages. Recover only your actual, documented cost, and do not label it rent. In a multiple dwelling, occupants are liable under State rules for willful or malicious damage that causes a code violation.

title: Relocation and Comparable Housing
bodyText: No New Jersey statute makes you provide or pay for alternate housing while you repair a unit or after a fire. But several eviction grounds under the Anti-Eviction Act (which covers all residential tenancies except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest-house rentals) carry relocation duties: (1) If you evict because housing inspectors cited the building and you must board it up, demolish it, remove tenants to comply, or correct an illegal occupancy, no warrant for possession may issue until the State relocation assistance laws have been complied with. (2) If a tenant is displaced because zoning or code officials cited an illegal occupancy, you owe the tenant relocation money equal to six times the monthly rent, due five days before removal; unpaid amounts accrue 18% yearly interest and can become a lien on the property. A town may instead handle this by ordinance and bill you. (3) If you evict a tenant to convert the building to a condominium or cooperative, the tenant may ask you, within 18 months after receiving the three-year notice, to offer comparable housing and a reasonable chance to see and rent it; the court will grant one-year stays of eviction until you do, unless you instead give hardship relocation compensation by waiving five months' rent. Senior and disabled tenants may have greater protection. (4) After a fire or other emergency makes a dwelling uninhabitable, a town may treat the tenant as a displaced person eligible for public relocation assistance; this is not a landlord duty.

title: Entering to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute lets a landlord enter a tenant's home to feed, care for or remove the tenant's animal when the tenant is away, hospitalized or detained. Entering a dwelling knowing you are not licensed or privileged to do so is a crime.

Occupants of multiple dwellings (three or more units) must give you access on reasonable notice only for inspections and repairs needed to comply with the law, and immediately for safety or structural emergencies.

If you believe an animal inside is suffering, call a municipal or county humane law enforcement officer or the police: they may enter private property with a warrant, or immediately if the animal's life or safety requires it, and take custody of the animal.

To plan ahead, you may use the optional clause "Animal Care", in which the tenant names a person to care for the animal and consents in advance to your letting that person in. For animals left after a tenant abandons the property, see "Abandoned Property Procedure".

title: Appliances You Will Not Maintain
bodyText: No New Jersey statute says whether appliances left in a rental are presumed to be supplied by the landlord, or lets a lease exclude them from your repair duty. In a multiple dwelling (three or more units), State rules make you responsible at all times for the safe maintenance of the building and its facilities, and require all required service equipment to be kept in good working order. No cooking is permitted in a unit unless it has, among other things, refrigeration in good operating condition and a safely connected cooking facility, so you may not exclude the refrigerator or stove in a unit where cooking is allowed. For other items you leave but do not want to maintain (for example, a window air conditioner or a second refrigerator in the basement), list them plainly in the lease as not part of the rental and not maintained by you, and offer to remove them. Never use such a list for heating equipment, a water heater, a gas appliance or anything else whose defect affects health or safety; a lease provision violating a clearly established tenant right can expose you to penalties under the Truth-in-Renting Act (which does not apply to premises of two or fewer units or owner-occupied premises of three or fewer). See also the library row on waiving habitability.

title: Asbestos
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a residential landlord to test for asbestos or to tell tenants that a building contains it. If you hire someone to apply, enclose, remove or encapsulate asbestos in a structure, the contractor must hold a State asbestos license from the Commissioner of Labor (with limited exceptions), and contracts for that work must say it will be done by licensed contractors and subcontractors. Selling or distributing any product that contains asbestos is banned in New Jersey. Cautious course: if you know or suspect asbestos-containing material in a unit is damaged or crumbling, have it handled by a licensed contractor before or during the tenancy, keep tenants out of the work area, and tell affected tenants in writing about the work and any area they should avoid. Federal rules on asbestos work and on renovation or demolition notices may also apply.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules in the Lease
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a planned community to disclose the association's obligations or to give the tenant a copy of the master deed, bylaws or association rules. Some association powers do reach the unit: a condominium association may enter the unit at reasonable hours to maintain or repair common elements, or for emergency repairs, and may charge you, as unit owner, for repairing common elements your tenant damages. In a planned community, tenants may vote or attend board meetings only where the bylaws allow. Cautious course: attach the association's current rules to the lease and have the tenant agree in writing to follow them. Under the Anti-Eviction Act, a tenant can be evicted for breaking rules only if the rules are reasonable and were accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the start of the term (the Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units). Check the master deed and bylaws for leasing restrictions before you rent.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: No New Jersey statute regulates automatic-renewal clauses in residential leases: none requires a reminder notice before a lease renews itself, bold type, or a limit on how early you may require a renewal decision. New Jersey's consumer auto-renewal laws cover online subscription services and service contracts, not leases. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (all residential tenancies except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest-house rentals), the end of a lease term does not end the tenant's right to stay: you may not evict or fail to renew except for good cause, and a lease term letting the tenancy end or not be renewed without good cause is unenforceable. At the end of a lease you may propose reasonable changes in its terms, including the length of the term, by written notice; a tenant who refuses them may be evicted on that ground after the required notice. For a tenancy the Act does not cover, the tenancy ends only by a notice to quit: one month for month-to-month, three months for year-to-year or at will, and one term for any other term. If you use an automatic-renewal clause, state the renewal term and how either side gives notice of non-renewal plainly.

title: Balcony and Structural Inspections
bodyText: New Jersey has no balcony-inspection law aimed at rental buildings, but its structural-inspection law reaches balconies in some condominium and cooperative buildings. It covers residential condominium or cooperative buildings whose main load-bearing system is concrete, masonry, steel or a hybrid (including heavy timber and buildings with podium decks). It does not cover frame-built buildings with combustible walls or roofs, single-family homes, or buildings that are not condominiums or cooperatives and consist mainly of rental dwellings. For a covered building, the owner of record or the association must have a licensed engineer inspect the load-bearing system, including attached balconies, within 15 years after the certificate of occupancy (or on the catch-up schedule for older buildings), within 60 days after observable damage, and then on the schedule the inspector sets (no more than five years between later inspections), and must carry out required corrective maintenance. Reports must be made available to any resident on request. If you rent out a unit in such a building, this duty falls on the association, not on you as unit owner; you may ask for the report. In any hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units), State rules require guard rails at least 30 inches high on balconies, exterior corridors, landings and porches with more than a three-foot drop, and the State inspects multiple dwellings on a two-, five- or seven-year cycle.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a residential landlord to disclose a unit's or building's bed bug history to a prospective tenant, or sets a deadline for treating bed bugs in a rental home. The one bed bug notice law covers hotels (including apartment hotels serving transient or permanent guests): a hotel operator aware of a bed bug or other vermin infestation not fully treated by a licensed exterminator within 24 hours must notify guests and those booking rooms, and guests may cancel without a fee. That law does not apply to ordinary residential leases. In a multiple dwelling (three or more units), you must eradicate pests, including bed bugs, when the infestation is in two or more units or in common areas, and must arrange preventive pest service by qualified persons at least once a year (see "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties"). Cautious course: do not rent a unit you know has an untreated infestation; answer a prospective tenant's questions about infestations truthfully, since misleading answers can expose you to claims under the Consumer Fraud Act; and use the optional clause "Bed Bugs and Other Pests" for reporting and treatment.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Leases
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute deals specifically with arbitration clauses in residential leases.

The general Arbitration Act applies: a written agreement to arbitrate an existing or future dispute is valid and enforceable except on grounds that would void any contract, and a court decides whether an agreement to arbitrate exists. Before a dispute arises, the parties cannot waive certain protections, including a party's right to be represented by a lawyer at the arbitration.

An arbitration clause cannot take away the court process for removing a tenant: under the Anti-Eviction Act (which covers all residential tenancies except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest-house rentals), a tenant may be removed only by the Superior Court for a good cause listed in the Act, and a lease term waiving rights under the Act is unenforceable.

An arbitration clause is lawful in New Jersey if it is drafted with care. If you want one, have a lawyer draft it to state clearly and plainly that the tenant is giving up the right to go to court for the covered disputes, keep possession actions and security-deposit claims in court, and preserve the right to a lawyer.

The library now offers an optional clause, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Changing the Fire and Re-Renting Rules by Lease
bodyText: New Jersey's two fire-and-casualty statutes can be changed by the lease. If a building is damaged by fire without the tenant's fault, you must repair it as quickly as possible, and if you don't, rent stops until it is fully repaired; if a building is totally destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault, rent is owed only to the date of destruction and the lease ends. Each statute says it does not apply where the parties have agreed otherwise in the lease. This library's lease keeps both statutory rules (see "Fire and Other Casualty"). Changing them does not change other law: in a multiple dwelling (three or more units), State rules keep the owner responsible for maintenance whatever the lease says, and the Anti-Eviction Act still governs removing a covered tenant. No statute addresses whether a lease may waive a landlord's duty to try to re-rent after a tenant leaves early; that rule comes from case law, so do not include such a waiver (see "Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early"). A lease provision violating a clearly established tenant right can expose a landlord covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act (not premises of two or fewer units or owner-occupied premises of three or fewer) to penalties.

title: Certificate of Occupancy
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to give a tenant a copy of, or disclose, the certificate of occupancy. Certificates still matter before you rent: a newly built building, or one altered under a construction permit, may not be used or occupied until the local enforcing agency issues a certificate of occupancy (an existing use may continue for 30 days after alterations finish). Before a new occupancy of a dwelling in a building with fewer than three units, you need either the municipal certificate (where a local ordinance requires one on change of occupancy) or a fire-safety certificate showing the required smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarm; renting without it can bring a fine of up to $500 (smoke alarms) or $100 (carbon monoxide). A hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units) must post its State certificate of inspection in a conspicuous place. Many towns also require a rental certificate of occupancy or registration under local ordinances; check yours.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination bars you from refusing to rent to someone, or setting different terms, because of familial status (being a parent, guardian or custodian of a child under 18, or being pregnant or securing custody of a child). You may not refuse to rent because a person's family includes children under 18, and a lease may not say it becomes void upon the birth of a child. You also may not advertise, or use an application or inquiry, that expresses a limitation or preference about familial status. These rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons, and (except for publicly assisted housing) the Act does not cover renting one unit of a two-family dwelling whose other unit the owner lives in, or renting rooms in a one-family home the owner or occupant lives in; federal fair housing law may still apply. Occupancy limits must rest on real space standards, not on children: in a multiple dwelling (three or more units), State rules require at least 150 square feet of usable floor area for the first occupant and 100 more for each additional occupant, plus bedroom minimums, and children under two do not count; an unemancipated minor may not live in a unit without its own required bathroom facilities. If a child under 11 lives in a unit, see "Window Guard Notice".

title: Cold-Weather Evictions
bodyText: No New Jersey statute bars residential evictions in winter or requires a special notice before a tenant must vacate in cold weather. Any removal still goes through the court: a warrant for possession must tell the tenant of the right to ask the court for a stay and that the tenant may be eligible for temporary housing assistance from the county welfare agency; it may be executed only by a court officer, no earlier than the third day (not counting weekends and court holidays) after it is served on the tenant, and only between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. unless the court orders otherwise. A tenant may also ask the court for a hardship stay (see the library row on hardship stays of eviction). The pandemic-era removal ban in State law applied only during the COVID-19 emergency and has expired. Separate State winter programs limit utility shutoffs for eligible households; they do not stop an eviction.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: In a hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units), State rules make lighting of common areas the owner's job: all interior common areas used by occupants must be lit during darkness well enough for people to move about safely; light switches in corridors, hallways, landings, stairways and vestibules must be of a type occupants cannot operate; entrances and exits must have exterior lights; and parking areas, walkways and unlocked garages used at night must be lit from half an hour before sunset to half an hour after sunrise (or on a dusk-to-dawn control). Inside units you must supply only kitchen and bathroom ceiling or wall fixtures, not lamps or replacement bulbs. A lease cannot relieve you of these duties. New Jersey's statutes contain nothing that addresses making a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric meter; the cautious course is not to wire common areas to a tenant's meter, and if an existing building is wired that way, to tell the tenant in writing before signing and credit the cost. For one- and two-family rentals, check local property maintenance codes.

title: Leases of Communal or Tribal Land
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires government approval before a residential lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land is valid. New Jersey law mentions tribes only in definitions and in programs unrelated to leasing. If you are renting property held in trust for a federally recognized tribe or its members, federal law may require approval of the lease by a federal agency; get legal advice before signing.

title: Rent After a Unit Is Condemned
bodyText: No New Jersey statute says in so many words that you may not collect rent once a unit is condemned, closed or ordered vacated. Do not read that as permission. A municipality that adopts an unfit-buildings ordinance can, after a complaint and a hearing, find a building unfit for human habitation or occupancy or use and order you to repair it or vacate and close it. If you do not comply, its officer can close the building and post a placard saying its use or occupation "is prohibited and unlawful", and the costs become a municipal lien. In a hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units, with some exclusions), the state housing inspectors can order the building vacated for an imminent hazard; until the violations are abated, you may not let anyone (other than a janitor, superintendent or resident caretaker) use it for living. If a fire destroys the building without the tenant's fault, the lease ends and rent stops; if fire damages it, rent stops until it is fully repaired (see "Fire and Other Casualty"). If the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation and an official posts the premises with a notice prohibiting occupancy (or a building inspector certifies the displacement will last more than seven days), you must have the security deposit, with its interest, available and return it within five business days of the tenant's demand, less lawful charges and rent due at the time of displacement. You may remove a tenant to board up or demolish a building after a citation for substantial health and safety violations, to comply with such a citation, or to correct an illegal occupancy only under the Anti-Eviction Act's code-enforcement ground, and no warrant for possession issues until the state relocation laws have been complied with. If a tenant is displaced because of an illegal occupancy, you owe relocation money equal to six times the monthly rent, due five days before the tenant is removed (or as the municipality's ordinance provides). If you have been held liable for a code penalty and code enforcement displaces tenants, you must repay the public agency's relocation costs. The cautious course: stop charging rent for any period a unit is under a vacate or closing order, and check your municipality's ordinance.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a tenant that a rental contains defective (for example, corrosive imported) drywall, and none sets a drywall standard or remediation duty for rentals. Your general maintenance and habitability duties still apply, and the Consumer Fraud Act can reach knowing concealment of a material fact in a rental (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). The cautious course: if you know the home has drywall that gives off odors or corrodes wiring or fixtures and it has not been fixed, tell the applicant in writing before the lease is signed.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets you name, in the lease, the person or company who must do repairs a tenant arranges, and no statute sets a tenant repair-and-deduct procedure that such a clause would control. The statutory route for serious conditions is rent receivership: a tenant or a municipal officer can ask a court to have rent paid into court and used for repairs (see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"). Whether a tenant may make a needed repair and deduct the cost from rent is a question for case law. For landlords covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act (not rentals of two or fewer units, owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer, or transient hotels), offering a lease term that violates clearly established tenant rights can cost up to $100 per offense and lets the tenant ask a court to end the lease. The cautious course: put no clause in the lease that names who must make repairs at your expense, limits what a tenant may do when you fail to repair, or bars deducting repair costs from rent. Tell tenants how to report repairs, and make them promptly yourself.

title: Disability Accommodations
bodyText:
New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination makes it unlawful to refuse to rent to someone, or to treat a tenant differently in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the facilities or services you provide, because of disability, including the disability of anyone who lives or will live in the home or anyone associated with the tenant. Disability is defined broadly and includes mental, psychological and developmental disabilities and HIV.

The Law does not reach renting one unit of a two-family house when you live in the other unit, or renting rooms in a one-family home you live in, unless the housing is publicly assisted; renting not more than one room in a single-family home is also outside it.

The statute itself does not spell out a duty to grant reasonable accommodations or modifications; the Division on Civil Rights' rules do (N.J.A.C. 13:13-3.4). You may not refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, or reasonable structural modifications, when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home, including public and common areas. You also may not refuse to let the tenant make reasonable modifications of the unit at the tenant's expense when they may be necessary for full enjoyment of it.

In a rental you may: where reasonable, make your permission conditional on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition (reasonable wear and tear excepted); where needed to be reasonably sure the money will be there, negotiate as part of that agreement payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not more than the cost of restoring, with the interest going to the tenant; and require a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike way with any required building permits.

You need not install or pay for special accessories or practices, but you may not charge a person with a disability extra compensation, an extra fee or an additional security deposit because of them (the rule's examples are a guide or service dog and a shower bar), though the tenant remains liable for specific damage to the premises.

The Division's published guidance adds that an accommodation may be refused only if it would be an undue burden, and that you may not require extra insurance or shorten a lease because of a disability; the federal Fair Housing Act has its own accommodation rules.

No New Jersey statute or rule requires the lease to say anything about accommodations or modifications. Treat every request seriously, answer it promptly in writing, and get advice before you deny one.

title: No Disaster-Displaced Guest Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, storm or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, suspends those terms during a declared emergency, or sets special rules for disaster-displaced people staying in hotels or other lodging. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms, local occupancy codes, and the eviction rules apply as usual. New Jersey's disaster rules for landlords are in "Duties After a Declared Disaster": chiefly, rent limits under a Governor's Notice of Rent Protection Emergency, fast return of the deposit when a tenant is displaced, and municipal relocation help. The cautious course: if a tenant asks to take in displaced family or friends after a disaster, answer in writing, and if you agree, say for how long.

title: Duties After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: When the Governor declares a state of emergency, the Governor may also issue a Notice of Rent Protection Emergency for the affected area. While that notice is in effect, within the emergency area and up to 10 miles beyond it if the notice says so: a rent increase you give a residential tenant after the declaration is presumed unreasonable if it is more than twice the rate of inflation (the regional CPI-W over the preceding nine months), and rent for a new lease is limited to the unit's fair market rent before the emergency adjusted by no more than twice that inflation rate. These limits add to, and never loosen, any local rent control. You may apply to the Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs for permission to charge more if the limits deny you a just and reasonable return. A violation can bring a penalty of six times the monthly rent you sought, is treated as consumer fraud, and lets the tenant ask a court to end a lease containing the unlawful term. The limits end when the emergency or the notice ends. If a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, the fast deposit-return rules apply (see "Fast Deposit Return Deadlines"). If fire damages the building without the tenant's fault, rent stops until it is repaired, and if the building is totally destroyed the lease ends (see "Fire and Other Casualty"). A municipality may treat tenants displaced from a building of two or more units by fire or another emergency as eligible for relocation assistance. No New Jersey statute ends a tenancy, or stops rent, simply because a disaster was declared or the unit cannot be reached, and none requires an emergency plan or shelter in a private rental.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute specifically bars renting the same home or room to two tenants for the same period, and none gives a tenant a special remedy, such as rent abatement, when you cannot deliver possession because someone else has it. The tenant's claims would rest on the lease, on general contract law and on the Consumer Fraud Act, which covers rentals and reaches deception and knowing omission of a material fact (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). The cautious course: never sign a second lease for a unit until the first tenancy has ended or the first tenant has given it up in writing, and if you cannot deliver possession on the start date, tell the tenant at once in writing and do not charge rent until you do.

title: Drug-Free Lease Addenda
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires, describes or gives special effect to a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum for private rentals. In New Jersey a lease promise about drugs works only through the Anti-Eviction Act: you may remove a tenant who, after written notice to cease, substantially breaks a reasonable lease covenant that was in the lease from the start of the term and for which the lease reserves a right of reentry. Use the library's optional "Criminal Activity" clause for that purpose rather than a separate addendum. Separately, the Act lets you remove a tenant who has been convicted of, pleaded guilty to, or (as a juvenile) been adjudicated delinquent for a drug offense under the Comprehensive Drug Reform Act on the leased premises or the building, complex or mobile home park, or who knowingly harbors such a person, unless the person completed or is on probation in a court-ordered drug rehabilitation program; the case must be brought within two years after the conviction or release from incarceration, whichever is later. These rules do not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or to transient hotels. Lawful adult cannabis use is treated separately (see "Cannabis in Rentals"). Federally assisted housing may require a federal addendum.

title: Submetered Electricity and Heat Billing
bodyText: No New Jersey statute sets rules for, or requires a lease disclosure about, billing tenants for electricity or gas through a submeter, and none says whether reselling metered electricity or gas to tenants makes you a regulated utility. By statute, metering, meter reading and billing for the delivery of electricity and gas stay under the Board of Public Utilities; check the Board's rules before you submeter or rebill. Heat is different. In a multiple dwelling (a building of three or more units, with some exclusions), you may not charge each unit a share of the building's heating cost by any method or device other than a separate meter approved by the Board of Public Utilities unless the Department of Community Affairs has approved the method and device. An approved system must give each unit its own thermostat, may apportion only fuel or current costs, and each bill must show the building's actual fuel or current cost for the period and the unit's share. The Department's rules also require you to give existing and prospective occupants written information about the system: its range of accuracy, the building's average heating cost per square foot over the last heating season (or an estimate), the square footage of the occupant's unit, and the maintenance schedule. Each bill must state that it is not from the utility and that the units' bills together will not exceed what you pay the utility to heat the units. You must maintain and inspect the system on the approved schedule.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: No New Jersey statute expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or other emergency help, voids a lease term that penalizes such calls, or gives a tenant a presumed defense to an eviction filed soon after a call. That does not make such terms safe. Calling for help is not one of the Anti-Eviction Act's grounds for removing a tenant, and a reprisal for a tenant's efforts to secure or enforce rights under the law, or for a good-faith complaint to a government authority about a health or safety violation, is unlawful (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). The library's optional "Criminal Activity" clause already says it does not apply to a request for police or other emergency help, or to criminal activity in which the tenant or a household member is the victim. The cautious course: put nothing in the lease that limits, counts or charges for calls for police, fire or medical help, and never treat such a call as a lease violation.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires a private landlord to collect an emergency contact from a tenant, and none limits how you use one a tenant gives you; if you ask for one, make it optional and use it only for emergencies.

The emergency-contact duties run the other way. Your landlord registration statement must name a representative of the owner or managing agent who can be reached at any time in an emergency affecting the premises, who has authority to make emergency decisions and repairs, and who has access to a current list of building tenants to give emergency personnel when needed.

In a tenant-occupied multiple dwelling (a building of three or more units, with some exclusions), you must also post, in at least one conspicuous place where tenants are most likely to see it and on the website of any management company that manages the building, emergency contact instructions with that representative's name, address and telephone number, and instructions for using the state's 24-hour social services information hotline, in English and Spanish.

A separate rule requires rooming and boarding houses, assisted living and similar facilities and senior public housing to collect emergency contacts for residents 62 and older and notify the contact within 24 hours of a resident's death; it does not apply to ordinary rentals.

title: Screening Building Employees
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to run a background check on a superintendent, manager, maintenance worker or other employee of a residential rental, and no state license or clearance exists for apartment staff. If you do screen, New Jersey limits how. If your business has 15 or more employees over 20 calendar weeks, the Opportunity to Compete Act bars you from asking about an applicant's criminal record, including an expunged record, on an application, orally or in an online form, during the initial application process, which ends after the first interview, unless the applicant brings it up first or a law requires a background check for the job. You may ask after the first interview and may refuse to hire because of a record, except one that has been expunged or pardoned, if that is consistent with other laws. Job advertisements may not say that people with arrest or conviction records will not be considered. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1,000, $5,000 and then $10,000 per violation, enforced by the Department of Labor; the Act gives applicants no private lawsuit. Municipal and county rules on criminal histories in private employment are preempted. Federal consumer-report rules also apply when you use a screening company.

title: Tenant Energy Usage Data
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage to you. The utility rule runs the other way: an electric or gas utility or supplier may not disclose, sell or transfer a customer's individual information, including name, address, telephone number, energy usage and payment history, to a third party without the customer's consent, and information disclosed under that rule may be used only to provide continued electric or gas service to that customer. Whether a tenant's consent can let you use the data for building benchmarking is therefore unsettled; the Board of Public Utilities' rules may answer it. Separately, the Board must require the owner or operator of each commercial building over 25,000 square feet to benchmark its energy and water use for the prior calendar year with the federal Portfolio Manager tool; whether that reaches an apartment building depends on the Board's rules. The library offers no lease clause for this. If you need a tenant's usage data, ask the tenant to share it or to sign the utility's own consent form, and do not make that a condition of the tenancy.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets you, or a tenant, end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event such as contamination, a chemical or fuel spill, a sewage backup, mold, radon or a flood, and none lets a lease create such a right for you. Where the Anti-Eviction Act applies (every rental except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotels), you may remove a tenant only on one of its listed grounds, and a lease term waiving those protections is unenforceable; the grounds include boarding up or demolishing the building, or complying with housing inspectors, after a citation for substantial health and safety violations (see "Rent After a Unit Is Condemned"). If a building is totally destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault, the lease ends and rent is owed only to that date (see "Fire and Other Casualty"). One tenant right exists: a landlord covered by the flood-disclosure law (not premises of two or fewer units, owner-occupied premises of three or fewer, or transient or seasonal rentals of less than 120 days) who fails to disclose that the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Risk Flood Hazard Area lets the tenant end the lease by written notice once the tenant learns of it, effective when the tenant surrenders possession, with prepaid rent refunded within 30 days (see "Flood Risk Disclosure Rider" clause). The library offers no environmental-event termination clause.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: No New Jersey statute says who owns a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when a tenancy ends, whether the tenant may or must remove it, or who pays to restore the space, and no statute gives a tenant a right to install one in the first place (see "No Tenant EV-Charging Right"). If you agree to let a tenant install a charger, settle ownership, removal and restoration in writing at the time you give consent, and treat any money you hold for those duties as part of the security deposit and its legal limit (see "Security Deposit Rules"). If the rental is a condominium or other common interest community unit, the association's rules bind you as the unit owner: the unit owner, and each later owner, is responsible as an assessment for damage from installing or removing a charger, its upkeep and restoring the area after removal, and must tell buyers about it.

title: EV Charging Requirements
bodyText: New Jersey's electric vehicle charging rules for rental property are construction and utility rules, not tenant rights; no statute requires you to let a tenant install a charger (see "No Tenant EV-Charging Right"). New construction: as a condition of preliminary site plan approval for a multiple dwelling of five or more units (including condominium and cooperative buildings and mixed-use developments), the developer or owner must prepare at least 15 percent of the required off-street parking spaces as Make-Ready spaces and install charging equipment in one-third of them, then another third within three years and the final third within six years after the certificate of occupancy; at least 5 percent of the equipment must be accessible for people with disabilities. Other new parking lots and garages need a smaller number of Make-Ready spaces, and single-family homes are exempt. These requirements apply to new construction and new parking created by an expansion, not to existing buildings. Installing chargers or Make-Ready spaces is a permitted accessory use needing no use variance. If you own, operate or manage charging equipment, you are not a public utility just for that, and charging a vehicle is treated as a service, not a sale of electricity. No state weights-and-measures registration rule for chargers was found. In a condominium or other common interest community, the association may not prohibit or unreasonably restrict a unit owner's charger in a designated parking space; that right belongs to the unit owner (you, if you own the unit), not to your tenant.

title: EV Charging in Shared Parking
bodyText: No New Jersey statute governs a tenant's charger in a parking area shared with other tenants: nothing lets a tenant put one there, sets a fee you may charge to reserve the space, or assigns responsibility for damage to it. Those terms are for you to set in writing if you agree to allow it. Shared-area rules exist only for condominiums and other common interest communities, and they protect unit owners against the association, not tenants against a landlord: the association's board must grant a unit owner exclusive or limited use of common elements needed to run utility lines or meters to the owner's designated space, may license a common-area parking space to a unit owner for a charger for a set period, may install shared chargers for all owners and adopt rules for them, and may create a new space for a charger at the owner's cost. A utility may charge no more than a residential rate (or its residential EV rate) for electricity delivered to such a development for a charger meant for a specific unit owner, and the development may set its own price for charging it provides as a service. New multifamily construction must include Make-Ready spaces (see "EV Charging Requirements").

title: Habitability Gaps in New Jersey
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no New Jersey statute. Each is explained in its own row. (1) No radon testing or disclosure duty for landlords; the radon statutes cover home sales, schools, child care centers, new construction and testers ("No Radon Rule for Landlords"). (2) No mold disclosure or remediation statute; mold is handled under general habitability law and housing codes ("No Mold Rule for Landlords"). (3) No defective drywall disclosure. (4) No statute that, in so many words, stops rent once a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, although closing and vacate orders make occupancy unlawful, displacement triggers a five-business-day deposit return, and illegal-occupancy displacement triggers relocation payments ("Rent After a Unit Is Condemned"). (5) No statute letting you name who must do repairs or setting a tenant repair-and-deduct procedure; whether a tenant may repair and deduct is a case-law question not covered here ("No Designated-Repairer Rule"). (6) No right for either side to end a lease because of an environmental or public-health event, apart from the tenant's flood-zone nondisclosure exit ("No Environmental-Event Termination Right").
