What New Jersey does have: rent receivership for serious conditions ("Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"), non-waivable maintenance duties in multiple dwellings ("Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived"), heat and pest duties ("Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)"), and fire and casualty rules ("Fire and Other Casualty"). These absences are statutory only.

title: Other Rules New Jersey Lacks
bodyText: Some rules found in other states have no New Jersey statute. Each is explained in its own row. (1) No statute bars renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; contract law and the Consumer Fraud Act apply ("No Double-Letting Statute"). (2) No required move-in or move-out inspection or condition report; the library offers an optional condition-report clause ("Move-In Condition Report" clause). (3) No rule letting tenants house disaster-displaced people despite the lease, or suspending occupancy limits in an emergency ("No Disaster-Displaced Guest Rule"). (4) No statute on drug-free or crime-free lease addenda; drug conduct is handled through the Anti-Eviction Act ("Drug-Free Lease Addenda"). (5) No statute expressly protecting a tenant's calls for police or emergency help, though calls are not a removal ground and reprisals for asserting legal rights are unlawful ("Calling Police or Emergency Help"). (6) No tenant right to install an electric vehicle charger, and no rule on chargers at move-out or in shared tenant parking; the charger rules protect condominium unit owners against associations and govern new construction ("No Tenant EV-Charging Right", "EV Chargers at Move-Out", "EV Charging in Shared Parking"). (7) No statute on billing tenants for submetered electricity or gas; utility rules, not reviewed, may apply ("Submetered Electricity and Heat Billing"). These absences are statutory only unless a row says otherwise.

title: Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Laws
bodyText: Four things landlords ask about, answered across all New Jersey statutes, not only the landlord-tenant laws. (1) Squatters: there is no special removal procedure outside court. Removal is by summary eviction, unlawful detainer or a possession action, and criminal trespass law may also apply; never use self-help ("Removing an Unauthorized Occupant"). (2) Cash receipts: present. A landlord covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act (not rentals of two or fewer units, owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer, or transient hotels) must give a printed or emailed receipt for every cash payment due under a residential lease, showing the amount, purpose, date received, both parties' printed names and who accepted it; failing to do so is a defense to a nonpayment eviction for those months ("Rent Receipts"). (3) Registration before eviction: present. If you have not filed the required landlord registration statement, no judgment for possession may be entered until you comply; the court continues the case up to 90 days and then dismisses it. The registration law does not apply to owner-occupied two-unit premises ("Landlord Registration Statement" clause). Business-registration rules can also stop an eviction. An out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing real property in New Jersey is transacting business here, and until it obtains a certificate of authority it may not maintain any action, including an eviction (N.J.S.A. 42:2C-59(b), 42:2C-65(a)); an out-of-state corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority faces the same bar (N.J.S.A. 14A:13-11(1)), though whether renting out property is transacting business for a corporation is a case-law question. A corporation that rents under an alternate name it has not registered may not maintain an action arising from a lease made under that name until it files the registration (N.J.S.A. 14A:2-2.1(6)). None of these failures voids the lease or stops you from defending a suit (see "Out-of-County Owner Must Name a Local Agent"). (4) Immigration status: no statute specifically addresses asking about or acting on a tenant's immigration status. The Law Against Discrimination bars housing discrimination based on national origin, ancestry and nationality, and the Division on Civil Rights says it protects everyone regardless of immigration status ("No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords"). Do not ask about immigration status.

title: Fair Housing Rules
bodyText: New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination covers owners, landlords, sublessors, managing agents, brokers and their employees. You may not refuse to rent, refuse to negotiate, say a unit is unavailable when it is available, or set different terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services because of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, nationality, marital status, civil union or domestic partnership status, pregnancy or breastfeeding, sex, gender identity or expression, affectional or sexual orientation, familial status, disability, service or liability for service in the U.S. Armed Forces, or source of lawful income used for rent. Source of lawful income includes Section 8 and other vouchers, rental assistance, benefits, child support and any lawful form of currency; see "Tenant Screening Limits" for the income rules. You may not refuse to rent because a household includes children under 18, or use a lease term that ends the tenancy on the birth of a child, except in qualifying housing for older persons. Ads, listings, signs, application forms and screening questions may not state or suggest any limit or preference on these grounds. A tenant with a disability who has a service or guide dog must get full and equal access, may not be charged extra for the dog, and is liable for damage the dog causes; a no-pets clause does not apply to it (see "Service and Assistance Animals" clause). The Division on Civil Rights also says you must make reasonable accommodations for a disability unless doing so would be an undue burden. Exemptions: the Law does not cover renting one apartment in a two-family house when you live in the other unit, or renting rooms in a one-family home you or the occupant lives in. These exemptions do not apply to publicly assisted housing. Even when an exemption applies, the Division's advertising rule still bars discriminatory ads. Religious organizations may give preference to members in housing they run, and housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rule. A person who is wronged can complain to the Division or sue in Superior Court, with tort damages; the Division can also seek penalties of up to $10,000 for a first violation, $25,000 for a second within five years, and $50,000 for more within seven years. Retaliating against someone who opposes discrimination or files a complaint is unlawful. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: Family Day Care in Rentals
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a landlord to let a tenant run a family day care home in a rental, or sets conditions such as insurance or liability waivers on which a landlord must allow one. A lease may address the subject. Related rules: a registered family day care home (child care for a fee for three to five children at a time, at least 15 hours a week, in the provider's home) is a permitted use in every residential zone, and must be treated the same as a single-family home. A deed restriction against using a single-family home as a family day care home can't be enforced unless the party enforcing it proves it is needed for the neighbors' health, safety and welfare. In a condominium, cooperative or horizontal property regime, the bylaws or deed restrictions may bar family day care; outside age-restricted or retiree communities, the association must prove the ban or any other restriction (such as noise or common-area limits) is reasonably related to residents' health, safety and welfare. If your rental is in such a community, the association's rules bind your tenant too (see hoa-compliance). Registration of family day care providers with the State is voluntary.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No New Jersey statute is worded as a general ban on charging a residential tenant for a service you don't provide. Several rules reach that result. The Consumer Fraud Act covers rentals and makes it unlawful to use deception, a false promise, misrepresentation or an unconscionable practice in renting or in your later performance; charging for a promised service you don't deliver risks a claim for three times the tenant's loss plus attorney's fees (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). You may not stop a tenant from getting cable television, demand or accept any payment for allowing it to be installed in the tenant's home, or charge a tenant who has cable different rent; you may set reasonable installation conditions to protect the building and other tenants. In a mobile home park, every fee must relate to and be identifiable with your actual costs, all fees must be disclosed in writing before occupancy, and an undisclosed fee can't be collected. The cautious course: charge only for services you actually provide, describe each one in the lease, and stop or credit a service charge when the service stops. Don't call any fee rent or additional rent (see "Fees Treated as Rent").

title: New Jersey Fire Code
bodyText: New Jersey has one statewide fire code, the Uniform Fire Code, adopted by the Department of Community Affairs under the Uniform Fire Safety Act. The Act says the code must be based mainly on the NFPA Life Safety Code and other national model fire codes, which may be adopted by reference with State changes. It covers fire detection and suppression systems, alarms, protective equipment, egress, and maintenance of fire protection systems. The code itself (N.J.A.C. 5:70) states which model-code editions apply and which buildings it reaches; check its current text. The code is enforced by the State or by a local fire department, county fire marshal or fire district that the town designates, and a town may adopt fire safety ordinances stricter than the State code. Under the Act, "owner" includes anyone who owns, manages, rents, leases or controls a building. You may not disable or fail to maintain any protective equipment, or ignore an enforcement order; penalties run up to $5,000 per violation, with each day after the correction date a new violation, plus up to $50,000 more for failing to abate after notice and the town's firefighting costs. The Act does not authorize a fire regulation or ordinance requiring a building that conforms in all respects to the State construction code to meet more restrictive standards. In a building of three or more units (a multiple dwelling under the Hotel and Multiple Dwelling Law), the State maintenance rules require the building to be kept up as the Uniform Fire Code requires, and no occupant may create a fire code violation or damage protective equipment. Where a town has rent control, improvements the fire laws require count as capital improvements whose cost may be passed on to tenants under the local ordinance. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms: see "Smoke Alarms".

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rentals
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental home or apartment building. The Uniform Fire Safety Act lets the State fire code (N.J.A.C. 5:70) require fire suppression systems in new or existing buildings, so any retrofit duty for your building type, such as a high-rise, would be in that code; check it with your local fire official. Statutes do require sprinklers in two settings: a newly built townhouse under the one- and two-family dwelling subcode, unless its permit or development application came in before the cutoff dates in the law, and student dormitories owned or recognized by a school or college (not private apartments rented to students). If your building has sprinklers, keep them working: anyone who disables or fails to properly maintain protective equipment faces penalties of up to $5,000 per violation, with each day after the correction date a new violation. In a building of three or more units, the State maintenance rules require all safeguards that the rules require, or that the law required when the building was built or altered, to be kept in good working order. A certified automatic fire suppression system installed in a residential building is exempt from property tax. Where a town has rent control, improvements the fire laws require count as capital improvements whose cost may be passed on to tenants under the local ordinance.

title: Firearms in Rentals
bodyText: No New Jersey landlord-tenant statute addresses firearms. No statute bars or requires a lease rule on firearms, protects a tenant's right to keep one, or protects firearms locked in vehicles in your parking area. State criminal law still shapes what a lease should say. A person may keep a lawfully possessed firearm at the person's residence or premises, which includes a tenant's own unit. Carrying a firearm on private property, including residential property, is a crime unless the owner has given express consent or posted a sign saying a permit holder may carry a concealed handgun there; this rule does not limit keeping a firearm in one's own residence. This rule has been challenged in federal court. So for common areas, grounds and parking areas you control, decide whether you consent to permit holders carrying, and say so plainly in the lease or by a sign; don't give consent by accident. In a vehicle, a firearm must be unloaded and in a closed, fastened case or gunbox, or locked unloaded in the trunk. Anyone who knows or should know that a child under 16 may get to a loaded firearm at premises the person controls must keep it in a locked box or container or another secure place, or use a trigger lock. If you add a firearms rule, write it as a lease rule applied evenly to everyone. Don't word it so that it blocks keeping a lawful firearm inside the unit unless you have had legal advice. Hunting and discharge near buildings: see farmland-hunting-rights.

title: No Pre-Lease Foreclosure Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a landlord to tell a prospective tenant, before signing a lease, that the property is in foreclosure or that the landlord has received a foreclosure complaint. Other rules apply once foreclosure is under way. A foreclosing party who serves a tenant with the foreclosure complaint, or first contacts a tenant during the case, must include the court-required notice of tenant rights. Whoever takes title at a sheriff's sale or by deed in lieu of foreclosure must give every tenant a prescribed English and Spanish notice within 10 business days, and foreclosure alone is not grounds to evict (see "Tenants in Foreclosed Properties"). In some sheriff's sales of a home owned by an individual, a tenant who has lived there at least a year and is not behind on rent may have a right of first refusal to buy it. The cautious course: if a foreclosure complaint has been filed against the property, tell a new tenant in writing before the lease is signed. The Consumer Fraud Act makes it unlawful to knowingly conceal or omit a material fact in renting with intent that others rely on the omission (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases").

title: No Foreign-Ownership Limit on Leasing
bodyText: No New Jersey statute bars foreign nationals, foreign governments or so-called foreign adversaries from leasing or owning land, and no statute requires a lease to a foreign person to be recorded, approved or labeled. New Jersey's alien land law runs the other way: an alien friend, meaning a foreign national domiciled and residing in the United States with federal permission to remain, has the same rights in New Jersey real estate as a native-born citizen. You have no duty under New Jersey law to find out whether an applicant is a foreign national. Refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of national origin, ancestry or nationality is unlawful under the Law Against Discrimination (see "Fair Housing Rules" and "No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords").

title: Tenant Can Pay and Stay
bodyText: In New Jersey a tenant sued for unpaid rent can usually keep the home by paying what is owed. By an older statute, in a possession action by a landlord owed a full year's rent who has a right of reentry, if the tenant pays or tenders all rent in arrears plus costs before trial, to you or into court, the action must be dismissed. For tenancies under the older removal statute, payment of the rent claimed plus accrued costs to the court clerk on or before final judgment stops the case. By law, in a nonpayment case under the Anti-Eviction Act, the tenant also has three business days after the warrant for removal is posted, or after a lockout, to pay all rent due and owing. You must accept the payment, whether made in cash, by certified check or money order, or through a rental assistance program or charity, and cooperate with any program or charity that has committed to pay. Give the tenant a dated receipt, and within two business days tell the court in writing that the rent was paid; the court then dismisses the case with prejudice. You may not add a late fee beyond the amount in your warrant application. A violation can cost up to $500 per offense. A lease clause can't take these rights away. Fees and charges count toward what must be paid only if the lease and the law allow them to be charged as rent; in this library no fee is treated as rent (see "Fees Treated as Rent"). Ending a tenancy for a breach other than rent still requires good cause and the notices in the Anti-Eviction Act (see "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)" and "Reservation of Right of Reentry" clause).

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: New Jersey's building and fire statutes mostly do not freeze a code at a named edition. The State Uniform Construction Code is built from national model codes adopted by the Department of Community Affairs. Once a model code is adopted as a subcode, later editions are adopted too, but no more often than every three years, and the Commissioner must first review each new edition and adopt only the provisions found essential; until then the edition already in effect stays in force. Check the current construction code (N.J.A.C. 5:23) for the editions that apply. The Uniform Fire Code is based on the NFPA Life Safety Code and other national fire codes, adopted by reference with State changes; its editions are in N.J.A.C. 5:70. A few statutes do name an edition. Which buildings are life hazard uses under the Uniform Fire Safety Act is tied to use groups in the 1981 edition of the BOCA Basic Building Code. Required sprinklers in newly built townhouses must follow the 2021 International Residential Code, Section R313.1, or a successor model code. For older buildings, equipment and safeguards that the law required when the building was built, altered or repaired must still be kept in good working order in a building of three or more units. A building that meets the construction code can't be required by a fire regulation or local ordinance to meet a stricter standard.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute gives a tenant's guests, or service providers and suppliers, a right to enter the building, bars a fee for guests, or makes guest rights non-waivable in buildings of three or more households. Guest limits are therefore set by the lease (see the library's guest policy clause).

Related rules still apply. Any rules you make about guests must be reasonable and accepted by the tenant in writing or made part of the lease at the start of the term before you can rely on breaking them as good cause for eviction, and you must first give a written notice to cease. A guest's disorderly conduct is a separate eviction ground only with a notice to cease. Apply guest rules evenly; rules that fall more heavily on families with children, or on a protected group, can violate the Law Against Discrimination. A guest who stays may become an occupant whom you can't remove without a court process.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be
bodyText: New Jersey's statutory repair remedy turns on how serious the problem is. A tenant or the town's public officer may ask a court to order rent paid into court and used for repairs only where there is a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, or another condition in substantial violation of the State or local housing or health code standards of fitness for human habitation, or any other condition dangerous to life, health or safety. Minor or cosmetic problems that are not substantial code violations and not dangerous do not qualify. You have a full defense if the condition did not exist or has been fixed, was caused maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use by the petitioning tenant or the tenant's family, or a tenant refused you entry to fix it. This remedy does not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, hotels, motels or guest houses, or public housing (see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"). New Jersey courts also apply a judge-made implied warranty of habitability with its own test of seriousness. The cautious course: treat any code violation affecting health or safety, and any loss of an essential service, as needing prompt repair.

title: No Habitability Presumption
bodyText: No New Jersey statute presumes that you breached a habitability duty or took too long to repair, and none presumes that you complied. In the statutory rent-into-court proceeding the tenant or public officer must affirmatively prove the conditions, and you must affirmatively prove any defense: that the condition did not exist or was fixed, was caused maliciously or by abnormal use by the petitioning tenant, or that a tenant refused you entry to fix it (see "How Serious a Defect Must Be"). A separate presumption does run against you: if a tenant gets a notice to quit, or a substantial change in the tenancy terms without cause, after trying to enforce lease or legal rights, after reporting a health or safety violation to a government agency (having first given you a reasonable time to fix it), after joining or organizing a lawful tenant group, or after winning a prior possession case against you, the law presumes it is retaliation (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). Keep dated records of repair requests, your responses and entry attempts.

title: No Required Habitability Statement
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation, or prescribes habitability wording. Your duties exist whether or not the lease mentions them: State and local housing and health codes apply, a tenant can ask a court to have rent paid into court for serious violations, and in a building of three or more units the State maintenance rules apply and no lease term relieves you of them (see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs", "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)" and "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived"). New Jersey does require certain other notices in or with the lease, such as the Truth in Renting statement, the flood notices, the window guard notice in multiple dwellings and the lead-safe certification exhibit (see "What a New Jersey Lease Must Contain"). The library's Maintenance & Repairs clause states your repair duty in plain terms; use it rather than drafting a separate habitability promise.

title: No Lease Contamination Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a residential lease to disclose soil or groundwater contamination, to state that a deed notice is recorded, or to incorporate recorded engineering or institutional controls. Related duties still reach you. If a property was cleaned up to a nonresidential standard, or with engineering or institutional controls (such as a cap or a no-groundwater-use restriction), a deed notice may be recorded on it, and both the owner and any lessee must maintain those controls; improperly altering or removing them carries penalties and remediation liability. An owner of a deed-notice site must tell anyone who plans to excavate there about the contamination and the measures needed to prevent exposure. Whoever is conducting a cleanup must notify property owners and tenants living within 200 feet of the site. The cautious course: if your rental is subject to a deed notice or other controls, tell the tenant in writing before signing, attach the restrictions, and bar digging, wells or other uses the controls prohibit. Knowingly hiding a material fact in renting can violate the Consumer Fraud Act (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). Lead paint and lead in drinking water have their own rules (see lead-based-paint and "Lead-Safe Certification Exhibit" clause).

title: Local Health Board Rental Rules
bodyText: In New Jersey, local boards of health and towns can add rental rules of their own. No statute requires you to give a tenant a copy of local health or housing rules on request, post them, or refer a tenant to the health department, and no statewide health-district rental code applies everywhere. A local board of health may adopt ordinances and rules on public health. These can include heat standards for buildings with more than two families where the owner has agreed to supply heat: from October 1 to May 1, at least 68 degrees from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. when it is below 55 degrees outside, and at least 55 degrees at other times when it is below 40 degrees outside. Where your board has adopted such a rule, you must supply the fuel and keep the heating system working regardless of any lease term shifting that duty, unless the tenant agrees in writing to heat a unit that has its own separately billed heating equipment. The State maintenance rules for buildings of three or more units set their own, stricter heat rule (see "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)"). If the heat fails, the tenant tried in good faith to tell you, you have not acted, 24 hours have passed since the tenant complained to the board, and it is below 55 degrees outside, the board may hire repairers and order parts as your agent. They bill you, and they can record a lien on the property. A town may also adopt the State Housing Code by ordinance, which sets minimum standards for water, plumbing, garbage storage, lighting, ventilation, heating, egress, maintenance and occupancy. Check your town's and health board's ordinances.

title: Renting in a Condo, Co-op or HOA
bodyText:
If your rental is in a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the association's documents can limit leasing. New Jersey law adds a few rules. A condominium master deed may restrict or limit leasing of units, so long as the restriction is otherwise lawful. Any restriction based on race, religion, national origin or another protected trait is void.

In a cooperative, rules that unreasonably keep a proprietary lessee from renting the unit are unenforceable, unless the co-op limited occupancy to owners from the start or by a properly amended bylaw adopted when the developer turned over control, and has strictly enforced it ever since. Even then, in a co-op of more than ten units under one roof, an owner whose unit has stayed unsold for four months at a break-even price may rent it, on the conditions in the law.

A co-op may still adopt reasonable rules, require a reasonable minimum lease term, and make tenants follow its rules on parking, pets, noise and occupancy. If it screens tenants, it must interview a prospective tenant within seven days after the tenant's name is submitted.

A condominium association may enter units at reasonable hours to repair common elements, and may charge you for common-element damage your tenant causes. A planned community's association may let tenants vote or join the association; a voting tenant votes in place of the owner, not in addition.

You remain the landlord: you file the landlord registration statement, and the Anti-Eviction Act and other tenant laws apply to your unit as to any other rental.

No New Jersey statute caps association lease-approval fees, lets an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind, or exempts owners who bought before a leasing restriction was adopted; check the governing documents. Have your tenant agree to follow the association's rules (see hoa-compliance).

title: Holdover Rates in New Jersey
bodyText:
New Jersey has no statute that caps, or expressly allows, a holdover rate you write into a lease (such as a percentage of the daily rent).

Instead, New Jersey statutes set the holdover measure themselves, in two cases. First, if a tenant gives you notice that the tenant will move out on a stated date and does not leave then, the tenant owes double the rent from that date for as long as the tenant stays (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-5). Second, if a tenant willfully stays after the lease term has ended and after you have made a written demand for possession, the tenant owes at the rate of double the yearly value of the property for the time the tenant keeps you out (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-6).

Most New Jersey rentals are covered by the Anti-Eviction Act. Covered premises exclude owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and hotels, motels and guest houses rented to transient or seasonal guests. For a covered tenant, the end of the lease term is not by itself a ground for removal or non-renewal (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3), so do not treat a covered tenant who stays after the term as a holdover owing a penalty rate unless you have good cause and have given the required notice.

The library does not offer a separate stipulated holdover rate for New Jersey. The Holdover clause carries the two statutory double-rent remedies in the cases where they apply. Don't add a second holdover charge on top of them. If you write a different figure into a lease anyway, a court could treat it as an unenforceable penalty, so the cautious course is not to use one.

title: Home-Based Businesses in New Jersey
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented dwelling, and none stops a lease from restricting business use. A lease may limit the home to residential use.

One related statute: registered family day care homes are a permitted use in all residential zoning districts, and a deed restriction against using a single-family dwelling as a family day care home is unenforceable unless it is necessary for the health, safety and welfare of the neighbors (N.J.S.A. 40:55D-66.5b). That statute speaks to zoning, deed restrictions and condominium or cooperative bylaws, not to leases.

Whether it limits a lease ban is a question only case law could settle. If a tenant asks to run a registered family day care home, the cautious course is to get legal advice before refusing. Your town's zoning ordinance may also regulate home occupations; check it.

For a tenant covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals, other than owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest house rentals), breaking a business-use restriction is a ground for removal only if the restriction is reasonable, was in the lease at the start of the term, the lease reserves a right of reentry for its breach, and the tenant keeps substantially breaking it after your written notice to cease (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(e)(1)). A house rule works the same way if it is reasonable and the tenant accepted it in writing or it was part of the lease at the start of the term (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(d)).

title: Incapacity and Early Termination in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey has no general rule that ends a tenancy, such as a month-to-month tenancy, when you or the tenant receive notice that a party has become incapable of contracting. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends only by the notice the law otherwise requires. New Jersey does give some tenants a statutory right to end a lease early because of illness, disability or a move into care (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.2). It applies to a lease for a term of one or more years of a home the tenant uses solely as a dwelling for the tenant or the tenant's family. The tenant, the spouse or a legal representative may end the lease by written notice, with the documents the statute lists, if: (a) the tenant or spouse suffers a disabling illness or accident, with a treating physician's certification that the person can no longer work, proof of lost income, and proof that pensions, insurance or other benefits are not enough to pay the rent; (b) the tenant or spouse, one of whom is 62 or older, is accepted into an assisted living facility, nursing home or continuing care retirement community, with a treating physician's certification of need and proof of acceptance; (c) the tenant or spouse, one of whom is 62 or older, is accepted into low- or moderate-income housing (and does not already live in such housing), with proof of the new lease or intent to lease; or (d) the home is not accessible to a household member with a disabling, likely permanent handicap, with a physician's certification and a statement that you were asked to make the unit accessible at your expense and were unable or unwilling to do so. The termination takes effect on the 40th day after you receive the notice. Rent is owed up to that day. The tenant must vacate and turn over possession at least five working days before that 40th day. See also the library's row on statutory early termination ("Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early"). The statute does not say whether a lease can take this right away. The cautious course is to treat it as one the lease cannot remove.

title: Inspection and Condemnation Orders in New Jersey
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about an outstanding housing inspection order, code violation notice or condemnation order before renting. What the law does control is renting a unit under such an order. In a hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units), if the state or local enforcing agency finds a violation that is an imminent hazard and orders that units be vacated or not occupied, you must not let anyone live in those units until the violation is corrected and the order is lifted (N.J.S.A. 55:13A-17; N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.13 and 5:10-26.2). The Uniform Fire Safety Act gives fire officials the same vacate-or-correct power for any building (N.J.S.A. 52:27D-208), and a municipal public officer can order an unfit building repaired or demolished (N.J.S.A. 40:48-2.5a). Separate disclosure duties apply on other topics, such as flood-zone notice and lead disclosures; see those rows. Hiding a known, serious defect from an applicant may also raise consumer-fraud issues (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). The cautious course is to disclose any outstanding order that affects the unit, and never to rent a unit that is under a vacate or no-occupancy order.

title: Inspection Notices and Deposit Penalties in New Jersey
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires a move-in or move-out inspection, or a notice telling the tenant about a right to one, so no statute sets a penalty for skipping an inspection or an inspection notice.

The penalties that do exist are in the Rent Security Deposit Act (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19 to -26). It applies to all dwelling rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, unless the tenant of such premises gives you 30 days' written notice invoking the Act.

If you fail to deposit or invest the security as required, or fail to give the written notice naming the bank or fund, account type, interest rate and amount (within 30 days of receiving the deposit, within 30 days of moving it, at each annual interest payment, and within 30 days after a sale), the tenant may give you written notice to apply the deposit, plus interest at 7% a year, to rent. After that you cannot demand a new deposit. For a missed annual interest payment or annual notice alone, the tenant must first give you written notice and 30 days to fix it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(c)).

If you do not return the deposit with an itemized list of deductions within 30 days after the lease ends, by personal delivery or registered or certified mail, a court that finds for the tenant must award double the amount owed plus costs, and may award attorney's fees (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).

In practice, the cost of skipping an inspection is proof: without a move-in record and photos you may not be able to show that damage happened during the tenancy.

title: Key Control in New Jersey
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a private landlord to adopt a key-control policy or to run background checks on employees who have access to tenants' units. Related rules you do have to follow: in a multiple dwelling (three or more units), the main entrance door lock must be operated by the tenant's key, and that key must not also open the tenant's own unit door; unit entrance doors need a dead-latching lockset or separate deadbolt, a chain door guard and a viewer (N.J.A.C. 5:10-19.2). If a state housing inspection is scheduled and a tenant has let you keep a key and gives you a key for the inspection, you must return it within 24 hours after the inspection (N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.10(e)). A court can order a lock change for a domestic-violence victim (see edu-dv rows and "Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early"). Criminal background checks are required by statute for employees of local public housing authorities (N.J.S.A. 40A:12A-22.1 ff.), not for private landlords' staff. Good practice: keep keys in a locked, logged system, rekey between tenants, and limit unit keys to staff who need them. If you screen employees, employment-screening laws apply; the Fair Chance in Housing Act covers screening of tenants, not staff.

title: Tenant Remedies for Landlord Breach in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey has no single statute listing a tenant's remedies when you breach the lease. Several statutes give remedies for particular breaches, and the courts supply the rest. Repairs and serious conditions: a tenant or the municipal public officer can ask a court to have rent paid to a court-appointed administrator and used for repairs where there is a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, or another substantial code violation or danger to life, health or safety (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-85 to -96; see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"). This does not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units. Retaliation: a tenant can sue for damages and injunctive relief if you serve a notice to quit, sue for possession, or substantially change the tenancy as a reprisal (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10; same owner-occupied exception; see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). Security deposit: double the amount wrongly kept, plus costs and possibly attorney's fees (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1; see "Security Deposit Rules"). Lockouts and self-help: see "Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal"; where a return to possession is inappropriate, the court awards treble damages (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-8). Unlawful lease terms: a tenant may petition a court to end a lease containing a term that violates clearly established tenant rights, and you face a penalty of up to $100 per offense (N.J.S.A. 46:8-47, -48). These two sections apply only to a Truth-in-Renting "landlord", which excludes premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, and transient or seasonal hotels, motels and guest houses (N.J.S.A. 46:8-44). Habitability: New Jersey courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability, and a statute mentions it (N.J.S.A. 52:27D-287.10(b)(11)). The remedies courts allow for it, such as rent abatement, repair-and-deduct or ending the lease, come from case law. The cautious course is to expect that a tenant facing a serious defect you haven't fixed after notice may raise it as a defense to a rent claim. What to do: answer repair requests in writing, fix health and safety problems first, and keep records.

title: Landlord Liens and Distraint in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey does not let you seize a residential tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. The old remedy of distraint (seizing and selling a tenant's goods for rent) still exists in statute, but "No distraint shall be permitted for money owed on a lease or other agreement for the occupation of any real property used solely as a residence of the tenant" (N.J.S.A. 2A:33-1). The distraint procedure in N.J.S.A. 2A:33-2 to -23 is therefore for non-residential leases only. Taking or locking up a tenant's property to force payment is also self-help, which New Jersey forbids (see "Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal"). Property a tenant leaves behind after the tenancy ends is handled under its own notice-and-storage rules (see "Property a Tenant Leaves Behind"). New Jersey does give you one statutory priority for rent. If another creditor of the tenant takes the tenant's goods from the leased premises by execution, attachment or other court process, that creditor must first pay you the rent due, up to one year's rent, before the goods are removed or sold. To claim it after the goods are removed, give the sheriff or officer written notice of the rent owed within 10 days after the removal (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-1 and -2). The statute does not limit this to non-residential leases. The library offers no lease clause granting you a lien or security interest in a residential tenant's goods. A clause letting you seize the goods would amount to the distraint the statute bars, and the cautious course is not to use one. To collect unpaid rent, sue for it and enforce any judgment through the courts. Personal property up to $1,000 in value, plus all clothing, is exempt from execution on a judgment (N.J.S.A. 2A:17-19).

title: Landlord Registration in New Jersey
bodyText:
New Jersey requires landlords to register each rental property. File a certificate of registration on the state form (N.J.S.A. 46:8-28): with the municipal clerk (or the official the clerk designates) for a one-unit rental or a two-unit premises you don't live in; or with the Department of Community Affairs, Bureau of Housing Inspection, for a multiple dwelling under the Hotel and Multiple Dwelling Law (three or more units), where you must also keep the validated certificate posted in the lobby or another conspicuous place, file an annual certification, and pay fees (N.J.S.A. 55:13A-12).

File when the first tenancy begins in a new or rebuilt building. File an amended certificate within 20 days after any listed information changes (N.J.S.A. 46:8-28.2).

The certificate lists the record owner, corporate agent and officers, an in-county agent for notices and service of process if the owner lives outside the county, the managing agent, the superintendent, a 24-hour emergency contact who has access to a current tenant list, every recorded mortgage holder, and the fuel-oil dealer if you supply oil heat.

Owners of tenant-occupied one- and two-family homes, including a two-family home where you live in one unit, must also file a certificate with the Bureau of Housing Inspection, with a fee (N.J.S.A. 46:8-28.5). An owner-occupied two-family home is exempt from this filing if it has been certified free of lead-based paint or as having a lead-free interior, was built in 1978 or later, or is a seasonal rental rented less than six months a year.

Scope: for the main registration act, "landlord" does not include owner-occupied two-unit premises (N.J.S.A. 46:8-27). Condominium, cooperative and similar unit owners who rent out their unit count as the landlord for filing.

Consequences: you cannot get a judgment for possession until you have registered. The court will postpone the case for up to 90 days and then dismiss it if you still have not complied (N.J.S.A. 46:8-33). The penalty is up to $500 per offense (N.J.S.A. 46:8-35). You must also give each tenant a copy of the certificate.

Two business filings can also apply. If you own through an out-of-state limited liability company, owning income-producing real property here is transacting business, so the company must obtain a certificate of authority, which names a New Jersey agent for service of process, and until it does it may not maintain any action, including an eviction (N.J.S.A. 42:2C-58, 42:2C-59(b), 42:2C-65(a)); an out-of-state corporation transacting business here needs a certificate of authority too (N.J.S.A. 14A:13-3(1), 14A:13-11(1)). And if you rent under a name other than your own real name, you must first file a trade-name certificate with the county clerk, with a duplicate for the Secretary of State, and doing business without one is a misdemeanor (N.J.S.A. 56:1-2, 56:1-4); a corporation registers an alternate name with the Secretary of State instead, and until it does it may not maintain an action arising from a lease made under that name (N.J.S.A. 14A:2-2.1(1), (6)).

Many towns also have their own rental registration, licensing or inspection ordinances, with separate fees. Check your town's ordinance.

title: Landlord Remedies After Default in New Jersey
bodyText: When a tenant defaults, New Jersey separates getting the unit back from collecting money. Possession: you recover possession only through a summary action for possession in the Special Civil Part (Landlord/Tenant). For most rentals you need a statutory good cause and the required notices (Anti-Eviction Act; see "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)" and "Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties"). The Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house rentals. A summary possession action cannot be joined with any other claim, and the tenant cannot counterclaim in it (R. 6:3-4(a)). So you do not get a money judgment for rent in the eviction case. In a nonpayment case, the tenant can stop the case by paying the rent claimed plus accrued costs to the court clerk on or before entry of final judgment (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-55). Money: sue separately for unpaid rent and damages, before or after the tenancy ends. Claims up to $5,000 between landlord and tenant for rent, security deposit or damages can go to the Small Claims Section. Claims up to $20,000 can go to the Special Civil Part. Larger claims go to the Law Division. If you file in a lower court, any amount over its limit is waived (R. 6:1-2). You can pursue both remedies. The security deposit cannot be applied to rent while the tenant stays in possession (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). No New Jersey statute sets a duty to re-rent (mitigate) after a tenant leaves early or governs rent acceleration. The cautious course is to make and document reasonable efforts to re-rent, and to claim only the rent lost while the unit stays empty despite those efforts. See "Default by Tenant" clause.

title: Police Cooperation and Crime-Free Terms in New Jersey
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum. None requires you or your tenants to cooperate with police investigations, or requires you, as a landlord, to give police tenant information or access to a unit; the general reporting duties below are the exception. No New Jersey statute bars a lease from penalizing a tenant for calling the police or emergency services. Duties that do apply: anyone, including a landlord, who has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused must report it immediately to the Division of Child Protection and Permanency (N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10); knowingly failing to report is a disorderly persons offense, or a fourth-degree crime if the abuse is sexual abuse (N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.14). Any member of the public who knows of a death from criminal violence, accident, suicide, or suspicious, unusual or unexplained circumstances, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately tell the local police the known facts, and willfully failing to report the death, or disturbing the body without the medical examiner's order, is a fourth-degree crime (N.J.S.A. 26:6B-10(a), (b)). Reporting suspected abuse of a vulnerable adult to county adult protective services is voluntary for a landlord, but no one may retaliate against a person who reports (N.J.S.A. 52:27D-409(a)(2), (d)). Criminal activity as a ground for removal is set by the Anti-Eviction Act, for example certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses, each with its own conditions and time limits (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(n)-(r); see "Criminal Activity" clause and "Good-Cause Eviction Rule"). Before applying a crime-free addendum, check that it does not go beyond those grounds. The Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house rentals. Domestic-violence victims have their own protections (see the edu-dv rows). The New Jersey Constitution protects people's houses against unreasonable searches (N.J. Const. art. I, ¶ 7). Whether you can consent to a police search of a tenant's unit is a question only case law could settle. Cautious course: let police into an occupied unit only with a warrant, the tenant's consent or a real emergency. Release tenant records only on a subpoena, warrant or other legal process, or with the tenant's consent. Never penalize a tenant for asking for police or emergency help.

title: New Jersey Lead Notices
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, New Jersey has three lead notice duties of its own.

1. Lead-safe certification. For a rental unit that must be inspected for lead-based paint hazards, give new tenants evidence of a valid lead-safe certification at tenant turnover and attach a copy to the lease as an exhibit (N.J.S.A. 52:27D-437.16(e)(2)).

Exempt units: certified free of lead-based paint; built in 1978 or later; in a multiple-family building registered with the Department of Community Affairs for at least 10 years with no outstanding lead-based paint violations from the last two cyclical inspections; or a one- or two-family seasonal rental rented less than six months a year to tenants without consecutive renewals.

2. Lead in drinking water. Before signing or renewing a lease, give the tenant a "Lead In Drinking Water Disclosure" statement (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-12.3c).

It is not required for a property built after 1986, a property whose service line the water system has determined is not lead, or a seasonal rental leased for fewer than six months a year. The duty begins 90 days after the state publishes its health notice and model statement. If you violate it and don't cure within 15 days after notice from the Department of Community Affairs, penalties are $100, $500, then $1,000 (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-12.9b).

3. Lead service lines. If a water system notifies you that your property has a lead service line: in an apartment building or other multi-unit dwelling, give every current resident a hard copy, post a copy in a common area until all lead lines are replaced, and tell each new resident before they move in and hand them a copy when they move in.

For any rental, the lease is conditioned on your not blocking the water system's replacement of the line; if you deny access, the tenant may end the lease without penalty (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-43(c)).

Tenants and other water users can ask the public water system for a free lead test (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-12.9a, as enacted by P.L.2025, c.144, s.4).

title: Initials and Signed Riders in New Jersey Leases
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease terms. Two statutes do require a separate rider that the tenant individually signs or otherwise acknowledges, in at least 12-point type, if you put the notice in a written lease instead of giving it separately: the flood-zone and flood-history notice, which you must give before the lease is signed or renewed (N.J.S.A. 46:8-50(a); see "Flood Risk Disclosure Rider" clause); and the Lead In Drinking Water Disclosure (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-12.3c(e); see "Lead in Drinking Water Disclosure" clause), where the landlord also signs or acknowledges the rider. The flood-notice rule uses its own definition of landlord. It excludes premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house rentals of less than 120 days, and seasonal rentals of less than 120 days (N.J.S.A. 46:8-50(a), (g)). Having the tenant initial other key terms is good practice, but no statute requires it.

title: Recording a Lease in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey does not require you to record or register a residential lease, and an unrecorded lease is valid between you and your tenant. A lease for life or for a term of at least two years, or a memorandum of such a lease, may be recorded with the county recording office (N.J.S.A. 46:26A-2(c)). Shorter leases are not on the list of recordable documents. Recording gives notice of the lease to later buyers, mortgage lenders and judgment creditors (N.J.S.A. 46:26A-12(a)). An unrecorded conveyance of an interest in real property has no effect against a later good-faith buyer or lender for value who had no notice and recorded first (N.J.S.A. 46:26A-12(c)). Whether that rule reaches an unrecorded lease, and whether a tenant's possession counts as notice, are questions only case law could settle. For most tenants it matters less, because the Anti-Eviction Act lets a new owner remove a tenant only for good cause (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3(b)), though a new owner not bound by the old lease may offer the tenant a different lease. That Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house rentals. If a long lease, option to purchase or below-market term must survive a sale or refinancing, record the lease or a memorandum of it. This is separate from landlord registration (see "Landlord Registration in New Jersey").

title: Long Leases and Signing Formalities in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey sets no maximum term for a private residential lease, and requires no seal, notarization or special form for a long lease. A lease of real estate for more than three years is enforceable only if the premises, the term and the identity of landlord and tenant are set out in a writing signed by or for the party it is enforced against, or are proved by clear and convincing evidence (N.J.S.A. 25:1-12). The general writing rule for conveyances does not apply to leases (N.J.S.A. 25:1-11(c)). Put any lease longer than three years in writing, signed by every owner. Married owners: a spouse is entitled to joint possession of real property the couple occupies as their principal matrimonial residence. Anyone who takes an interest from the other spouse, including a tenant, takes it subject to that right unless the spouse has released, subordinated or extinguished it in writing, or a court has ended it (N.J.S.A. 3B:28-3). If you rent out a home a married couple lives in as their principal residence, such as a room or part of it, have both spouses sign the lease. A lease for life or for a term of at least two years may be recorded (see "Recording a Lease in New Jersey").

title: Month-to-Month Versus Fixed-Term Terms in New Jersey
bodyText: No New Jersey statute bars you from charging a month-to-month tenant more rent, or imposing different terms, than a tenant on a fixed term (or the reverse). No statute caps the rent difference between lease types. Limits that do apply: for tenants covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, you may remove a tenant at the end of a lease for refusing new terms only if the changes are reasonable changes of substance and the tenant was given written notice. For tenants with protected status after a condominium or cooperative conversion, you must also prove the changes do not substantially reduce the tenant's rights (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(i)). A tenant who fails to pay a rent increase can be removed only if the increase is not unconscionable and complies with any rent-control ordinance (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(f); see "Local Rent Control and Registration"). The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house rentals. Those tenancies end by notice to quit: one month for month-to-month, three months for year-to-year or at-will, and one term for other terms (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-56). Practical point: a large month-to-month premium aimed at pushing a covered tenant out could be challenged as unconscionable or retaliatory (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). Keep any difference tied to a real cost or risk.

title: Type Size in New Jersey Leases
bodyText: No New Jersey statute sets a minimum type size for a whole printed lease, and no statute makes a lease in small type inadmissible or unenforceable for that reason alone. Specific type-size rules do apply to particular parts of a residential lease: if the lease lets you recover attorney's fees from the tenant, it must contain the statutory reciprocal-fee sentence in bold, in a font at least one point larger than the rest of that clause or 11 points, whichever is larger (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.67; see "Default by Tenant" clause); a flood-zone notice placed in the lease must be a separate rider, individually signed or acknowledged by the tenant, in at least 12-point type (N.J.S.A. 46:8-50(a)); and a Lead In Drinking Water Disclosure placed in the lease must be a separate rider, signed or acknowledged by tenant and landlord, in at least 12-point type (N.J.S.A. 58:12A-12.3c(e)). Under the Plain Language Act, which covers residential leases, one of the guidelines a court or the Attorney General may consider is whether conditions and exceptions to the main promise get equal prominence and are in at least 10-point type (N.J.S.A. 56:12-10(b)(3)). A lessor whose lease fails the Act is liable for the tenant's actual damages if the violation substantially confused the tenant about the lease, plus up to $50 punitive damages and attorney's fees and costs up to $2,500 (N.J.S.A. 56:12-3; see "Plain Language Rules for New Jersey Leases"). Practical rule: print the whole lease in at least 10-point type, and print the riders listed above in at least 12-point type.

title: Deadlines to Sue for Rent in New Jersey
bodyText: Most suits for unpaid rent or other lease money must be filed within six years after the claim arises. That six-year period covers contract claims, express or implied, not under seal, and also claims for trespass or tortious injury to real or personal property, such as property damage (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-1). A suit for rent founded on a lease under seal has 16 years, and a payment on that lease starts a new 16-year period. That rule does not apply when the suit on a sealed instrument is brought by a merchant or a bank, finance company or other financial institution; they have six years (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-4). Few modern leases are under seal, and whether yours counts is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course is to plan on six years. Personal-injury claims, such as a tenant's injury claim against you, must be filed within two years (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-2). For a simple contract, a spoken acknowledgment or promise to pay does not extend the deadline. It must be in a writing signed by the person to be charged. One co-tenant's written acknowledgment does not bind the others. A payment of principal or interest keeps its usual effect (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-24). Whether a part payment restarts the six-year period is not stated in these sections; that is case law. Track each unpaid month separately: each installment of rent starts its own period when it falls due.

title: Shifting Maintenance to Tenants in New Jersey
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute lets a lease shift a landlord's repair or maintenance duties to the tenant, sets what consideration such a shift needs, or requires a separate agreement for it.

In a hotel or multiple dwelling (three or more units), the state maintenance regulations say no lease, contract or agreement relieves the owner, managing agent or superintendent of the owner's duties. Tenants have their own duties, which a lease also cannot remove (N.J.A.C. 5:10-4.1(a), (b)).

So a lease can add tenant duties, such as keeping the unit clean or changing furnace filters, but you stay responsible to the code enforcer.

One exception runs the other way: if a tenant agrees in the lease to supply heat through a furnace or boiler that also heats other units, the tenant is responsible for that heat in the same way as the owner (N.J.A.C. 5:10-5.6(a)). Shifting heating fuel cost to a tenant has its own limits.

Any lease term waiving a tenant's right to the rent-receivership remedy for serious code violations is void (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-96). That remedy does not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units.

For one- and two-family rentals, the state regulations do not apply; local property-maintenance codes may.

Whether a lease can make a tenant responsible for conditions that affect habitability is case law. The cautious course is to keep structural, system and safety repairs with you, and to shift only routine upkeep, such as lawn care, snow removal or small repairs, stated specifically in the lease.

title: Utility Meter Charges in New Jersey
bodyText: No New Jersey statute creates an energy-efficiency "meter conservation charge" on a rental's utility bill, requires you to tell new tenants about one, or regulates submetering of water or electricity to tenants. The related statute covers heat in multiple dwellings (three or more units). If you charge each unit a share of the building's heating costs by any method other than separate meters approved by the Board of Public Utilities ("indirect apportionment"), the method and any device must first be certified by the Commissioner of Community Affairs (N.J.S.A. 55:13A-7.8 to -7.11). Certification requires that: the method be reliable and accurate; it be inspected and maintained on schedule; it distribute costs fairly based on actual use; each unit have its own thermostat; each bill state the building's actual fuel or current cost for the period and the unit's share; and no cost other than fuel or current be apportioned. Failing to maintain the system or to fix a malfunction promptly is a code violation. Shifting heating fuel cost to a tenant has other limits too (see "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)"). Reselling or submetering utilities may also fall under Board of Public Utilities rules. Check them before billing tenants for metered water, gas or electricity.

title: No Meth-Lab Disclosure Statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a tenant that a rental was once used to make methamphetamine, to report a suspected drug lab, to have a former lab tested or cleaned before renting, or to keep anyone out of a contaminated unit. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'methamphetamine', 'decontaminate' and 'production facility' found only criminal and drug-control laws. One of them matters to you: anyone who knowingly maintains or operates premises used to manufacture methamphetamine (or certain other drugs) commits a first-degree crime. The cautious course: if you know or suspect a unit was used as a drug lab, have it professionally assessed and cleaned before you rent it, and do not hide what you know. Concealing a known hazard can raise consumer-fraud and habitability problems (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). Removing a tenant for drug offenses on the premises is covered in "Criminal Activity" clause.

title: No Military or Air-Zone Lease Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a tenant that a rental is near a military base or airfield, or in a military noise zone or accident potential zone, and none gives a tenant a right to end a lease for that reason. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'military installation', 'accident potential' and military noise terms found no landlord or lease duty. Two related laws reach sales, not leases. A person who sells or transfers property in a delineated airport safety zone (under the Air Safety and Zoning Act of 1983) must tell the buyer before the contract of sale is signed. Sellers of newly built homes must give buyers a notice about lists of off-site conditions, which include airport safety zones; that act excludes units built solely for lease. The statute does not say whether a lease counts as a 'transfer'. The cautious course: if you know the property is in an airport safety zone shown on the municipal tax map, tell the applicant in writing before the lease is signed.

title: Unpaid Water and Sewer Charges Are a Lien
bodyText: In New Jersey, unpaid public water and sewer charges become a lien on the property itself, even if your tenant used the service and the lease makes the tenant pay. Charges of a municipal or county water or sewer utility are a first lien on the property served. Unpaid service charges of a sewerage authority or a municipal utilities authority are a lien on the parcel that ranks ahead of any owner, lessee, tenant or mortgagee, except municipal taxes. For a water commission, the owner is liable for water used by the occupier, and the charge is a lien on the building. These liens are enforced like property-tax liens, and the utility can shut off service after written notice to the owner of record. No New Jersey statute lets you avoid the lien by filing an affidavit, by putting the account in the tenant's name, or by a lease clause. What you can do: keep the account in your name and bill the tenant under the lease, or check the utility's balance regularly if the tenant pays it directly. A lease term making the tenant pay is a contract claim against the tenant only; it does not stop the lien. Private (investor-owned) water companies are regulated by the Board of Public Utilities.

title: Out-of-County Owner Must Name a Local Agent
bodyText: New Jersey ties the out-of-area owner's agent to landlord registration, not to the lease text. If any record owner's address is not in the county where the rental is, the registration certificate you file must name a person who lives in that county and is authorized to accept notices from tenants, issue receipts for them, and accept service of process for the owner. This applies to an owner who lives out of state and also to one who lives in New Jersey but in another county. You file the certificate with the municipal clerk for a one-unit rental or a two-unit building you do not live in, or with the Department of Community Affairs for a multiple dwelling, and you give each tenant a copy when the tenancy begins (see "Landlord Registration Statement" clause). Until you comply, a court will not enter a judgment for possession; it can continue the case up to 90 days and then dismiss it. Owner-occupied two-unit premises are not covered. If you own through an out-of-state limited liability company, owning income-producing real property here is transacting business, so the company must obtain a certificate of authority naming a New Jersey agent for service of process; until it does, it may not maintain any action, including an eviction, and it is treated as having appointed the State filing office as its agent for service in suits arising from its New Jersey business (N.J.S.A. 42:2C-58, 42:2C-59(b), 42:2C-65(a), (d)). An out-of-state corporation transacting business here faces the same bar on suing until it obtains a certificate of authority (N.J.S.A. 14A:13-11(1)). If you rent under a trade name and live outside New Jersey, the trade-name certificate you file with the county clerk must appoint the county clerk as your attorney to accept service of process in suits arising from that business (N.J.S.A. 56:1-2). No New Jersey statute requires a tenant to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner.

title: No Rule on Move-Out Forms; Notice to Quit Content
bodyText: No New Jersey statute governs a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, requires a warning when such a form adds terms the lease does not contain, or bars work that makes the unit hard to live in while a notice to quit is running. Keep any move-out form to the move-out date and a forwarding address. A term added in a notice or form is not part of the lease unless the tenant actually agrees to it, and it cannot take away a right New Jersey law gives the tenant, such as the security deposit rights. Your own notice to quit has content rules. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient hotels), the notice must specify in detail the cause of termination, give the notice period for that ground, and be served personally, by leaving a copy with a household member over 14, or by certified mail (with regular mail if the certified letter is not claimed). For tenancies outside that act, the notice to quit runs one month for month-to-month, three months for year-to-year or at will, and one term for other terms. See "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)".

title: Nuisance: Eviction Ground and Owner Exposure
bodyText: New Jersey deals with nuisances through the eviction law, the criminal code and local ordinances. Eviction: for tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel guests), one good cause is that the tenant, after written notice to cease, has continued to be so disorderly as to destroy the peace and quiet of other occupants or the neighborhood. You must give that written notice to cease first, and then a notice to quit at least three days before you file. Other grounds cover drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses on the premises (see "Criminal Activity" clause and "Good-Cause Eviction Rule"). Criminal and civil exposure: a person who knowingly maintains premises where people gather to engage in unlawful conduct, or who creates a condition endangering a considerable number of people, commits the disorderly persons offense of maintaining a nuisance. If the owner of the building is convicted, the court may close the building for up to one year. For a house of prostitution or obscenity premises, the Attorney General or county prosecutor may also sue to close the place; an owner who did not know of the use can get the property released by agreeing to take whatever steps are needed to stop it. Review your town's ordinance, which may fine owners for repeated tenant conduct. Act promptly in writing when you learn of nuisance conduct.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a tenant, before the lease is signed, about a former military ordnance site nearby, a planned demolition, or a gas or electric meter that also serves areas outside the tenant's unit. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'ordnance', 'munitions', 'demolition permit' and shared, master or separate metering found no landlord disclosure. Demolition is handled at the eviction stage instead. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient hotels), you may remove a tenant to permanently board up or demolish only if housing inspectors have cited you for substantial health and safety violations and it is economically unfeasible to correct them, after three months' notice; retiring a building from residential use takes 18 months' notice and must wait for any lease to expire. See "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)". If you already plan to demolish or retire the building, the cautious course is to say so in writing before the tenant signs. If the tenant pays for a meter that also serves common areas or other units, say so in the lease and how you will adjust the charge.

title: Elevators, Garages and Shared Facilities
bodyText: No New Jersey statute puts a special duty on a residential landlord for a garage door opener, laundry room, clubhouse, gym or similar facility, or says when you may close one. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'garage door' and 'amenities' found no such rule. In buildings of three or more units (multiple dwellings under the state maintenance rules), some facility rules do apply. Elevators must be kept in good working order and free of hazards, with a current certificate of compliance. Elevator service may be suspended only when unavoidable or for servicing or repairs, for the minimum time needed; if you know in advance, you must post a notice telling occupants the time, how long and why. Each self-service elevator needs a mirror so people can see inside before entering. Garages used by occupants after dark, and parking areas and walkways used at night, must be lit. No lease term relieves you of these maintenance duties. For one- and two-unit rentals, check local property-maintenance codes. If you offer shared facilities, list them in the lease and say whether access is included in rent and when they may be closed for repair.

title: Owner Move-In: Statute Controls, Not the Lease
bodyText: A lease clause cannot give you an owner move-in right in New Jersey; the eviction statute decides it. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (all residential rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient or seasonal hotel guests, plus two narrow family-trust and family-member exceptions), owner move-in is good cause only in these cases (plus the condominium-conversion sale case described below): (1) you own a building of three residential units or less and seek to personally occupy a unit, or have contracted to sell a unit to a buyer who wants to personally occupy it and the contract calls for it to be vacant at closing; or (2) you own three or fewer condominium or cooperative units, the tenant's initial tenancy began by rental from an owner of three or fewer units after the master deed or cooperative agreement was recorded, and you seek to personally occupy the unit or have contracted to sell it to a buyer who will personally occupy it under a contract calling for vacancy at closing. You must give two months' written notice stating the cause in detail, and where a written lease is in effect you cannot file until the lease expires. So you cannot end a fixed term early to move in, and an owner of a building with four or more units (other than the condominium cases, including a sale of a unit to an owner-occupant buyer in a building constructed as or being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, where the tenancy began after the master deed, cooperative agreement or subdivision plat was recorded and the tenant received the statement required by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.9) has no owner move-in ground at all. A lease term letting you end or not renew the tenancy for any other reason is unenforceable. If the tenant leaves after your notice and you or the buyer arbitrarily fail to personally occupy the unit for at least six months, and instead rent it to someone else or register a conversion, the owner is liable for three times the tenant's damages plus attorney fees and costs. Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units are outside the act; that tenancy ends at the end of its term or by notice to quit (one month for month-to-month, three months for year-to-year). See "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)".

title: Parking Rules: Make Them Part of the Lease
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, prescribes a heading or type size for them, limits mid-term changes to them, or limits the vehicle information you may ask for.

Two rules still shape how you handle parking rules. First, for tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient hotels), a tenant can be evicted for continuing, after written notice to cease, to substantially break your rules only if the rules are reasonable and were accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the beginning of the term.

So attach your parking rules to the lease, or have the tenant sign them. A rule adopted mid-term is not an eviction ground unless the tenant accepts it in writing.

Second, towing a tenant's or guest's car without consent requires a towing contract, posted entrance signs and your authorization of each tow, except at a single-family home or an owner-occupied building of six or fewer units.

title: No Statutory Pesticide Notice to Tenants
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to give tenants notice before a pesticide is applied in a rental unit or common area, or to hand over a pest-control company's notice with the lease. No New Jersey statute uses 'pesticide' near tenant, landlord, resident, apartment or multiple dwelling; the state's pesticide notice-and-posting law covers schools only. Pesticide use is regulated by the Department of Environmental Protection's Pesticide Control Regulations (N.J.A.C. 7:30), which may set notice or posting duties for applications at residential buildings. Check those rules, or ask your licensed applicator, before relying on this row. The cautious course: use a licensed pest-control applicator, give tenants written notice before any treatment inside a unit or in shared areas (what will be applied, where and when, and any preparation or time to stay out), and post the notice in common areas. Your duty to control pests in buildings of three or more units is in "Heat, Pests and Other Owner Duties (Buildings of 3+ Units)"; tenant cooperation with treatment is in "Bed Bugs and Other Pests" clause.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or other notice about caring for pets if the tenant is evicted or loses the home. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'fact sheet' and for pets, dogs, cats and domesticated animals near tenant, lessee or eviction terms found none. One related rule applies after a tenant leaves: when you store property a tenant left behind after an eviction or surrender, you must allow an animal control agency or humane society to remove any abandoned pets or livestock (see "Property a Tenant Leaves Behind"). The cautious course: if you learn a pet has been left in a vacated unit, call animal control or a humane society right away.

title: No Political Access Statute; Organizing Protected
bodyText: No New Jersey statute gives political candidates, campaign workers or canvassers a right to enter an apartment building, and none sets rules for political signs or literature in rental housing. A search of every New Jersey statute for canvassing, candidates, campaign or election signs, and flags near tenant, apartment or landlord terms found none. One statute does protect tenants' civic and organizing activity: in all rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, you may not serve a notice to quit, sue for possession, or substantially change the tenancy (including refusing to renew without cause) as a reprisal for a tenant organizing, joining or taking part in any lawful organization.
