A notice to quit or such a change after that activity is presumed to be a reprisal, and the tenant can sue for damages (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). New Jersey's courts have also applied the state constitution's free-speech clause to some private property; that is case law, not covered here. The cautious course: apply any rule on signs, flyers or solicitation in common areas evenly to all causes and groups, put it in your written rules, and do not single out political or tenant-organizing activity.

title: Pool Fences, Electrical Certificates and Health Rules
bodyText: New Jersey pool rules for rental property come from three sources. (1) Fence: in a building of three or more units (a multiple dwelling under the state maintenance rules), any outdoor swimming pool, decorative pool or pond holding 24 inches or more of water must be enclosed by a fence, wall or building at least four feet high, without outside handholds or footholds, made of material toddlers cannot get through, with a self-closing, self-latching gate (latch no more than six inches below the top) and hardware for permanent locking. No overhead electrical wires may be within 15 feet of a pool, and metal fences or railings near it must be grounded. (2) Electrical certificates: a pool, hot tub or spa on any property other than a one- or two-family home may not be opened until it has a valid bonding and grounding certificate (good for five years) and an electrical certificate of compliance, renewed by annual inspection and, for a seasonal pool, before each season opens. Post both in or about the pump house. (3) Health rules: pools open to residents may be public recreational bathing facilities under the Department of Health's rules (N.J.A.C. 8:26), with health-authority inspections and lifeguard and first-aid requirements. A statutory exemption from the lifeguard rules covers hotels, motels, mobile home parks, campgrounds, retirement communities and nonprofit common interest communities that limit the pool to residents and guests; ordinary apartment complexes are not on that list. Ask your local health department about those Health Department rules before opening a pool. For a single-family or two-family rental, check your local construction and property-maintenance codes. If you allow tenants to use a pool, put the pool rules in the lease or signed rules.

title: No Portable Cooling Device Statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute gives a tenant the right to install a window or portable air conditioner, requires you to provide cooling, or limits what a lease may say about cooling devices. A search of every New Jersey statute for air conditioning, cooling devices and window or portable units near tenant, landlord or rental terms found only definitions and health-facility rules. So a lease may allow, condition or forbid window and portable units. If you allow them, a written rule helps: require safe installation that does not damage the window or frame, a unit that does not overload the circuit, no unit in a window needed as a fire exit or fitted with a required child window guard, and repair of any damage the tenant causes. If you supply air conditioning, say so in the lease and maintain it. A building's own code rules (fire egress, window guards in multiple dwellings, local ordinances) still apply.

title: Tenant Right to Plug-In Balcony Solar (2027)
bodyText:
Starting March 1, 2027, a New Jersey landlord may not prohibit a tenant who pays for the electric service used in the unit from using a portable solar generation device, or placing one, within the tenant's leased premises, including any leased balcony or patio.

A portable solar generation device is a moveable plug-in solar device of no more than 1,200 watts that connects through a standard 120-volt outlet, sits on the customer's side of the meter, is listed or certified to UL 3700 or a comparable plug-in solar safety standard, and cannot send power to the grid during an outage. The combined output of all such devices in one dwelling unit may not exceed 1,200 watts unless an interconnection agreement is obtained.

The tenant must give you written notice at least 14 days before placing or using a device, with documentation that it meets those requirements and its proposed location. You may respond with reasonable restrictions on its physical dimensions, placement or manner of placement. You may prohibit or restrict placement anywhere else on your property, such as roofs or common areas, and may impose any restrictions needed to make the device comply with its product listing, the State Uniform Construction Code and the National Electrical Code.

The tenant is responsible for damage to the leased premises caused by the device. You are not liable for failing to maintain a habitable dwelling or provide an essential service because of a condition caused solely by the device. You may require the tenant to indemnify you for injury or property damage caused by negligent installation, maintenance or use of the device by the tenant, an occupant, or the tenant's contractor or agent.

If you pay for the unit's electricity, this right does not apply. The utility cannot require its approval or charge a fee, and a town cannot require a permit. Until March 1, 2027, no statute requires you to allow these devices.

title: Small-Landlord Exemptions Turn on the Building
bodyText: New Jersey's small-landlord exemptions turn on the building or premises being rented, and usually on whether you live there, not on how many units you own in total. The main thresholds: (1) Anti-Eviction Act (good cause to evict or refuse renewal), reprisal law and rent receivership: do not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units. (2) Security deposit law: covers every rental except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, and even those are covered once the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking it. (3) Truth-in-Renting Act: does not cover rental premises of not more than two units, or owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, or transient hotels. (4) Landlord registration: does not cover owner-occupied two-unit premises. (5) Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-history screening): does not cover owner-occupied premises of not more than four units. (6) Application fee cap: does not cover a unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling. (7) Law Against Discrimination: does not cover renting one unit of a two-family home whose other unit the owner lives in, or rooms in a one-family home the owner or occupant lives in (except publicly assisted housing). (8) Multiple dwelling maintenance rules: apply to buildings of three or more units (and certain groups of ten or more two-unit buildings). (9) Towing rules: do not cover a single-family home or an owner-occupied building of six or fewer units. (10) Owner move-in eviction: available only to the owner of a building of three residential units or less, or of three or fewer condominium or cooperative units; separately, in a building of any size constructed as or being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, an owner who has contracted to sell a unit to a buyer who will live in it may evict a tenant whose initial tenancy began after the master deed, cooperative agreement or subdivision plat was recorded, if the tenant was given the statement required by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.9. Read each exemption's words exactly: 'owner-occupied' is a separate condition from the unit count, so a three-unit building you do not live in is covered by every law in items 1, 2, 4 and 5. The one count of units owned is the condominium owner-move-in ground. Check each row's scope note before relying on an exemption.

title: No Possession Bond or Confessed Judgment
bodyText: New Jersey has no statutory bond by which a tenant agrees in advance to deliver possession at the end of the term and lets the landlord take a confessed judgment for possession. A search of every New Jersey statute for 'confess' and for bonds near tenant, lessee or delivery of possession found none for leases. Do not put a confession-of-judgment or similar clause in a lease. New Jersey law says no judgment by confession may be entered on a warrant of attorney included in the body of a bond, note or any instrument for the payment of money. A lease that obliges the tenant to pay rent is likely such an instrument, though only case law could settle that. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act (most rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units and transient hotels), a lease term by which the tenant waives rights under that act is unenforceable. To recover possession you file a summary dispossess action in the Special Civil Part (see "Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties"); a tenant who holds over can owe you for the holdover period (see "Holdover" clause).

title: No Written-Promise Rule; Promises Can Be Fraud
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. A search of every New Jersey statute for promise terms near tenant, landlord or lease found none. Your promises still matter. New Jersey's Consumer Fraud Act covers the rental of real estate: a false promise or misrepresentation made in connection with renting, or in your later performance, is an unlawful practice whether or not anyone was actually misled (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases"). The cautious course: put every promised repair or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum, with a description and a completion date, make no oral promises you do not intend to keep, and tell the tenant in writing promptly if a promised item will be late and why. Your ongoing repair duties in buildings of three or more units cannot be cut down by the lease (see "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived").

title: No Proposition 65-Style Warning
bodyText: New Jersey has no law like California's Proposition 65 requiring a landlord to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and no statute requiring a formaldehyde or similar chemical warning in a lease. A search of every New Jersey statute for carcinogens, reproductive toxicity and formaldehyde near tenant, landlord, rental or dwelling terms found only environmental and workplace right-to-know definitions, and a search for 'warning' near tenant or lessee found no lease warning duty. Specific hazard rules still apply and are covered in their own rows: lead-based paint (federal disclosure and New Jersey's lead-safe certification), lead in drinking water, flood risk, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Do not hide a known hazard: concealing a material fact when renting can violate the Consumer Fraud Act (see "Consumer Fraud Act and Leases").

title: Property Tax Rebates to Tenants (5+ Units)
bodyText: New Jersey does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes. It does require you to share property tax decreases with tenants in larger buildings, under the Tenants' Property Tax Rebate Act. Scope: a building or complex in which five or more housing units are rented or offered for rent, whether or not you live there, except transient hotels, buildings under a tax abatement agreement, buildings in towns whose rent control ordinance gives no automatic increase when property taxes rise, cooperatives, most condominium units, continuing care retirement communities, and assisted living and similar care facilities. How it works: when your property taxes for the current year are lower than in the base year (1998, or a later year set by the statute, such as a year taxes rose above the base or the first year the property was rented), the municipal tax collector computes the reduction and notifies you. You remove the share attributable to nonresidential rents and to units you or your employees occupy, and divide the rest among residential tenants in proportion to rent. You pay each tenant one-twelfth of the annual amount each month, as a rent credit or a direct payment, with the first payment cumulative (covering the year's months through the month after you receive the collector's notice) and the last by December 31 (or, if the notice arrives after November 1, in monthly payments through the next June 30, with no cumulative first payment needed). Only tenants in residence during the year are paid, for the months they lived there; use best efforts to find the forwarding address of a tenant who moved. Within 30 days after the collector's notice, file a form certifying the rebate with the rent leveling board (or the tax collector if there is none), and post in a prominent place in the building a notice listing the yearly and monthly rebate for each rent category. A tenant you fail to pay can recover twice the rebate or $100, whichever is greater, and you face a penalty of up to $100 per offense.

title: No Protected-Class Questions or Records
bodyText: New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination makes it unlawful for you, your agents, employees or broker to use a rental application form, or to make any record or inquiry about a prospective rental, that expresses directly or indirectly any limitation, specification or discrimination as to race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, pregnancy or breastfeeding, sex, gender identity or expression, affectional or sexual orientation, familial status, disability, military service or liability for service, nationality, or source of lawful income used for rent. The same rule covers ads, statements, notices and signs. An ad, form, record or inquiry that appears to be yours is presumed to have been authorized by you. Keep application forms and screening questions free of these subjects. A narrow exception lets you state a single-sex qualification for housing planned for and occupied only by one sex, with people qualified by gender identity or expression. The Law Against Discrimination does not apply to renting one unit of a two-family house when you live in the other unit, or to renting rooms in a one-family house you live in, unless the housing is publicly assisted. Federal fair housing law separately bars discriminatory ads and statements even for some owners New Jersey exempts, so the cautious course is to keep every ad and form neutral. If you own or manage 25 or more dwelling units in New Jersey under one management or common ownership, whether at one location or spread across several (including scattered single-family homes), the Division on Civil Rights' reporting rule requires an annual demographic report. For it, you must give leaseholders the Division's Tenant/Applicant Inquiry document with the signed lease and each renewal offer (or yearly if the term is one year or less), and give it to each applicant once the application process is complete. You may not ask applicants for that information before their application process is complete, may not require anyone to fill it in, and may not take adverse action, including raising rent, based on what tenants report. Criminal-history questions are limited separately by the Fair Chance in Housing Act (see the screening rules row).

title: Lease Void if Used for Prostitution
bodyText: A New Jersey statute makes a lease void at once if the tenant uses the dwelling or other premises for prostitution or assignation. The statute says you may then enter and use the same remedies to recover possession as against a tenant holding over after the lease ends. Separately, a person who knowingly keeps premises as a house of prostitution, or where people gather to engage in unlawful conduct, commits the crime or offense of maintaining a nuisance; after a conviction the court may order the place closed for up to one year, and the Attorney General or county prosecutor may sue to abate a house of prostitution. For most residential tenancies, the Anti-Eviction Act says a tenant may be removed only on one of its listed grounds. It does not list prostitution as such, but it covers disorderly conduct after written notice to cease, breach of reasonable lease covenants after notice, drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses. Whether the older void-lease statute lets you skip those grounds is a question only case law can settle. The cautious course is to treat it as no substitute for the Anti-Eviction Act: give the notices that Act requires and file in court. Never lock out or remove a tenant yourself. The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, transient or seasonal hotel and guest-house rentals, or certain family-trust units. No other New Jersey statute found voids a residential lease for other unlawful uses.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Possession Covenant
bodyText: No New Jersey statute writes a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into residential leases. The only statutory quiet-possession covenant is for deeds: when a grantor's deed says the grantee shall have quiet possession, the statute spells out what those words mean. It does not reach leases. Any quiet-enjoyment right a tenant has comes from the lease itself or from case law. New Jersey statutes do protect a residential tenant's possession in other ways. You may not enter and take possession of a dwelling without the tenant's consent except through a court eviction; doing so is a disorderly persons offense. The Anti-Eviction Act limits removal to its listed grounds for most tenancies. See the self-help eviction and Anti-Eviction Act rows.

title: No State Recycling-Notice Duty
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell tenants where and how to recycle. The state recycling law puts that notice duty on the municipality: at least once every six months, it must notify residents of local recycling opportunities and of its source-separation ordinance. Each municipality must have an ordinance requiring people who generate solid waste to separate listed recyclables, so your tenants and your building must follow the local rules. If the municipality collects trash from, or reimburses, a multifamily dwelling, the property must meet the same recycling requirements as other homes in town. If it does not, the municipality may stop collection or cut reimbursement, but only after sending you written notice of noncompliance and 30 days' written notice of a proposed reduction, during which you may come into compliance. New multifamily developments of three or more units that need site plan or subdivision approval must include recycling collection or storage space under the local ordinance. Check your municipal recycling ordinance, which may set its own duties for owners.

title: No Religious-Display Statute for Rentals
bodyText: No New Jersey statute gives tenants a specific right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, and none bars landlords from regulating them as such. The Law Against Discrimination still applies to rules about displays. You may not discriminate because of creed, national origin, ancestry or other protected traits in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the facilities and services you provide. A rule that bans or singles out religious items, or is enforced against one faith or culture only, risks a discrimination claim. Write any rule on door, hallway or window decorations in neutral terms, tie it to a real purpose such as fire safety or maintenance, and enforce it the same way for everyone. A separate statute stops homeowners' and condominium associations from banning the U.S. flag or signs supporting U.S. troops; it governs associations, not landlords.

title: When Rent Can't Be Demanded or Enforced
bodyText: No New Jersey statute bars you, across the board, from demanding or collecting rent just because a unit has code violations. But several statutes limit rent or its enforcement in specific situations. First, a municipality may adopt an ordinance under the substandard multiple dwelling law (buildings with 3 or more apartments or tenant households). If its public officer finds your building substandard after notice and a hearing, and you do not make the ordered repairs within the time set, rent control is imposed. It then becomes unlawful to demand or receive more than the maximum rent set, or to demand possession or evict a tenant for refusing to pay more than that maximum. Existing leases are not impaired until their term ends. Second, where there is a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, or another substantial housing-code or safety violation, a tenant or the municipal officer can ask a court to order rent paid into court and used for repairs (see the rent receivership row). Third, if you have not filed and given tenants the landlord registration statement, a court will not enter judgment for possession until you comply; it continues the case for up to 90 days and then dismisses it. Whether a tenant may withhold or reduce rent on habitability grounds outside these statutes is a matter of case law. The cautious course is to fix cited conditions promptly and keep your registration current.

title: How to Raise the Rent
bodyText:
New Jersey has no single statute setting a fixed number of days' notice before a rent increase. For most residential tenancies, the Anti-Eviction Act controls how an increase is made and enforced.

You may remove a tenant who fails to pay an increased rent only if you gave a valid notice to quit and a notice of the increase, the increase is not unconscionable, and it complies with every other law and municipal ordinance on rent increases.

The Act does not say how much notice a valid notice to quit needs; the cautious course is the general notice-to-quit periods (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-56): one month's notice for a month-to-month tenancy, three months' notice for a year-to-year tenancy or tenancy at will, and one term's notice for other terms. So give written notice of the new rent at least that far ahead of the date it starts, and time it for the end of a rental period.

During a fixed-term lease you cannot raise the rent unless the lease itself provides for it (see the scheduled rent changes clause). At the end of a lease, you may also propose reasonable changes to the lease terms, including rent, with one month's written notice; refusal of reasonable changes is a ground for removal.

Many New Jersey municipalities have rent control ordinances that cap increases and add their own notice and registration rules; check the local ordinance first (see the local rent control row).

A large increase soon after a tenant complains or asserts rights is presumed retaliatory. When the Governor issues a Notice of Rent Protection Emergency during a declared state of emergency, an increase above twice the rate of inflation in the affected zone is presumed unreasonable.

The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, transient or seasonal hotel and guest-house rentals, or certain family-trust units; for those, the increase takes effect only by ending the tenancy with the same notice to quit periods. Manufactured home park sites have their own annual cap under a separate law.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: No New Jersey statute creates a rent-reporting program, requires you to offer positive rent reporting, or requires a notice before you report late rent to a credit bureau. Federal credit reporting law governs anyone who furnishes data to a consumer reporting agency. One New Jersey rule remains in force. For rent that accrued during the COVID-19 covered period, March 1, 2020 through August 31, 2021, you may not at any time furnish information about nonpayment or late payment of residential rent, a missed rent increase, or related eviction filings, to another residential landlord or to a debt collection or credit reporting agency. You also may not refuse to rent to someone, or put a tenant on a list for other landlords, because of that record. This does not apply to payments missed before March 1, 2020, and does not stop you from sharing information with your own attorney or property manager or from giving notices the Anti-Eviction Act requires. The Attorney General or the tenant may sue; after a chance to correct a first violation, a court may order retraction, fines of up to $500, $1,000 and then $2,500 per violation, counsel fees and damages.

title: Sales and Occupancy Tax on Rent
bodyText: New Jersey sales tax does not reach ordinary residential leases. It applies to rent for occupancy of a room in a hotel or a "transient accommodation", and not to a permanent resident: anyone who occupies the room for at least 90 consecutive days is a permanent resident for that period. A transient accommodation is a room, group of rooms or other living space, including a house or apartment, that is booked through a transient space marketplace (an online booking platform or travel agency) or is a "professionally managed unit": a self-contained rental unit owned or controlled by someone who offers two or more other units for rent during the calendar year. Leases of real property for a term of at least 90 consecutive days are expressly not transient accommodations, nor is a private home rented with no hotel-type services where the keys are handed over at a licensed real estate broker's office. Where the tax applies, a state hotel and transient accommodation occupancy fee is added, and the municipality may impose its own occupancy tax of up to 3 percent. If you rent furnished units for short stays, register and collect these taxes; if you rent only under leases of 90 days or more, they do not apply.

title: State Inspections of Multiple Dwellings
bodyText: If your building is a multiple dwelling under the Hotel and Multiple Dwelling Law (generally three or more units occupied by people living independently, or a group of ten or more two-unit buildings under common ownership on one parcel), the state Bureau of Housing Inspection inspects it on a tiered cycle of two, five or seven years depending on how quickly past violations were fixed. You must apply for a certificate of inspection, pay the inspection fee within 30 days of the inspection, and post the certificate in a conspicuous place. When the Bureau tells you an inspection is scheduled, you must notify each occupant of the time and ask each one either to admit the inspector or to authorize you to do so. An occupant who was notified, lets you keep a key, and has not objected in writing is treated as consenting. An occupant who consents but cannot be present must, on notice, give you a key, which you must return within 24 hours after the inspection. You must help the inspector reach all areas and, on request, accompany the inspector through common areas and units where the occupant is absent. Inspecting a private dwelling unit still requires the occupant's consent, except in an emergency or under a search warrant; a lease clause cannot remove the tenant's right to object in writing. If the inspection finds a potentially hazardous violation that you do not fix by the deadline, you must hand each resident the state's notice and post it in the lobby and on each floor, may not lease the affected unit until a certificate of inspection issues, and must notify residents again once it is fixed. Many municipalities also require inspections or certificates of occupancy when a unit changes tenants; check the local ordinance.

title: Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute stops you from requiring renter's insurance, limits the carrier the tenant may choose, sets rules for force-placed coverage, or requires a statement that you will not insure the tenant's belongings.

If your lease requires renter's insurance, say so in the lease (see the tenant's property and renter's insurance clause), and do not charge any fee for it that the lease and New Jersey's fee rules do not allow.

Two statutes do apply. First, every residential lease must contain the state's flood insurance notice, which tells tenants that a standard renter's policy does not typically cover flood damage (see the renter flood insurance notice clause).

Second, if you own a building or complex with 10 or more units occupied by people living independently, you must give each new tenant, no more than 30 days after the tenant moves in, information about crime insurance through the Federal Crime Insurance Program and where to apply, and you may not do anything that makes a tenant ineligible for that coverage; the penalty is up to $200 per offense.

The federal program named in that statute may no longer be offered; the cautious course is still to give the notice, stating where tenants can get information about crime and theft coverage.

title: Ending a Tenancy When Repairs Are Unfeasible
bodyText: New Jersey has no statute that lets you end a lease simply because repairs would cost more than a set amount. For tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, the closest ground is narrow. You may seek removal only if local or state housing inspectors have cited you for substantial violations affecting tenants' health and safety and it is economically unfeasible to eliminate them, so you will permanently board up or demolish the premises; or if you must remove the tenant to comply with the inspectors' citation; or to correct an illegal occupancy you were cited for. You must give three months' written notice specifying the cause in detail. If you rely on the need to comply with a citation, you must notify the Department of Community Affairs when you serve the notice, and the Department may tell the court whether you can comply without removing the tenant. No warrant for possession issues until state relocation assistance laws are met. For an illegal-occupancy removal, you owe the tenant relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent, payable five days before removal, under the municipal ordinance or, if there is none, directly by statute; unpaid amounts carry 18 percent interest and become a lien. If you board up or demolish and then allow residential use within five years, you are liable to the former tenant for three times the damages plus attorney fees. Permanently retiring a building from residential use is a separate ground needing 18 months' notice and, if a lease is in effect, waiting until it expires. Fire and other casualty damage is covered in the casualty row. The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, transient or seasonal hotel and guest-house rentals, or certain family-trust units.

title: No Opt-Out Notice for Rent Receivership
bodyText: New Jersey has no notice you can give to opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The rent receivership law, which lets a tenant or municipal officer ask a court to have rent paid into court and used for repairs, applies to all rental dwellings except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units. That exception applies automatically; no notice is required or available to create it. Any lease term waiving the law's protections for tenants is void. The only exemption notice in this area concerns rent control: owners of newly built multiple dwellings that are exempt from local rent control must tell prospective tenants in writing, before signing, that the building is exempt and for how long (see the rent control exemption notice clause).

title: Repair Requests and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: You may ask tenants in the lease to report needed repairs promptly and in writing; the shared maintenance clause does so. But that lease term cannot narrow the tenant's statutory remedies, which turn on whether the problem was brought to your attention, not on the form of the notice. Before a tenant can ask a court to have rent paid into court for repairs, the tenant must show that the condition was brought to the attention of you or the manager you designated and that you did not act within a reasonable time. The statute does not require written notice, and any lease term waiving the rent receivership law's protections is void. Similarly, the anti-reprisal law protects a tenant's good-faith complaint to a government agency about a health or safety violation once the tenant has first brought it to your or your agent's attention and given you a reasonable time to correct it. Treat any repair report, whether by phone, text, email, in person or through a portal, as notice. Log the date and your response. Your defenses in a rent-into-court case include that the condition did not exist or has been fixed, that the tenant caused it maliciously or by abnormal use, or that a tenant refused you entry to fix it. The rent receivership law does not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units; the anti-reprisal law has the same exception.

title: New Jersey Lease-Time Disclosures Checklist
bodyText:
New Jersey has no single disclosure statute or state form that must be the first page of every lease, and no statewide notice of whether a unit is covered by a just-cause or rent-increase law. Instead, separate laws require separate disclosures, several of them with their own exemptions. Before or at signing, check each:
- (1) the state Truth in Renting statement, given to each new tenant at or before move-in and kept posted, for landlords other than those with two or fewer units, owner-occupied premises of three or fewer units, or transient and seasonal hotels (Truth in Renting statement clause)
- (2) a copy of your landlord registration certificate at the start of each new tenancy, unless the premises are an owner-occupied two-unit building (landlord registration clause)
- (3) the flood risk rider and the flood insurance notice (flood clauses)
- (4) the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, and the lead-safe certification where required (lead clauses)
- (5) the Lead In Drinking Water Disclosure for properties built before 1986 not cleared of lead service lines, once the state model statement is published (lead in drinking water clause)
- (6) the window guard notice for multiple dwellings (window guard clause)
- (7) the rent control exemption statement for exempt newly built multiple dwellings (rent control exemption clause)
- (8) the condominium or cooperative conversion statement where it applies (conversion statement clause)
- (9) steam radiator cover, private well test results and management website or social services hotline notices where they apply (those clauses)
- (10) within 30 days after you receive a security deposit, written notice of the bank, account type, interest rate and amount (security deposit rows).

If you own 25 or more units under one management, give the Division on Civil Rights Tenant/Applicant Inquiry document with the signed lease and each renewal offer (protected-class inquiry row). If you own a building or complex of 10 or more units, give new tenants crime insurance information within 30 days of move-in (renter's insurance rules row).

If you give the tenant an option to buy, note that a seller of New Jersey real property must disclose flood-zone status and known flood risks on the property condition disclosure statement before the purchaser becomes obligated under a contract to buy. A tenant holding an option is arguably not obligated until it exercises the option, but the statute does not say; the cautious course is to give the completed statement when you grant the option.

title: State Tenant Rights Guide and Posters
bodyText: New Jersey's state rights guide is the Truth in Renting statement, a summary of the main legal rights and responsibilities of tenants and landlords that the Department of Community Affairs publishes in English and Spanish and updates annually. You must give a copy of the current statement to each new tenant at or before move-in, give every tenant a copy within 30 days after the Department makes a new statement available, and keep a copy posted where it is prominent and accessible to all tenants. No signed acknowledgment is required, but getting one is good proof of delivery (the Truth in Renting statement clause does this). The penalty is up to $100 per offense. This duty applies to landlords renting for terms of at least one month, but not to dwelling units in premises of two or fewer units, owner-occupied premises of three or fewer units, or transient and seasonal hotels, motels and guest houses. Separately, the Law Against Discrimination makes it unlawful to refuse to post or display the civil rights notices the Attorney General requires by regulation. The Division on Civil Rights' guidance says housing providers must display its official housing poster where actual and prospective tenants can easily see it and give residents a copy every year and on request, with fines up to $10,000 for failing to display it.

title: Making Building Rules Enforceable
bodyText:
Under the Anti-Eviction Act, you may seek removal of a tenant for breaking your rules only if the tenant keeps substantially violating them after written notice to cease, and only if the rules are reasonable and were either accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the beginning of the lease term. You must then give one month's written notice, specifying the cause in detail, before filing.

So attach your rules to the lease, or have the tenant sign them, at signing. A rule you adopt mid-term that the tenant has not accepted in writing is not a ground for removal. You can add new rules at renewal: at the end of a lease you may propose reasonable changes to its terms, with one month's written notice, and a tenant's refusal to accept reasonable changes is itself a ground for removal.

Do not change rules or other terms in reprisal for a tenant's complaint, lawful request or tenant-organization activity; a substantial change without cause after such activity is presumed retaliatory.

The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, transient or seasonal hotel and guest-house rentals, or certain family-trust units; the anti-reprisal law excludes owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell a New Jersey rental, assign your lease, or change managers, several duties follow. Security deposits: when you convey the property or assign your lease, turn each deposit plus the tenant's share of interest over to the buyer or assignee at delivery of the deed or assignment or within five days after, and notify each tenant by registered or certified mail of the transfer and the new holder's name and address. Doing so releases you from liability for that deposit. The buyer must obtain the deposits from you, and is responsible for investing them, paying interest, giving the required notices and returning them whether or not you actually turned them over. Within 30 days after the transfer, the holder must give each tenant written notice of the bank, account type, interest rate and deposit amount. These deposit rules do not apply to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units unless the tenant has invoked them by 30 days' written notice. Registration: within 20 days after any change in the information on your landlord registration certificate, including a new owner, a new managing agent, superintendent or emergency contact, file an amended certificate (a fee applies only when ownership changes), and give each tenant a copy within seven days after filing it with the municipality, or after receiving the validated certificate from the Department of Community Affairs for a multiple dwelling. Registration does not apply to owner-occupied two-unit premises. Tenants: a buyer or other successor may remove a tenant of premises covered by the Anti-Eviction Act only for good cause, except where federal law controls or a public agency removes occupants under eminent domain or code enforcement with relocation assistance. If you have served notice to board up, demolish or retire the building from residential use, you must tell the buyer in writing before signing the contract; failing to do so carries a civil penalty of $2,500 to $10,000 and treble damages. For a lender's foreclosure, see the foreclosure row.

title: Code Exceptions and Variances
bodyText:
If the Commissioner of Community Affairs grants you, as owner of a multiple dwelling (generally three or more units), an exception to a state housing regulation that affects occupants' safety, you must give every applicant and occupant of the affected units a written notice citing the regulation and stating the exception granted, attached to the lease of each affected unit; for an exception covering common areas, attach it to every lease in the building.

Exceptions are granted only on a written application showing undue hardship and that the exception won't unreasonably endanger occupants.

Fire safety variances under the Uniform Fire Safety Act follow a similar hardship test, are decided within 30 days and are kept open for public inspection, but that statute adds no tenant notice.

Local zoning and land use variances, the state sanitary code and the fire code (N.J.A.C. 5:70) are outside this library; check them and your municipal code.

title: Seasonal rentals in New Jersey
bodyText:
New Jersey has no single seasonal-lease statute, but several laws treat a seasonal rental differently. Most of them define "seasonal" as a residential term of not more than 125 consecutive days by a person who has a permanent residence elsewhere. That definition does not cover housing for seasonal, temporary or migrant farm workers. You have the burden of proving the rental is seasonal.

Eviction: The Anti-Eviction Act's good-cause rules do not apply to a hotel, motel or other guest house, or part of one, rented to a transient guest or seasonal tenant (or to owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units). The exception is worded for hotels, motels and guest houses; it does not say that every seasonal house or apartment rental is outside the Act. Unless your rental clearly fits the exception, treat the tenant as covered by the good-cause rules.

Fast removal for disorder or damage: For a furnished unit rented for seasonal use in premises of five or fewer units, if you win possession because the tenant habitually disturbed the peace after written notice to cease or willfully or by gross negligence damaged the premises, the court must issue the warrant for removal within 2 days of judgment. It can be stayed only with your consent.

Security deposit: For a seasonal rental you do not have to put the deposit in an interest-bearing account or money market fund. The other security-deposit rules (the deposit stays the tenant's money held in trust, the 1.5-month cap, the 30-day return with an itemized list) are not excluded by that provision and still apply, except in owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, where the deposit law applies only if the tenant gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26).

Private well water: If the unit's drinking water comes from a private well, for a seasonal rental you must either post the most recent test results in a readily visible place inside the unit or give the new tenant a written copy.

Other exemptions: Seasonal rentals of less than 120 days are exempt from the flood-zone notice; the Safe Housing Act (domestic-violence lease termination) does not apply to seasonal leases; and the window-guard requirement does not apply to seasonal rental units (125 days or less). The Truth-in-Renting Act's definition of landlord excludes hotels, motels and guest houses serving transient or seasonal guests.

title: Required locks and door security
bodyText:
Multiple dwellings (generally buildings with three or more units, and groups of ten or more two-unit buildings under common ownership): the state Hotel and Multiple Dwelling regulations require you to provide and keep these security features:
- Each unit entrance door must have a medium-duty dead-latching lockset or a separate dead bolt lock.
- Each unit entrance door must have a chain door guard that allows partial opening, and the main unit entrance door must have a viewing device (peephole) that lets the occupant see a person just outside.
- Building entrance doors serving two or more units must have heavy-duty dead-latching locksets. The tenant's key must open the main entrance lock, but that key must not also open the tenant's unit door.
- Exterior doors leading to interior common areas must be self-closing and self-locking and kept closed. The main entrance must have a doorman, a buzzer and latch-release system (only with an intercom), individual door bells, or another approved entry system. Buildings with fewer than six units may use one common-area bell audible in every unit.
- Exterior doors to common basement, cellar or storage areas must be self-closing and lockable.
- All exit doors must open freely from the inside at all times.
- Every openable window or sliding door that gives easy access (basement windows, windows onto fire escapes, porches, balconies and similar) must have a locking device. Grilles lockable only from inside may not be put on windows that provide access to exits.
- Exposed hinges on building and unit entrance doors must use non-removable pins or be altered so the door cannot be lifted off.
Hotels have similar unit-door lock, viewer-or-chain and window-lock rules.

One- and two-family rentals: no New Jersey statute, and nothing in the State Housing Code (N.J.A.C. 5:28, which towns adopt by ordinance), sets a lock or peephole standard. Check your municipality's housing code.

No New Jersey statute requires you to rekey or change locks between tenants. The one statutory lock-change duty is a court order in a domestic-violence restraining order: you must change the locks within 48 hours of the victim's written request or the victim may do it (see the domestic-violence rows).

title: No work-card rule for senior housing staff
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires the staff of senior (55 and older) rental housing to hold a work card or pass a fingerprint or criminal background check. The background-check statutes cover licensed health care settings such as assisted living, not ordinary apartments for older residents. If you screen employees who hold keys, follow your own written policy and the employment and consumer-report laws that apply to you.

If you operate housing for older persons, New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination lets you turn away families with children only if the housing qualifies: housing under a qualifying state or federal elderly program; housing intended for and solely occupied by persons 62 or older; or housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit, with significant facilities and services for older persons (or a showing that the housing is needed), at least 80 percent of units occupied by at least one person 55 or older, and published policies showing that intent.

title: Penalties for refusing a service or guide dog
bodyText:
A tenant or applicant with a disability who has a service or guide dog, or keeps a retired one as a pet, is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations. You may not charge extra for the dog, and a no-pet lease clause does not apply to it. The tenant is liable for damage the dog does. (The lease wording is in the service and assistance animal clause.)

If you refuse the dog, two penalty laws can apply:
- New Jersey's service and guide dog law sets a fine of $100 to $500 for a violation of that law that is not otherwise prohibited by the Law Against Discrimination, and for anyone who intentionally interferes with the rights of a person with a disability accompanied by a guide or service dog, or with the dog's ability to work.
- Refusing housing because of a disability is also a violation of the Law Against Discrimination. In a Division on Civil Rights case or certain court cases, each violation can carry a penalty of up to $10,000, up to $25,000 with one prior violation in five years, and up to $50,000 with two or more in seven years, on top of other relief.

The statute does not say whether the $100 to $500 fine is criminal or civil. Do not refuse a service or guide dog because of a no-pet rule, size, breed or a pet fee.

title: Fake guide dog penalty
bodyText:
New Jersey's only statute on misrepresenting an assistance animal is narrow. It fines anyone $100 to $500 who fits a dog with a harness of the type commonly used by blind persons to represent that the dog is a guide dog when the dog has not had guide-dog training. The statute is not limited to particular places, so it can apply in housing, but it covers only that act. No New Jersey statute penalizes falsely claiming a service dog, emotional support animal or other assistance animal in any other way.

The fine is enforced by the state, not by you. Don't accuse a tenant of fraud or deny a request just because you doubt an animal. Where the disability or the need for the animal is not obvious, you may ask for reliable documentation as allowed by law (see the service and assistance animal clause).

title: Servicemember tenants in New Jersey
bodyText:
New Jersey's Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act protects tenants in "military service": active federal military service, and active duty in the state's military service under an order of the Governor (for example, National Guard on state active duty). Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) also applies and may give more protection.

Lease termination: If a tenant signed the lease and then entered military service, and the tenant or the tenant's dependents occupy the home, the tenant may end the lease by written notice to you or your agent at any time after service begins. Notice may be mailed. For a lease with monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following the notice. For other leases, it takes effect on the last day of the month after the month of notice; you must prorate unpaid rent and refund rent paid in advance for the period after termination. Once terminated, the tenant and any co-signer owe nothing more except for damage to the property, and you may not charge any early-termination penalty or fee. A court may modify the relief if you apply before the termination date. Knowingly holding the tenant's belongings or blocking their removal to collect rent for the period after termination is a disorderly persons offense (up to 6 months and $1,000).

Eviction: You may not evict the spouse, children or dependents of a person in military service from a home rented for $150 a month or less except with leave of court, and the court may stay the case up to 3 months. Federal law sets its own, higher rent ceiling. In any case where the tenant is in military service, the court may stay the case during service and for 60 days after.

Default judgments: Before a default judgment you must file an affidavit stating whether the tenant is in military service. Knowingly filing a false affidavit is perjury.

Discrimination: You may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, someone because of service or liability for service in the U.S. Armed Forces.

title: Sex offender registry and disclosure
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to tell tenants or applicants about registered sex offenders nearby or to put a registry notice in the lease. The registry law says no action may be brought against any person for failing to investigate or disclose information from the State Police Internet sex offender registry.

Be careful with the registry itself. Information from it may be used for lawful purposes consistent with public safety, but, except as another law authorizes, it may not be used to apply for, obtain or deny housing. Using registry information to commit an offense is itself a crime or disorderly persons offense. The Fair Chance in Housing Act is the law that does authorize one housing use: in buildings it covers, you may consider whether an applicant is subject to a lifetime registration requirement under a state sex offender registration program. The Act does not apply to owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units.

title: No state offender residency rule
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute bars a registered sex offender from living within a set distance of a school, child care center or park, limits how many registered offenders may live in one dwelling, or makes it an offense for a landlord to rent to one. Parole or court supervision conditions may limit where a particular person lives, but those bind the offender, not you. Some towns have adopted their own residency ordinances; check your municipality, and get legal advice before relying on one.

If you screen applicants, follow the Fair Chance in Housing Act (you may consider a lifetime registration requirement) and do not use registry information to deny housing except as that Act allows. See the sex offender registry row.

title: No first-page occupancy notice rule
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires a single-family lease to carry a notice on its first page, in a larger font, about whether the lease must be notarized or signed by a licensed manager to show lawful occupancy. New Jersey has no statutory presumption that an occupant is unlawful because the lease was not notarized or lacked the landlord's contact details.

New Jersey does set type-size or boldface rules for some specific lease notices, and those rows carry the wording: the flood risk rider (separate, signed rider in at least 12-point type), the attorney-fee reciprocity sentence (bold, at least 11 points and one point larger than the clause), and, in multiple dwellings, the window guard notice and the social services hotline notice (prominent boldface).

title: No shoreline access disclosure rule
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to tell a tenant about public access to the beach or shoreline, or to put a shoreline notice in the lease.

If you rent waterfront property, know the background rules. State law declares that the public has rights under the public trust doctrine to use tidal waters and the adjacent shorelines for navigation, fishing, bathing and other recreation. The Department of Environmental Protection may require public access as a condition of a waterfront permit. If public access has been required on your property as a condition of a DEP approval or by agreement with DEP, you and your tenant (as owner, lessee or occupant) are liable to people using that access only in limited cases, such as willful or malicious failure to guard or warn against a danger. Don't write lease rules that tell tenants to block or interfere with public access the property is required to provide.

title: No shutdown rent protection
bodyText: No New Jersey statute gives federal or state government workers extra time to pay rent, or delays eviction, during a government shutdown or furlough. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due when the lease says, and any late fee must follow New Jersey's late-fee rules. If you agree to a payment plan with a furloughed tenant, put it in writing. Tenants who are in military service have separate protections (see the servicemember row), and some court-ordered hardship stays may be available in an eviction case.

title: No state single-family zone rental limit
bodyText: No New Jersey statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone, or requires the owner to live on the lot before renting it out. No New Jersey statute requires an owner to live in an accessory dwelling unit or the main house before renting either one. Zoning is set by each municipality under the state's land use law, and many towns have their own rules on rental permits, certificates of occupancy, occupancy limits, short-term rentals and accessory apartments. Check your town's ordinances before you rent a single-family home or a unit on the same lot.

title: No smart lock statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute specifically regulates smart locks, keypads, key fobs or app-based entry systems in residential rentals. You may use them, but the general rules still apply. In a multiple dwelling, unit and building entrance doors must still meet the state lock standards (dead-latching lockset or dead bolt, chain guard and viewer; building entry systems with a buzzer release only if there is an intercom). Your entry into the unit is governed by your lease and New Jersey's entry rules whether you use a key or an app. If a court orders a lock change for a domestic-violence victim, change the code or credentials as well as any physical lock. If your system collects tenants' personal or biometric data, check New Jersey's consumer data privacy law and federal law before using it.

title: No late-benefit eviction defense
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires the court to postpone or dismiss a nonpayment eviction because a tenant's Social Security, other government benefit, or housing voucher payment arrived late. Related rules do apply:
- Grace period: if rent is due on the 1st and the tenant is a senior receiving Social Security old-age, Railroad Retirement or another government pension in place of Social Security, or receives Social Security Disability, SSI or Work First New Jersey benefits, you must allow five business days before charging any late fee.
- Paying to stop the case: in a nonpayment case, if the tenant pays the court clerk the rent claimed plus accrued court costs at any time on or before final judgment, the case must stop.
- Assistance notice: the warrant for possession must tell the tenant they may be eligible for temporary housing assistance and how to contact the county welfare agency.
The COVID-19 eviction limits for rent that accrued during the pandemic's covered period are not a general late-benefit defense.

title: Source of income discrimination
No special district lease statement
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a lease to state that the property is in a special improvement district, redevelopment area or other special taxing district, or that the tenant knows about district assessments. Those assessments are charged to the property owner. If you want the tenant to pay any part of a district charge, the lease must say so clearly as a stated amount or method, and it must not be labelled additional rent (see the fees-as-rent row). Many municipalities have special improvement districts set by ordinance; check yours if you are asked about them.

title: No sprinkler disclosure statute
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to tell tenants in the lease, or anywhere else, whether the building or unit has an automatic fire sprinkler system. Sprinkler installation and maintenance are set by the State Uniform Construction Code and the State Fire Prevention Code, which apply to the building whether or not you disclose. Some newly built townhouses must have sprinklers. If the building has a sprinkler system, consider telling tenants not to hang items from sprinkler heads or block them.

title: When a lease must be in writing
bodyText:
In New Jersey, a lease for more than three years is not enforceable unless either (a) the premises, the term and the identity of the landlord and tenant are set out in a writing signed by or for the party against whom it is being enforced, or (b) those same facts are proved by clear and convincing evidence. A lease of three years or less can be oral, although a written lease is always the better practice and some notices must be given in writing.

A promise by a guarantor or co-signer to pay someone else's rent is enforceable only if it is in a writing signed by the guarantor or the guarantor's agent.

An unwritten interest in real estate is not effective against a later good-faith buyer for value, or a lienholder, who had no notice of it. A tenant in possession may give notice, but keep every lease in writing and signed.

title: New Jersey money limits at a glance
bodyText:
New Jersey sets these money limits for residential rentals, whatever the lease says. Each has its own row with details and exceptions.
- Security deposit: no more than 1.5 months' rent. Any added security collected in a year may not exceed 10 percent of the current deposit. A deposit wrongfully kept can cost you double the amount. (The deposit law does not apply to owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units unless the tenant invokes it by 30 days' written notice.)
- Application fee: since May 1, 2026, no more than $50, adjusted each January from 2027 for inflation; the cap does not apply to a unit in a one- or two-family dwelling or to a real estate licensee who is not the landlord.
- Late fees: no general statutory cap or grace period. If rent is due on the 1st and the tenant is a senior on Social Security or a similar pension, or receives SSDI, SSI or Work First New Jersey, no late fee until after five business days. After a warrant for removal is posted or a lockout for nonpayment, a tenant who pays all rent due within three business days cannot be charged a late fee above the amount in the warrant application.
- Bounced checks and failed electronic transfers: no cap on a lease returned-payment fee is set by statute. If you sue after a 35-day certified-mail demand, you may recover the amount plus fees, costs and damages of $100 or triple the amount, whichever is greater, but not more than $500 above the amount.
- Holdover: double rent if the tenant gave notice to quit and stays; double the yearly value for a willful holdover after the term and a written demand.
- Window guards (multiple dwellings): you may pass on to the requesting tenant no more than $20 per window guard installed.
- Rent increases: no statewide cap, but an unconscionable increase cannot support an eviction, and local rent control ordinances may set limits.

title: No stigmatized property statute
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute addresses "stigmatized" or "psychologically impacted" property. No statute says whether you must, or need not, tell a tenant that a death, murder or suicide occurred in the unit, or that a prior occupant had HIV or another illness. There is also no statute protecting you from liability for staying silent about these facts.

Two rules still matter:
- The Consumer Fraud Act covers rentals and makes a misrepresentation, or a knowing concealment or omission of a material fact with intent that the tenant rely on it, unlawful. Whether a particular event is a material fact is not settled by statute. Answer a tenant's direct question truthfully, and do not make misleading statements.
- Under the Law Against Discrimination, AIDS and HIV infection are disabilities. Never refuse to rent, or comment on a prior or current occupant's diagnosis, because of HIV or AIDS.

title: Stove and refrigerator rules
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to supply a stove or refrigerator in every rental. The state rules work this way:

Multiple dwellings (generally three or more units): no cooking is allowed in a unit unless it has at least a kitchen sink with hot and cold water, ventilation that removes cooking odors to the outside, food storage free from infestation, refrigeration in good working order that keeps food above 32 and below 50 degrees Fahrenheit, a safely connected electric or gas cooking facility, storage for dishes and utensils, and two electrical outlets. Gasoline stoves and portable kerosene or similar portable fuel-burning cooking appliances are prohibited. Microwave ovens may be used in rooming units. As owner you are responsible at all times for safe maintenance of the building and its facilities, and required equipment must be kept in good working order. If you store an old refrigerator on the premises, remove its doors first.

One- and two-family homes: the State Housing Code, which towns adopt by ordinance, requires a kitchen sink but does not require a stove or refrigerator. Where that code applies, you may not shut off a service or facility it requires except temporarily during actual repairs or in an emergency the Public Officer authorizes, and if a service or utility you agreed to supply is discontinued you must take immediate steps to restore it. Check your municipal code.

Say in the lease which appliances you provide and who repairs them.

title: Renting to students in New Jersey
bodyText:
New Jersey has no separate landlord-tenant code for students. A student who rents from you is a tenant like any other. The Anti-Eviction Act's good-cause rules, the security-deposit rules and the other tenant protections apply unless one of their general exceptions applies (for example, owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units). Being a student, or the school year ending, is not by itself a ground for eviction; use a fixed-term lease and follow the good-cause and notice rules.

Rooming and boarding houses: the state licensing law for rooming and boarding houses does not cover a dormitory owned or operated by a nonprofit school for its students, or a single-room-occupancy building occupied only by full-time students at an approved college. A building of shared rooms that serves a mix of students and others may need a rooming or boarding house license.

Safety exceptions: if the state has granted the owner of a multiple dwelling or school dormitory an exception from a Hotel and Multiple Dwelling safety regulation, written notice citing the regulation and the exception must be attached to the lease (or the dormitory housing agreement) of each affected unit, and to all leases if the exception covers common areas.

If you rent to minors or to students with co-signers, get each guarantee in a signed writing.

title: Voucher inspections and refusals
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute lets you turn down a voucher holder because the housing program will inspect the unit, and no statute creates a special or faster eviction when a subsidized tenant refuses to let a program inspector in.

The rule that governs runs the other way. Under the Law Against Discrimination you may not refuse to rent because of the source of lawful income a tenant will use, including by refusing to accept a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance as payment. The Division on Civil Rights' guidance says a landlord cannot justify refusing a voucher holder by saying they do not want to deal with the paperwork or the program's inspection. These rules do not cover renting one unit of an owner-occupied two-family house or rooms in an owner-occupied one-family home, unless the housing is publicly assisted.

If a tenant refuses access you are entitled to under the lease, the ordinary rules apply. In housing covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, a substantial breach of a reasonable lease covenant can be good cause only after written notice to cease, where the lease reserves a right of reentry and the covenant was in the lease from the start.

title: No State Rule on Subsidy Abatement for Unfit Units
bodyText: No New Jersey statute sets what happens to a housing subsidy (such as a Section 8 voucher payment) when the unit fails an inspection or is unfit, or says how the rent is split between you and the tenant while repairs are pending. For voucher units that comes from the federal program rules and your contract with the housing authority, not state law: follow the housing authority's inspection notice and deadlines and keep repair records. Do not try to collect a withheld subsidy payment from the tenant without checking the program rules and your contract first. New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination bars treating a tenant differently in the terms or conditions of a rental because of the source of lawful income used for rent, which includes Section 8 vouchers and other rental assistance (this does not apply to renting one unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit, or rooms in a one-family home you live in, unless the housing is publicly assisted). For any tenant, subsidized or not, state law lets the tenant or the municipality ask a court to have rent paid into court and used for repairs when the unit has serious defects; see the row on rent deposited with the court for repairs.

title: Late Fees When Rental Assistance Pays Rent
bodyText:
Rental assistance payments: If you accept State or federal rental assistance on a tenant's behalf for rent that is due and owing, state law makes it a condition of taking that money that you waive all late fees charged for the rent unpaid during the period the assistance covers. The law was passed with New Jersey's COVID-19 tenant protections, but this sentence is not limited to the COVID period by its words. The cautious course is to waive those late fees whenever such assistance pays past-due rent.

The tenant's own share: Charge a late fee only on the part of the rent the tenant owes, never on a late payment from a housing authority or assistance program. The Law Against Discrimination bars treating a tenant differently in the terms or conditions of a rental because of the source of lawful income used for rent, including Section 8 vouchers and other rental assistance. It does not apply to renting one unit of a two-family house where you live in the other, or rooms in a one-family home you live in, unless the housing is publicly assisted.

Grace period: If rent is due on the 1st and the tenant is a senior on a Social Security or similar government pension, or receives Social Security Disability, SSI or Work First New Jersey benefits, no late charge may cover the first five business days (see "Senior and Benefit-Recipient Grace Period").

Payments in an eviction case: When a tenant has three business days to pay after a warrant for removal is posted or a lockout is executed in a nonpayment case, you must accept payment made through a federal, State or local rental assistance program or a bona fide charity, and cooperate with a program that has committed to pay the rent due.

Federal voucher rules (the HUD tenancy addendum) may limit charges further.

title: Court-Appointed Receivers for Neglected Buildings
bodyText:
New Jersey's Multifamily Housing Preservation and Receivership Act lets a court take a neglected residential building out of your hands. It covers buildings at least half residential by floor space. It does not cover a one- to four-unit building where the owner lives in one unit as a principal residence.

Who can sue: any tenant, a group chosen by more than half the tenants, a mortgage or lien holder, the municipal public officer, a local nonprofit, or a qualified entity registered with the Department of Community Affairs.

When a building qualifies: (1) code violations endanger tenants' health and safety and have gone unfixed for at least 90 days before the complaint; or (2) a clear pattern of repeat violations, such as citations at least four separate times in 12 months or six times in two years, and you did not make timely, proper repairs. The complaint must show you got notice of the conditions and did not act in time. The court hears it in a summary (fast) proceeding.

Your defenses and options: For a repeat-violation complaint, the court may dismiss if you prove the repairs were timely and of proper quality and the building is adequately maintained, or if the violations were mostly minor. It may dismiss a tenant's complaint if that tenant is in default of a material obligation. You may offer a written plan to fix the conditions by set dates; the court may accept it, require a bond, and order receivership if you miss the dates.

If a receiver is appointed: the receiver takes possession, collects rents, makes repairs, may borrow against the building (in some cases ahead of existing mortgages), signs leases of up to one year, may evict for cause, and after more than a year may ask the court to sell the building. You stay liable for taxes, liens, mortgages and your earlier expenses. You can petition to get the building back by paying the receivership's costs and taxes, taking on its debts, and usually posting a bond of up to 50% of market value that is forfeited for a later serious code violation.

This is separate from a tenant's or municipality's action to have rent paid into court for repairs (see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"). Keep code violations fixed promptly and keep proof of every repair.

title: Property Tax Increases and Tax Rebates
bodyText:
Passing on increases: No New Jersey statute bars or regulates a lease term that makes the tenant pay a share of a property tax or insurance increase. Such a share exists only if the lease creates it; use the optional tax and insurance increase clause, which states the tenant's percentage, requires the bill and your calculation, and refunds the same share of any later reduction.

Many New Jersey towns have rent control or rent leveling ordinances that limit or set rules for tax surcharges; check the local ordinance before using the clause. For tenants covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, a rent increase can support an eviction only if it is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws and local ordinances.

Passing on decreases (Tenants' Property Tax Rebate Act): If you own a building or complex with five or more rental housing units, and the property tax falls below the base-year amount, you must give the residential tenants a rebate. The municipal tax collector sends you a notice of the reduction.

You divide it among residential tenants in proportion to their rents (after taking out the share for commercial rents and units you or your employees occupy), and pay it monthly, either as a rent credit or directly. Within 30 days of the notice, file the required certification with the rent leveling board (or tax collector) and post a notice in a prominent place listing the rebate per year and per month for each rent category.

If a tenant dies and the lease ends under the death-termination law, pay any rebate owed to the estate or surviving spouse. Failing to pay costs twice the rebate or $100, whichever is greater, plus penalties of up to $100 per offense. Owner occupancy does not matter.

The act does not apply to hotels and motels for transient or seasonal guests, buildings under a tax abatement agreement, buildings in towns whose rent control ordinance has no automatic increase for tax increases, cooperatives, most condominium units, continuing care communities, or assisted living and similar care facilities.

title: Tenants' Right to Cable Television
bodyText:
You (or your agent) may not forbid or prevent a tenant from getting cable television service in the unit the tenant lives in. You may not demand or accept any payment, in any form, as a condition of allowing the cable installation. You may not charge a cable subscriber different rent or otherwise treat that tenant differently because the tenant gets cable. The rule covers any dwelling, and "owner" includes condominium associations, housing cooperatives and mobile home park owners.

What you may do: require that the cable installation meet reasonable conditions needed to protect the safety, functioning, appearance and value of the property and the convenience, safety and well-being of other tenants. The cable company installing service for a tenant must agree to indemnify you for damage caused by installing, operating or removing its equipment and for liability arising from it.

A knowing violation of the cable television law is a misdemeanor, and the Board of Public Utilities can seek civil penalties of up to $1,000 for a first offense and more for repeat offenses.

This state law speaks only to cable television. Satellite dishes and antennas are governed by federal rules not covered here; check them before limiting a tenant's dish or antenna.

title: Ending a Tenancy at Will
bodyText:
New Jersey law recognizes tenancies at will (an open-ended tenancy with no agreed term or rent period), but no statute defines one or says when it arises. If you treat an arrangement as a tenancy at will, two different rules can apply.

Tenancies outside the Anti-Eviction Act (for example, owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, or a hotel, motel or guest house rented to transient or seasonal guests): before a court will order removal of a tenant at will who stays after the tenancy ends, you must end it with a written notice to quit given 3 months ahead, and prove to the court that you gave it. For comparison, a month-to-month tenancy needs one month's notice and a year-to-year tenancy three months.

All other residential tenancies: the Anti-Eviction Act applies whatever the tenancy is called. You may remove the tenant only for one of the good causes the Act lists, with the notice that cause requires (see "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)"). Simply giving notice that you want to end the tenancy is not enough.

Because the line between a tenancy at will and a periodic tenancy is not set by statute, a written lease with a stated term or rent period avoids the question. If an occupant pays rent monthly, the cautious course is to treat the tenancy as month-to-month or as covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, as applicable.

title: No State Rule on a Tenant's Bankruptcy
bodyText: No New Jersey statute or Part VI court rule (the landlord-tenant rules) says what happens to an eviction, a judgment for possession or a warrant of removal when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law controls. A bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay that can stop eviction and rent collection, with exceptions set by federal law. When you learn a tenant has filed, stop collection and eviction steps and get legal advice before taking any further action, including asking the court officer to carry out a warrant. A lease clause that ends the tenancy because the tenant files for bankruptcy may not be enforceable under federal law. The state law on bankruptcy in this area runs the other way: if a landlord who holds a security deposit goes bankrupt, the tenant's claim to deposit money not yet properly spent is a statutory trust.

title: Protecting Tenants' Personal Information
bodyText:
New Jersey has no general statute that bars a landlord from sharing a tenant's information. Several specific rules apply.

Domestic-violence documents: You may not disclose documents a tenant gives you to end a lease as a domestic-violence victim, enter them in any shared database or give them to anyone, except as evidence in an eviction or a suit for rent or damages, with the tenant's consent, or as the law requires (see "Keeping Domestic-Violence Documents Confidential"). That law does not apply to seasonal leases.

Social Security numbers: Do not publicly post or display a tenant's Social Security number (or four or more consecutive digits of it), print it on mailed materials unless the law requires it, or make it available to the public. You may use it internally for verification, and an application sent by mail may include it, but never on a postcard or visible through the envelope.

Data breaches and disposal: If your business keeps computerized records with a tenant's name plus a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, financial account or card number with its access code, or online login with password, you must notify affected New Jersey residents of a security breach without unreasonable delay, after first reporting it to the State Police.
