When you no longer keep records containing that kind of information, shred, erase or otherwise make them unreadable. Willful, knowing or reckless violations are Consumer Fraud Act violations.

COVID-period rent: You may not report unpaid or late rent that accrued from March 1, 2020 through August 31, 2021, or related court filings, to another landlord, a debt collector or a credit reporting agency.

Larger operators: The New Jersey Data Privacy Act applies only to businesses that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers a year, or at least 25,000 if they make money from selling personal data.

Treat tenant files as confidential and share them only as the tenancy requires.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
Ending the lease: If a tenant who rented the property only as a home for themselves (or with family) dies during a lease of one year or more, the lease can be ended early by written notice from the executor or administrator of the estate. If the lease was signed jointly by a married couple, the surviving spouse can give the notice, and a tenant can end the lease after a spouse's death. The termination takes effect on the 40th day after you receive the written notice. Rent is owed up to that date, and the property must be vacated and turned over to you at least five working days before the 40th day. This right does not apply if the lease explicitly provides otherwise. This library's leases do not include a term opting out of it. The broader early-termination rules are summarized in "Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early".

Property tax rebates: If you owe a tenant a property tax rebate under the Tenants' Property Tax Rebate Act (buildings of five or more units) and the lease ends this way, pay any rebate owed before termination to the executor or administrator or the surviving spouse. Failing to do so costs twice the rebate or $100, whichever is greater.

Belongings and deposit: New Jersey's procedure for disposing of property a tenant leaves behind applies only after a warrant for removal is executed or the tenant gives written notice of giving up possession. A tenant's death is not one of those triggers. No statute says who may collect a deceased tenant's belongings or receive the security deposit. Deal with the executor or administrator (or follow a court's direction), keep the belongings safe, and return the deposit with the itemized list to the estate within the deposit law's deadlines. Get legal advice before releasing property to anyone else.

Other household members: If others still live in the unit, do not treat the death as ending their right to stay. Under the Anti-Eviction Act, removing a remaining occupant needs a court order on a listed good cause.

title: No State Rule on Tenant Flags and Signs
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute gives tenants a right to display flags, political signs or religious items, or limits what a landlord may put in a lease about displays. Display rules are a matter for the lease, applied evenly to all tenants.

Condominiums, cooperatives and other associations: If your rental is in a community run by a homeowners' association (including a condominium, private community, retirement community or cooperative), the association may not adopt or enforce a rule limiting or banning display of the U.S. flag or yellow ribbons and signs supporting U.S. troops, or charge a fee for such a display. It may require removal only when the display threatens public safety, restricts necessary maintenance, interferes with another's property rights, or is not displayed in the proper manner (such as under the federal Flag Code). Any association rule against these displays is void.

Evenness: Apply any display rule the same way to everyone. A rule enforced against one tenant's religious items but not another's could raise a discrimination claim under the Law Against Discrimination.

title: Housing Your Own Employee
bodyText:
If you house a superintendent, janitor or other employee as part of the job, the Anti-Eviction Act still protects that person as a tenant. One of the Act's good causes for removal is that you conditioned the tenancy on, and gave it in consideration for, the tenant's employment by you, and that employment is being ended.

To use it you must give a written notice to quit at least three days before filing for possession. The notice must state the cause in detail and be served in person, by leaving a copy at the home with a family member over 14, or by certified mail (and regular mail if the certified letter is not claimed).

You still need a court judgment; you may not lock the employee out. This cause applies only if the tenancy was in fact tied to the job, so put that in writing at the start (see the optional clause).

Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units are outside the Act; there the tenancy ends with an ordinary notice to quit for its rental period. A firing tied to the employee's complaints or tenant organizing can raise a retaliation claim. Whether you may deduct rent from wages is governed by wage law, not covered here.

title: No State Rule on Renter's Insurance Claims
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires a tenant to carry renter's insurance, bars a lease from requiring it, or governs how a tenant's or landlord's insurance claims are handled between you, such as notice of a loss, who claims first, or what happens to insurance proceeds. The lease decides; the library's renter's insurance clause ("Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause) covers New Jersey.

One related rule does exist: every residential lease must contain the state's flood insurance notice. It tells tenants that flood insurance may be available to renters through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program and that a standard renter's policy does not typically cover flood damage (see "Renter Flood Insurance Notice" clause). Unless your rental is exempt, you must also give the separate flood-risk disclosure before signing or renewal (see "Flood Risk Disclosure Rider" clause).

A tenant's insurance claim does not change the security deposit rules: you may not deduct from the deposit while the tenant is still in possession, and damage claims at move-out still go on the itemized list sent within 30 days.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute regulates tenant portals as such, but three rules limit how you use one.

Payments: You may not require a tenant or applicant to pay rent or any other amount under the lease by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers and ACH. A portal can be offered, but always accept at least one other way to pay (see "Acceptable Payment Methods" clause). The ban is in the Truth-in-Renting Act, whose definition of landlord excludes rental premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, and hotels or guest houses for transient or seasonal guests. Applying it to every rental is the simpler course. If you take cash, give a printed or emailed receipt.

Signatures and notices: New Jersey's electronic-transactions law applies only when both sides have agreed to deal electronically. A tenant who agreed may refuse further electronic dealings, and the lease cannot waive that right. So do not make the portal the only way the tenant can sign, give notice or request repairs; let the tenant also use the lease's ordinary notice methods.

Eviction notices: Notices to quit and other eviction notices must be served by the methods the eviction statutes require (personal delivery, leaving a copy at the home with a family member over 14, or certified mail, with regular mail if the certified letter is not claimed). Posting one on a portal is not enough (see "Electronic Notices").

title: Keeping Tenant Records
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute requires you to keep a rent ledger or to give a tenant their account history on request. Several rules still make good records necessary.

Receipts: Give a printed or emailed receipt for every cash payment, showing the amount, what it was for, the date received, the printed names of landlord and tenant, and who accepted it. A tenant can use a missing receipt as a defense to a nonpayment eviction for the months involved. In a nonpayment case, give a dated receipt for each payment made within the three business days after a warrant for removal is posted or a lockout is executed.

Eviction filings: The court's verified complaint for nonpayment of rent asks whether a written rent ledger exists for the tenant and whether it is attached. Keep one, so you can show every charge and payment.

Security deposits: Keep records of where the deposit is held and the interest earned, because the deposit law requires written notices to the tenant (see "Security Deposit Rules").

Protecting the records: Keep domestic-violence documents a tenant gives you confidential (see "Keeping Domestic-Violence Documents Confidential"). Keep Social Security numbers out of public view. When you dispose of records that contain a tenant's name with a Social Security, driver's license or account number, shred, erase or otherwise make them unreadable. If computerized records with that information are breached, you must notify the affected residents (see "Protecting Tenants' Personal Information").

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Are Not Made
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute gives a tenant a general right to make repairs and deduct the cost from rent. Tenants do have these statutory remedies, and the courts recognize others not covered here.

Rent paid into court: For rentals other than owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units (the act's 'housing space' also excludes public housing and hotel, motel or guest-house space), a tenant or a municipal officer can ask a court to have rent paid into court and used for repairs when the unit lacks heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, or has another serious code violation. A lease cannot waive this (see "Rent Deposited With the Court for Repairs"). In buildings with persistent violations, a court can appoint a receiver (see "Court-Appointed Receivers for Neglected Buildings").

No heat: Where you fail to restore heat, the local board of health may act as your agent to hire repairers and order parts for the furnace or boiler. It may do so when at least 24 hours have passed since the tenant complained to it, the tenant first made a good-faith attempt to tell you, you did not act, and it is below 55°F outside. The repairer bills you and can file a lien on the property. A municipality may also adopt an ordinance letting its health officer order fuel oil and have the burner refired for you after a shorter wait (12 hours at 33-55°F, 4 hours at 32°F or below). Your negligence that leads to that action can cost up to $300 per affected unit.

Fire damage: If a building is damaged by fire that was not the tenant's fault, you must repair it as quickly as possible, and if you do not, rent stops until it is fully repaired, unless the lease says otherwise (see "Fire and Other Casualty").

Retaliation: You may not retaliate against a tenant for complaining to you or to officials about code violations (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). Courts also apply judge-made rules on rent abatement and tenant self-help repairs; fix reported defects promptly and keep records.

title: Tenant Organizing Is Protected
bodyText:
New Jersey protects tenants who organize mainly by barring reprisals; no statute separately gives tenants a right to meet in common areas or hand out materials. You may not serve a notice to quit or bring an eviction case because a tenant is an organizer of, a member of, or involved in the activities of any lawful organization, such as a tenants' association. You also may not substantially change the tenancy terms in reprisal for that activity and then evict for refusing the new terms. A substantial change includes refusing, without cause, to renew a lease or continue a tenancy.

If you serve a notice to quit or substantially change the terms without cause after a tenant organizes, joins or takes part in such an organization, a court presumes it was a reprisal unless you prove otherwise. No reprisal is presumed from refusing a renewal the tenant requested more than 90 days before the lease or renewal date ends. If the tenant proves reprisal, the court enters judgment for the tenant, and the tenant can sue you for damages and other relief, including an injunction. These rules cover all rental dwellings, including mobile homes and mobile home spaces, except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units. See also "Retaliation Is Prohibited".

Tenants' organizations and utilities: If a utility gives notice that it will shut off electric, gas, water or sewer service because the landlord has not paid, and cannot bill tenants individually, it must let a tenants' organization representing every tenant accept the billing. Members who pay may deduct their share from rent. The share of the landlord's past-due bill may not exceed 15% of the tenant's rent.

title: Truth in Renting Statement
bodyText:
New Jersey's Department of Community Affairs publishes the Truth in Renting statement, a summary of the main legal rights and responsibilities of tenants and landlords, in English and Spanish. It updates the statement annually and posts it on its website.

You must give a copy of the current statement to each new tenant at or before move-in. Within 30 days after the Department issues a new edition, give a copy to each existing tenant. You must also keep a current copy posted where all your tenants can see and reach it. A tenant's waiver or refusal of the statement does not excuse you. A violation can cost up to $100 per offense.

Who must comply: landlords covered by the Truth-in-Renting Act, which excludes rental premises of not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, and hotels or guest houses serving transient or seasonal guests.

Senior citizen housing projects (three or more units occupied solely by people 62 or older, with some exceptions): give the statement at the signing of each lease and each renewal, have the resident sign a receipt form, keep the form for one year, and post the statement.

title: No State Rule on Rental Security Cameras
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or video doorbell, or limits a landlord's cameras at a rental property. The lease decides installation (for example, your alterations clause can require written consent before anything is mounted or wired). General criminal laws still apply to everyone's cameras.

Private spaces: It is a crime to photograph, film or record someone whose intimate parts are exposed, or who is engaged in sexual activity, without consent where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed. Never place a camera inside a unit, bathroom or other private space. Posting prior notice and acting for a lawful purpose is a defense, but that does not make cameras in private spaces a good idea.

Audio: Recording a private conversation with a device is lawful only if the person recording is a party to the conversation or one of the parties has consented in advance. A camera or doorbell that records sound in common areas or picks up other people's private conversations can create liability. Turning audio off is the cautious course.

Camera registries: Some municipalities run a voluntary registry for privately owned outdoor security cameras to help police. Registering does not require you to hand over footage unless other law requires it.

title: Duties State Rules Place on Tenants
bodyText:
In a multiple dwelling (a building of three or more units, with some exclusions), New Jersey's maintenance rules put these duties on each occupant directly, whatever the lease says:

- Responsibility for violations: an occupant is responsible for code violations caused by the willful act, gross negligence, neglect or abuse of the occupant, a household member or a guest, including in common areas. Adults answer for violations by minors in their care that they knew of or allowed. Every occupant is liable for willfully or maliciously damaging the premises.
- Access: give the owner or the owner's agents access to the unit for inspections and required repairs on reasonable notice, ordinarily one day (immediately in a safety or structural emergency).
- Reporting: promptly report any condition, failed service or defective equipment that violates the rules to the owner, superintendent or the owner's emergency contact.
- Cleanliness: keep the unit safe and sanitary to the extent of the occupant's own use, prevent garbage build-up that could cause infestation, put garbage in the receptacles provided (never out windows or in hallways, stairways or fire escapes), keep plumbing fixtures clean and not clog them, and keep cooking equipment and surfaces free of grease.
- Screens and safety equipment: do not damage or remove screens or protective equipment, or deface required notices or signs, and create no fire code violation.
- Storage: store items only in the unit or a designated common storage area, labeled with the occupant's name and unit number.
- Occupancy: do not exceed the occupancy standards or cook where required cooking facilities are not installed.
- Heat: an occupant who agrees by contract or lease to supply heat from equipment that also heats other units has the owner's heating duties.

The owner's own duties are not reduced by these rules or by the lease. For one- and two-unit rentals, local housing codes may set similar duties.

title: Changing Lease Terms or Raising Rent
bodyText:
New Jersey has no statute that sets a standard notice period for changing a lease term or raising rent. How a change works depends on whether the tenancy is covered by the Anti-Eviction Act.

Covered tenancies (most residential rentals, but not owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units or transient or seasonal hotel and guest-house rentals): You may propose reasonable changes of substance in the lease terms, including the length of the term, at the end of a lease. If the tenant refuses them after written notice, that can be good cause for removal, but only after a further one month's written notice that states the cause in detail. For a tenant protected under the senior/disabled condominium-conversion laws, or who received a conversion termination notice, you must prove the change is reasonable and does not substantially reduce the tenant's prior rights. A rent increase can support an eviction for nonpayment only after a valid notice to quit and notice of the increase, and only if the increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws and local rent ordinances. Every change must also comply with any local rent control ordinance.

Non-covered tenancies: A change takes effect when the current rental period ends, after a notice to quit that ends the old terms (one month for month-to-month; three months for year-to-year or at will; one term for other periods).

Always: A change made as a reprisal for a tenant's complaints, efforts to enforce rights, or tenant-organization activity is unlawful (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited"). During a declared Rent Protection Emergency, an increase above twice the recent inflation rate in the emergency zone is presumed unreasonable. During a fixed-term lease, you may change terms only as the lease allows or by agreement.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: New Jersey's towing rules for rental property are explained in "Towing From Rental Property" (filed under parking and vehicle rules). In short: to have an unauthorized vehicle towed without the owner's consent, you must have a private-property towing contract. You must post a sign of at least 36 by 36 inches at every vehicle entrance stating the parking rules, that violators will be towed at the owner's expense, the tow company's contact details and charges, and the storage address and redemption hours. You must authorize removal of each particular vehicle, and the car must go to secure storage within a reasonable distance. In a residential community with clearly marked assigned spaces, a simpler entrance sign is allowed if you document approval of each tow. Tow companies may not patrol your lot and tow on their own; each tow needs your specific request. These rules do not apply to a lot with a single-family home or an owner-occupied building of not more than six units, to a car blocking a driveway or garage entrance, or to tows ordered by police.

title: No Good-Cause Exemption Notice in New Jersey
bodyText: Some states make a landlord whose property is exempt from their tenant protection law (a statewide just-cause eviction rule or rent cap) give the tenant a written exemption notice. No New Jersey statute does this. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap. Its good-cause eviction law, the Anti-Eviction Act, covers residential tenancies except, by its own terms: owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units; hotels, motels and guest houses rented to transient or seasonal guests; and a unit held in trust for, or permanently occupied by, an immediate family member of the owner who has a developmental disability. Those exclusions apply automatically. There is no exemption notice to give and nothing to file. Do not put a statement in the lease claiming an exemption the property does not have. The one exemption notice New Jersey does require is different: if a newly built multiple dwelling is exempt from municipal rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1 et seq., you must give each prospective tenant a written statement before the lease and put an exemption provision in the lease (see "Rent Control Exemption Notice" clause).

title: Tenant Rights Notices in New Jersey
bodyText: New Jersey has no statute requiring a lease notice like other states' tenant protection act notices (a statement of a statewide rent cap or just-cause rule), and no general right for a tenant to buy the property or get notice when you sell it. Two notice duties do apply. First, the Truth in Renting statement: the Department of Community Affairs publishes a statement of tenants' and landlords' rights (in English and Spanish, updated on its website). You must give a copy to each new tenant at or before move-in, give every tenant a copy within 30 days after the Department makes a new statement available, and keep a current copy posted where all tenants can see it. This duty does not apply to rental premises with not more than two units, owner-occupied premises of not more than three units, or hotels, motels and guest houses for transient or seasonal guests (see "Truth in Renting Statement" clause). Second, conversion: if you intend to convert a multiple dwelling (other than a hotel or motel) or a mobile home park to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, you must give tenants 60 days' notice of your intention and the full plan of conversion before serving any eviction notice, send a duplicate to the municipal clerk, and tell tenants of their right to buy at a stated price. A tenant in occupancy has the exclusive right to buy the unit for the first 90 days after notice that it can be bought, and you may not show it to anyone else in that time unless the tenant has waived the right in writing (see "Condominium or Cooperative Conversion Statement" clause). New Jersey's statute actually named the Tenant Protection Act of 1992, and the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act, are conversion laws: in a covered county, before you file to register a conversion you must notify the municipal agency and give it a list of every tenant, stamped addressed envelopes and copies of the statutory notice and application, which the agency mails to each tenant; qualified tenants can get a protected tenancy.

title: No Sunset on New Jersey Tenant Laws
bodyText: No New Jersey statute puts its core tenant protections on a dated repeal clock. The Anti-Eviction Act (good cause for removal), the Rent Security Deposit Act and the Truth-in-Renting Act have no expiry date. Treat them as permanent. The one time-limited eviction rule found is the COVID-19 law that let the Governor stop residential evictions during the declared public health emergency; its stated end dates for that executive order were in 2021, so it does not limit evictions now. Check for any new emergency law or order after a declared emergency before you file for possession.

title: Lease Translation and Spanish Notices
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to translate a lease into the tenant's language, whatever language you advertised or negotiated in. A few specific notices must be in English and Spanish. In a multiple dwelling (generally a building of three or more units, with some exclusions), the lease notice giving the management company's website and the social services hotline instructions, and the posted emergency contact and hotline information, must be made available in English and Spanish (see "Management Website and Social Services Hotline Notice" clause). The Truth in Renting statement you must hand out is published by the Department of Community Affairs in English and Spanish; give the tenant the Department's current statement (see "Truth in Renting Statement" clause). If you take title to a tenant-occupied property at a sheriff's sale or by deed in lieu of foreclosure, the notice to tenants you must give within 10 business days must be in English and Spanish, in the form the statute sets out. Practical step: if a tenant reads another language better than English, you may give a courtesy translation, but say in writing which version controls.

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under Trespass Law
bodyText: New Jersey's criminal trespass law has no landlord-specific trespass-warning form. A person commits the petty disorderly persons offense of defiant trespass if, knowing he is not licensed or privileged to be there, he enters or remains in a place after notice against trespass is given by telling him directly, by posting in a way likely to come to intruders' attention, or by fencing or another enclosure plainly meant to keep intruders out. It is a defense that the place was open to the public and the person complied with all lawful conditions on access, or that the person reasonably believed the owner or another person with power to allow entry would have let him in. So you or your manager may tell a non-tenant who has no right to be there to leave common areas you control, and may post no-trespassing notices. But the tenant's unit is in the tenant's possession, and a tenant may generally let guests in to see the tenant; no New Jersey statute lets you bar a tenant's invited guest, and whether you can is a question for case law. The cautious course: give a written, specific notice to the barred person, tell the tenant, and enforce any building rule against guests only if it is reasonable and was accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the start of the term (the Anti-Eviction Act rule standard). Never lock out a tenant or remove a tenant's belongings yourself: taking possession without a court warrant is an offense (see "Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal").

title: Separately Charged Parking
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires you to offer parking separately from the rent, forbids a separate parking charge, or sets rules for a separate residential parking agreement. If you charge for parking separately, put the space, the charge and how either side can end the parking arrangement in a separate written addendum, and do not call the charge rent; in this library an unpaid parking charge is not treated as rent and will not support an eviction for nonpayment. A municipal rent control ordinance may count parking charges toward the regulated rent; check yours. One statewide parking duty applies regardless: if you own a multiple dwelling (generally three or more units, with some exclusions) that provides parking to its occupants and a person with a physical disability lives there, you must set aside at least one percent of the occupant spaces, and at least one space, as accessible parking as close as possible to the main entrances, with a sign showing the International Symbol of Access and the words "This space reserved for drivers with physical disabilities." Where possible the space must be 12 feet wide, and curb ramps must be provided where applicable.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant
bodyText: This applies only if you lease the property as the holder of a life estate, not as its full owner. New Jersey has no usufruct; the closest interest is a life estate. Two statutes address it. First, if your lease ends on your death and you die on or before a rent day, your executor or administrator may recover from the tenant the whole rent due that day if you die on it, or, if you die before it, a share of the rent for the part of the period you were alive. Second, if you lease your life estate and then keep occupying the property or taking its profits and commit or allow waste, the remainderman or reversioner may sue you for the value wasted and treble damages, but only if you were liable for waste before you leased. No New Jersey statute says whether the tenant's lease or Anti-Eviction Act protection survives against the remainderman when the life estate ends; that is a question for case law. The cautious course: tell the tenant in writing, before the lease is signed, that you hold only a life estate and that the lease may end when it ends, and do not sign a lease for a term that the remainderman has not agreed to in writing.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText:
Heat is the one utility New Jersey statutes address. In a multiple dwelling (a building of three or more units, with some exclusions), you may not charge each unit a share of the building's heating cost by any method or device other than separate meters approved by the Board of Public Utilities, unless the Commissioner of Community Affairs has approved the method and device.

An approved system must be reliable and accurate, be inspected and maintained on a schedule, split costs fairly based on actual use, and give each unit its own thermostat. Each bill must show the building's actual fuel or current cost for the period and the unit's share, and only fuel or current costs may be split. Failing to keep up the maintenance schedule or to fix a malfunction promptly is a violation of the Hotel and Multiple Dwelling Law.

For water, sewer, electricity and gas, no New Jersey statute permits, forbids or sets a method for dividing a master-metered bill among tenants, and none makes a lease term charging tenants for a shared meter unenforceable. By statute, metering and billing for electricity and gas stay under the Board of Public Utilities. Before you split any shared electric, gas or water bill, check the rules or ask the Board. Otherwise, include the utility in the rent or have the tenant hold an account for a meter serving only the unit.

title: Utility Deposits You Collect
bodyText: New Jersey has no separate rule for a utility deposit a landlord collects. Any money a tenant pays you as security for the lease, or to be applied to lease payments when due, is a security deposit under the Rent Security Deposit Act, whatever you call it. So a "utility deposit" you hold counts toward the cap of one and a half months' rent; you must hold it in trust with the rest of the deposit, in an interest-bearing account, and give the required notices; you may not deduct from it while the tenant is still in possession; and you must return it, with interest and an itemized list of any lawful charges, within 30 days after the lease ends. The Act applies to all dwelling rentals except owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, unless the tenant of such premises gives you 30 days' written notice invoking it (see "Security Deposit Rules"). A deposit the tenant pays directly to a utility company is between the tenant and the utility; if it goes unclaimed for more than one year after service ends, it is presumed abandoned under the unclaimed property law.

title: Utility Disclosures With the Lease
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a general utility disclosure attached to the lease, such as a statement of average utility costs or a utility billing history. Who pays which utility is a lease term (see utilities-responsibility and utilities-paid-by-landlord). A few specific utility-related disclosures do apply. If you charge units in a multiple dwelling (three or more units, with some exclusions) a share of the building's heating cost through an approved indirect apportionment system, the Department of Community Affairs' rules require you to give existing and prospective occupants written information about the system: its range of accuracy when working properly, the building's average apportioned heating cost per square foot over the last heating season (or an estimate), the square footage of the occupant's unit, and the maintenance schedule (see "Submetered Electricity and Heat Billing" and "Splitting Shared Utility Bills"). If the tenant will supply heat in a multiple dwelling, the tenant's agreement must be in writing (see "Tenant-Supplied Heat" clause). Drinking-water notices (lead in drinking water and lead service lines) and private well test results have their own rows (see "Lead in Drinking Water Disclosure" clause, "Lead Service Line Notice" clause and "Private Well Water Test Results" clause).

title: Cutting Off Utilities You Supply
bodyText: No New Jersey statute lets you interrupt electricity, gas, heat or water you supply or submeter because the tenant has not paid you for it, and none sets a notice procedure for doing so. Do not do it. Shutting off, or causing to be shut off, vital services such as heat, electricity or water in an effort to regain possession is forcible entry and detainer; after a warning by police or another public official, doing it or refusing to restore the tenant is a disorderly persons offense, and a second conviction within five years is a fourth-degree crime (see "Lockouts and Utility Shut-Offs Are Illegal"). In a hotel or multiple dwelling (generally three or more units, with some exclusions), the Department of Community Affairs' rules also bar you from intentionally shutting off any service, facility, equipment or utility the rules require you to supply, or knowingly letting it stay off, where it affects an occupied unit, building, exterior space or common area. That rule does not apply to a temporary interruption needed while actual repairs or alterations are under way, or during a temporary emergency caused by a public utility or public agency or approved by the Department; even then you must make repairs quickly and, as far as possible, provide temporary or alternate service until permanent service is restored. If a tenant does not pay a utility charge you lawfully bill, your remedy is to collect it as a debt, not to cut service. Whether you may resell or bill submetered electricity or gas at all depends on Board of Public Utilities rules (see "Submetered Electricity and Heat Billing").

title: Utility Accounts in Your Name
bodyText:
If a utility account for your tenants' homes is in your name, keep it paid. New Jersey statutes protect tenants if you do not.

If an electric, gas, water or sewer public utility notifies a tenant that service is in danger of being cut off because you have not paid, any rent the tenant then uses to keep the service on is not unpaid rent, so you cannot evict for it.

If the utility has given tenants written notice of a proposed shutoff, the tenants want service to continue, and the utility finds it cannot bill each tenant separately, the utility must let a tenants' organization representing every tenant accept the bills, including your unpaid arrears, and keep service on while payments are made. Each paying tenant may then deduct his or her share from the rent, but the share of your arrears may not be more than 15 percent of the rent otherwise due.

A tenant or the municipality may also ask a court to have rents paid into court and used to fix a lack of heat, running water, light or electricity.

The state's winter and summer shutoff protection programs cover residential tenants of a building whose owner is the utility's non-residential customer of record.

The reverse case is covered too: if you or someone else in the building uses, or diverts from a tenant, electric, gas or water service that is billed to the tenant without the tenant's consent, and you do not correct it within 30 days after notice by certified mail from the tenant, the municipal officer or the utility, any of them may ask a court to have rents paid into court and used to correct it.

When a utility shuts off gas, electric or water service to a customer in a building of three or more units for safety reasons, it must notify the local police chief or the State Police within 12 hours, unless service is fully restored first. Whether the utility must also notify each tenant before shutting off service for your nonpayment is set by Board of Public Utilities rules.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: New Jersey utility shutoff rules govern the utility, not you, but they affect your tenants and any account in your name. A public utility may not discontinue, curtail or abandon service without the Board of Public Utilities' permission after notice. It may terminate a customer's service for violating its approved tariff on at least 3 days' notice unless the Board's rules or orders provide otherwise, and without notice where a hazardous condition exists. Seasonal programs protect eligible residential customers. Under the Winter Termination Program, local authorities, municipal utilities and rural electric cooperatives may not cut off service from November 15 through March 15 to a residential customer the Department of Community Affairs finds qualified, and the Board's program covers electric, gas, water and sewer public utilities. Under the Summer Termination Program created in 2025, a public utility may not cut off electric, sewer or water service from June 15 through August 31 to an eligible residential customer, and an eligible customer cut off for nonpayment before June 15 gets service restored on June 15 with no reconnection fee; local authorities, municipal utilities and rural electric cooperatives have a parallel program run by the Department of Community Affairs. Neither program applies to shutoffs for a utility emergency. For all of these programs, "residential customer" includes a residential tenant where the owner, or the owner's agent, is the utility's non-residential customer of record. An electric utility also may not cut off a medical customer who uses electric life-sustaining equipment, for 90 days, if the shutoff would aggravate the condition and the customer meets the Board's proof requirements. Eligibility details are in Board and Department rules. What this means for you: a tenant on one of these programs may keep service even while behind, and a shutoff for nonpayment of an account in your name can be stayed for your tenants; never shut off a utility yourself (see "Cutting Off Utilities You Supply").

title: No Submetering Lease Disclosure
bodyText: No New Jersey statute requires a lease disclosure when you bill tenants for water, sewer, electricity or gas through a submeter or by splitting a master-metered bill, and no statute sets submeter billing limits or late-fee caps for those utilities. That does not mean submetering is unregulated. Check them, or ask the Board, before you submeter or rebill electricity, gas or water. Heat is different: in a multiple dwelling (three or more units, with some exclusions), charging units a share of the building's heating cost requires a system approved by the Department of Community Affairs, and its rules require written information to existing and prospective occupants and specific statements on each bill (see "Submetered Electricity and Heat Billing", "Splitting Shared Utility Bills" and "Utility Disclosures With the Lease").

title: Veteran Rent Concessions
bodyText: No New Jersey statute gives a private landlord a tax credit, grant or other incentive for renting to veterans or servicemembers, or sets rules for a veteran rent discount. Be careful before offering one. The Law Against Discrimination makes it unlawful to refuse to rent to, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental against, any person because of service in the Armed Forces of the United States or liability for that service, and to advertise any limitation or specification based on it. The statute has no exception allowing a private landlord to favor veterans, and whether a veterans-only concession is unlawful discrimination against other applicants is a question for case law. The cautious course is to offer any concession on terms open to everyone, or to get legal advice first. The Law Against Discrimination does not apply to renting one unit of a two-family house whose other unit the owner lives in, or rooms in an owner-occupied one-family house, unless the housing is publicly assisted. Two statutory veteran rules do apply. You must count a military or veteran housing allowance, supported by U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs documentation, as income when deciding whether a servicemember or veteran meets your minimum income requirement (see "Tenant Screening Limits"). And in an affordable housing project, a municipality may agree with the developer or owner to give low- and moderate-income veterans who served in time of war or other emergency a preference for up to 50 percent of the affordable units.

title: Hot Water Temperature Rules
bodyText: New Jersey's hot water temperature rules are in Department of Community Affairs regulations, not statutes. In a hotel or multiple dwelling (generally three or more units, with some exclusions), each building must have a hot water heater and distribution system that works even when the heating system is off and delivers water at the outlets at no less than 120 and no more than 140 degrees Fahrenheit at all times, based on the expected need from the number of fixtures and use of the building. Sidearm water heaters are prohibited. Every kitchen sink, bathroom sink, tub and shower must have both hot and cold water. The State Housing Code, which municipal public officers use to judge whether any dwelling is fit to live in, sets the same 120 to 140 degree range for every dwelling's water heating facilities, which must be installed and kept in good and safe working condition. In a building of two or more units with a common source of heat for domestic hot water, you are responsible for its proper operation at all times. Neither rule requires you to reset a unit's water heater at each new tenancy, and no New Jersey statute sets a water heater temperature; but check the setting at turnover so the unit meets the range. Do not shut off hot water except for a temporary interruption needed for actual repairs or alterations or in an authorized emergency.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText:
No New Jersey statute mentions waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture. There is no tenant right to keep one, no landlord duty to allow one, and no statutory insurance or installation requirement. You may prohibit waterbeds in the lease, or allow one only with your written consent and on reasonable conditions such as a proper frame and liner, an approved location and liability insurance.

If you rely on the rule to end a tenancy covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, it must be a lease covenant or a reasonable rule accepted in writing by the tenant or made part of the lease at the start of the term, and the tenant must have continued to violate it after written notice to cease. You may not deduct damage costs from the security deposit while the tenant is still in possession.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: New Jersey has no single rule that every landlord-tenant notice be in writing; each statute sets its own. The main written notices are these. Eviction notices: for a tenancy covered by the Anti-Eviction Act, no judgment of possession may be entered, except for nonpayment of rent, unless you made written demand and gave written notice for delivery of possession, for the period the ground requires (for example three days for disorderly conduct or damage, one month for rule or lease violations or habitual late payment). The notice must state the cause in detail and be served in person, left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail (and by regular mail if the certified letter is not claimed). For disorderly conduct, rule violations and lease covenant violations, you must first give a written notice to cease (see "Good-Cause Eviction (Anti-Eviction Act)" and "Good-Cause Eviction Rule"). Security deposit notices: within 30 days of receiving a deposit, at each annual interest payment, and after moving it or selling the property, you must notify the tenant in writing of the bank, account type, interest rate and amount (see "Security Deposit Rules"). Tenant's written notices: a tenant of an owner-occupied building of not more than two rental units may invoke the Rent Security Deposit Act by 30 days' written notice; and a tenant ending a lease of one year or more early because of death or disability ends it on the fortieth day after you receive written notice (see "Tenant Rights to End a Lease Early"). Utility diversion: a tenant, municipal officer or utility must notify you by certified mail of a wrongful diversion before going to court. Oral leases are allowed, but put every notice you give in writing and keep proof of delivery.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: New Jersey follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (N.J.S.A. 12A:3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (N.J.S.A. 12A:1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: New Jersey's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (New Jersey's landlord-tenant and eviction statutes searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how New Jersey's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText:
New Jersey's general interest statute allows at most 6% a year without a written contract, and at most 16% a year under a written contract that specifies a rate (N.J.S.A. 31:1-1(a)).

Whether it reaches a tenant's unpaid charges is unsettled, so if your lease charges interest, state a simple annual rate no higher than 16%. Don't use an interest term to add interest to Rent: rent paid late is covered only by the late fee term.
